papers.title: EMU and trade: The euro effect on the agricultural sector
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper uses a structural gravity model to examine the partial equilibrium effects of the European Monetary Union (EMU) on trade for the agricultural sector. We find robust evidence that EMU has increased trade both between members and between EMU and non‐EMU member countries. This positive link is found in most member countries. Moreover, the overall impact of EMU on trade between members has not been different for late and early joiners. The year‐by‐year and period‐by‐period analyses show that the effect of EMU is increasing over time. In addition, we conduct a counterfactual general equilibrium experiment that reveals a remarkable welfare‐enhancing effect of EMU for its member countries.
papers.journal_name: Canadian Journal of Agricultural Economics/Revue canadienne d'agroeconomie

papers.title: Survey: Competition in Higher Education
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper provides a bibliometric mapping and economic interpretation of the literature on competition in higher education. Drawing on 1470 Scopus‐indexed articles (1961–2023), we combine descriptive bibliometrics, a keyword co‐occurrence network, and a multiple correspondence analysis (MCA) of harmonized author‐assigned keywords with a unified economic framework that distinguishes two functions of competition: an evaluative–optimizing mechanism, in which institutions are compared against criteria treated as known in advance, and a generative–discovery mechanism, in which decentralized experimentation reveals information that cannot be fully specified beforehand. Both the co‐occurrence network (modularity ) and the MCA reveal a pronounced conceptual asymmetry: the field is organized around a large, central, internally elaborated vocabulary of rankings, performance, quality assurance, reputation, efficiency, and institutional positioning, while discovery‐oriented concerns—innovation, institutional diversity, scientific incentives, and the organization of knowledge production—are less central and less coherently consolidated within the retained author‐keyword structure. We connect this asymmetry to the policy chronology—massification, performance‐based funding, deregulation, the Bologna process, and global rankings—through which the evaluative–optimizing function has been progressively institutionalized. The contribution is threefold: a large‐scale map of the field, an economic distinction between two functions of competition, and a reading of why the literature's conceptual structure has taken its present, asymmetric form.

papers.title: Cultivating New Economic Momentum: A Bibliometric Analysis of Cross‐Border Integration Between Artificial Intelligence and InsurTech
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Against the backdrop of digital economy development and global economic momentum transformation, the integration of artificial intelligence and InsurTech has become a key driver of high‐quality economic growth. Based on 137 empirical papers from the Web of Science Core Collection (2012–2026), this paper conducts a bibliometric analysis to systematically review the research evolution, core themes, methodologies and global distribution of AI–InsurTech integration, focusing on its economic effects and momentum transmission mechanisms. Results show that studies have shifted from technology application to economic efficiency and institutional governance, forming five core knowledge clusters. Micro‐level research dominates while macroeconomic analysis remains insufficient. The global research pattern features the rapid rise of Asia and steady development in Europe and the US, and empirical methods are moving toward rigorous causal identification. We identify three major gaps in theoretical mechanisms, causal identification and institutional ethics, and propose future research directions. This study clarifies the logic of technology–finance integration driving economic momentum transformation and provides implications for theory and policy.

papers.title: Spatially coordinated conservation auctions under imperfect information about ecological spillovers
Agricultural extension services for farm resilience in Russian–Ukrainian Conflict
Recreational Marijuana Laws and Workplace Absence
papers.abstract: A near majority of states have now passed recreational marijuana laws (RMLs), but their impact on labor market behavior remains unclear. This study provides new causal evidence on the relationship between RMLs and workplace absence. Using a generalized difference-in-differences framework to exploit the staggered rollout of RMLs, I first document that the onset of legal recreational sales is accompanied by a 50% increase in the prevalence of prior-month adult marijuana use in treated states relative to control states. Next, I show that retail market access leads to a 14% increase in the incidence of prior-week workplace absence. Supplemental analyses of health outcomes suggest that part of the effect may be driven by increases in self-reported mental health problems following the opening of recreational dispensaries. These findings suggest that marijuana legalization may affect labor market outcomes along margins not typically captured by employment status alone.

papers.title: The Diminishing Value of Bundling Under Inventory Scarcity
papers.abstract: We study the impact of inventory constraints on bundling in a dynamic pricing setting, challenging the classical view that bundling consistently enhances revenue. Traditional bundling theory, which typically assumes abundant inventory and static pricing, often asserts that bundling generates higher revenue than selling products individually. However, we show that limited inventory, in fact, distorts the revenue-extraction capability of bundling, favoring the sale of products or services separately. We study the optimal dynamic mixed bundling strategy in a large market regime where the market size grows relative to limited inventory. Leveraging this framework, we derive optimal dynamic pricing policies and value functions for commonly used bundling strategies, including mixed bundling, pure bundling, bundle size pricing, and component pricing. Our analysis reveals that as inventory becomes more constrained relative to market size, the optimal dynamic mixed bundling strategy converges to a dynamic component pricing strategy, outperforming both dynamic bundle size pricing and dynamic pure bundling. Moreover, the performance gap between these strategies increases with the number of items, a factor typically viewed as favoring bundling when inventory is abundant. Notably, our numerical experiments reveal that these structural insights extend to policies derived from the standard fluid regime. As the market size grows relative to the inventory, the dynamic mixed bundling policy obtained by resolving the deterministic fluid problem also reduces to a dynamic component pricing policy. This paper was accepted by Karan Girotra, operations management. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03120 .

papers.title: Experimenting Under Stochastic Congestion
papers.abstract: We study randomized experiments in a service system when stochastic congestion can arise from temporarily limited supply or excess demand. Such congestion gives rise to cross-unit interference between the waiting customers, and analytic strategies that do not account for this interference may be biased. In current practice, one of the most widely used ways to address stochastic congestion is to use switchback experiments that turn a target intervention on and off for the whole system in alternation. We find, however, that under a queueing model for stochastic congestion, the standard way of analyzing switchbacks is inefficient and that estimators that leverage the queueing model can be materially more accurate. Additionally, we show how the queueing model enables estimation of total policy gradients from unit-level randomized experiments, thus giving practitioners an alternative experimental approach they can use without needing to precommit to a fixed switchback length before data collection. This paper was accepted by Vivek Farias, data science. Funding: This work was supported by the ONR [Grant N000142412091]. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08306 .

papers.title: Coworking: Finding Value Through Work Companions
papers.abstract: Many workers have the flexibility to work across different work locations, and some choose to join coworking spaces, where they work alongside others with different employers, occupations, and backgrounds. Yet, little is known about the nature of relationships formed within this type of work location, where individuals lack shared goals and a common organizational umbrella. Thus, we ask: How do workers manage and find value from relationships within coworking spaces? Applying grounded theory techniques to collect and analyze observational, archival, and interview data collected from 80 workers in 21 coworking spaces, we derive a theoretical model that centers around the novel construct of work companions – individuals who work alongside one another with a shared focus on work but without family, friendship, or employment relationship obligations. The coworking space environment, overseen by one or more space managers, provides favorable conditions for the formation of work companions. Through interaction flexibility, coworking space members socially engage or parallel work with work companions, extracting both personal and professional value. Relational embeddedness, defined as the existence of family, friendship, or employment relationships, imposes obligations that make work companion interactions less flexible, creating a boundary condition to these findings. Introducing the work companion construct and elaborating relationships among coworking space members offers promising avenues for future research and informs management practice on work companions, coworking, and remote work.

papers.title: When deep acting is damaging: Emotional labour and negative emotions in contemporary debt collection
papers.abstract: Emotional labour, the appropriation of workers’ emotions for commercial gain, is central to our understanding of service work. This study focuses on the impact of deep acting, emotional labour and empathy through an in-depth analysis of a hard-to-reach and rarely studied occupation, debt collectors. It details the ways clients’ traumas and emotional demands triggered workers’ memories of their own traumatic life events such as bereavement or violence, prompting authentic feelings/deep acting that was damaging. These observations challenge the existing assumption that surface acting is more harmful than deep acting because surface acting entails faking emotions, creating dissonance between the way workers really feel and the way they are expected to act. Such conclusions have been drawn almost entirely from studies of positive emotions. Significantly, this research demonstrates that, when dealing with negative emotions, deep acting and authentic feeling can be more damaging to workers than surface acting.

papers.title: Managerial Information Processing Systems and Sustainability Performance: The Roles of Green Exploitation–Exploration and Resource Orchestration
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT In recent years, scholarly attention has increasingly focused on the role of green innovation ambidexterity (GIA) and resource orchestration in improving firms' sustainability performance (SP). However, prior research has largely overlooked managerial information processing as a critical driver shaping these capabilities. Drawing on information processing, dynamic capabilities, and resource orchestration theories, this study investigates how managers' information processing systems shape firms' SP through EGI, ERG, and resource orchestration capability (ROC). Data were collected from 413 firm managers operating in Türkiye and analyzed using consistent partial least squares structural equation modeling with bootstrap mediation analysis. The findings show that analytical information processing systems (AIPS) have significant positive effects on exploitative green innovation (EGI), explorative green innovation (ERG), ROC, and SP. In contrast, experiential information processing systems (EIPS) directly influence only EGI and ROC. The results further reveal that EGI and ROC shape SP, whereas ERG has no significant effect in the baseline specification. By integrating managerial information processing, EGI, ERG, and ROC, this study reveals how firms build cognitively driven green strategies in emerging markets.

papers.title: The Impact of Institutional Pressures on Firms' Low‐Carbon Behaviors: A Configuration Approach
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Although the institutional environment is recognized as crucial for firms' low‐carbon development, how configurations of institutional pressures collectively shape firms' low‐carbon behaviors remains underexplored. Drawing on institutional theory, configuration theory, and resource‐based view, this study investigated the impact of institutional pressure configurations on firms' low‐carbon behaviors and the moderating role of artificial intelligence (AI) capability. The study used cluster analysis, analysis of variance (ANOVA), and OLS regressions with panel data from Chinese A‐share listed firms (2007–2022) to verify our research propositions. The results reveal three distinct firm clusters based on institutional pressure profiles. These configurations exert varying effects on both hard and soft low‐carbon behaviors. Generally, more intense pressures promote greater hard low‐carbon behaviors; conversely, high‐pressure firms are associated with significantly fewer soft low‐carbon behaviors compared to low‐pressure firms. Furthermore, a firm's AI capability enhances the positive influence of more intense institutional pressure on the adoption of hard low‐carbon behaviors and mitigates the negative influence of high institutional pressure on the adoption of soft low‐carbon behaviors. This study extends institutional perspectives on firms' environmental behaviors and provides actionable guidance for low‐carbon management.

papers.title: Effects of AI disclosure in service recovery communication: The role of framing strategies
Exploring the supply chain resilience of food banks: a dynamic capabilities perspective
papers.abstract: Purpose While supply chain resilience (SCR) has been extensively studied in for-profit contexts, nonprofit supply chains (NPSCs) remain underexplored. Drawing on dynamic capabilities theory (DCT), this study aims to investigate how food banks enact and integrate resilience capabilities under systemic disruptions. Using the COVID-19 pandemic as an empirical setting, this study investigates strategies deployed across pre-crisis, crisis and post-crisis phases. Design/methodology/approach Based on 21 semi-structured interviews with Moissons and community-based organizations across Québec (Canada), this study adopts an abductive, interpretive approach to identify the dynamic capabilities (DCs) underpinning proactive, concurrent and reactive responses. Findings Nonprofit SCR is enabled by six interdependent dynamic capacities: anticipation, adaptability, agility, collaboration, recovery and learning, aligned with the sensing, seizing and transforming processes. Horizontal collaboration emerges as a pivotal mechanism enabling network-level adaptation despite severe resource constraints. Findings further show that collaboration also functions as a compensatory mechanism when formal reconfiguration capacity is limited. Practical implications Findings guide nonprofit managers and policymakers in strengthening supply chain continuity during systemic disruptions. Practitioners can enhance resilience by institutionalizing peer collaboration and leveraging digital coordination tools, while policymakers can better align regulatory frameworks and funding mechanisms with the flexibility needs of NPSCs. Originality/value This study extends DCT to resource-constrained NPSCs and develops a temporal, process-based framework of resilience. Unlike prior DCT applications in for-profit and vertically coordinated supply chains, which emphasize firm-level optimization and hierarchical coordination, this study demonstrates how resilience emerges under chronic resource scarcity, volunteer dependence and fragmented operations. Horizontal governance structures further shape how capabilities are enacted across decentralized actors. The study highlights that resilience is achieved through compensatory, network-based mechanisms rather than formal reconfiguration capacities typical of firm-centric models. It provides empirically grounded insights into how DCs unfold across crisis phases in decentralized nonprofit networks, with implications for other systemic disruptions and comparative research.
papers.journal_name: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

papers.title: An employee lens on the dark and bright sides of customer dissatisfaction
papers.abstract: Purpose Customer dissatisfaction has long been studied in the hospitality marketing literature for its powerful impacts on customer outcomes, but it has rarely been examined from the perspective of hospitality employees. Drawing on the theory of workplace anxiety, this research aims to explore how perceived customer dissatisfaction impacts employees’ emotional state of anxiety and subsequent behavioral responses, and how perceived leader empowerment functions as a motivational contingency that shapes these responses. Design/methodology/approach Study 1 employed an experimental causal-chain approach using a recall paradigm to support causal relationships between perceived customer dissatisfaction and two behaviors through workplace anxiety. In Study 2, an experience sampling methodology design with U.S. hospitality frontline employees was conducted via CloudResearch. Findings Perceived customer dissatisfaction increases employees’ workplace anxiety, which in turn, leads to voice behavior. Moreover, employees who perceive higher leader empowerment are less likely to withdraw when experiencing workplace anxiety. Practical implications Organizations can turn customer dissatisfaction into opportunities for learning and improvement by recognizing workplace anxiety as a motivator for positive behavior and by empowering employees to manage their emotions and respond proactively. Such practices can help build a more resilient, adaptive and productive workforce. Originality/value This research shifts customer dissatisfaction from a customer-focused to an employee-focused perspective. Customer dissatisfaction can be perceived as a high job demand that triggers employees’ workplace anxiety and results in divergent behavioral responses, namely, voice and withdrawal, contingent on leader empowerment.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

papers.title: From service delivery to crafting memorable experiences: guest perspectives
papers.abstract: Purpose This study explores the role of employees in shaping memorable hotel experiences (MHEs) through customer perceptions. It aims to identify employee attributes that strongly influence memorable guest experiences. Design/methodology/approach A three-stage mixed-method design was applied to 30,783 TripAdvisor reviews from 100 hotels across the world’s ten most visited cities. Text mining and sentiment analysis identified experience factors, and their relative contributions were quantified through regression modeling. A hermeneutic analysis of a 500-review subsample then interpreted the experiential meanings underlying staff-related patterns. Findings Five employee attribute dimensions were identified as significant contributors to MHEs: emotional resonance, functional mastery, proactive resolution, personalized connection and flexibility. The analysis further reveals new guest insights into the role of authenticity and personal engagement in shaping their experiences. Practical implications The findings provide actionable insights for hospitality practitioners seeking to enhance human resource strategies and service design. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature on experience co-creation and customer experience management by identifying the dimensions of staff service most valued by guests, extending current understanding of experience formation within the hospitality context.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

papers.title: When trust is not enough: buyer orchestration modes and innovation in coopetitive automotive supply networks
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how buyer orchestration modes shape knowledge-sharing dynamics and innovation outcomes among competing suppliers in multi-tier automotive supply networks. While prior coopetition research emphasizes trust and voluntary collaboration as drivers of innovation, we investigate the underexplored role of the buyer as an active governance agent whose orchestration choices – ranging from coercive enforcement to collaborative co-development – shape whether competing suppliers share knowledge deeply enough to produce innovation. Design/methodology/approach Using multiple-perspective interviews, we conducted 28 in-depth interviews across six coopetitive relationships involving eight organizations in the Austrian and German automotive supply industries. Cases were purposefully selected to capture variation in buyer orchestration modes (enforcer, mandator, coordinator, facilitator, co-developer, partner), relationship formation (voluntary vs involuntary) and trust configurations. Data were analyzed using within-case and cross-case methods, with the relational view (RV) as the analytical lens. Findings We identify three theoretically distinct orchestration regimes – coercive, facilitative and collaborative – that shape how RV's four mechanisms (relation-specific assets, knowledge-sharing routines, complementary resources and governance) operate in coopetitive settings. Coercive orchestration (enforcer and mandator) generates compliance-based knowledge exchange but suppresses exploratory sharing – even when inter-supplier trust is high. Facilitative orchestration (coordinator and facilitator) creates structural conditions for sharing but cannot generate the relational motivation required for breakthrough innovation without pre-existing trust. Only collaborative orchestration (co-developer and partner), where the buyer signals vulnerability through co-investment of its own technical and organizational resources, enables suppliers to transition from protective to exploratory knowledge sharing, producing high innovation. Practical implications Supply chain managers should recognize that mandating collaboration is insufficient for innovation; the buyer's orchestration mode – not merely the existence of trust or voluntary engagement – is the primary lever. We provide actionable guidance for selecting and transitioning between orchestration modes based on relational conditions and innovation objectives. Originality/value This study reconceptualizes the buyer from a peripheral contextual node to the node that owns the primary governance mechanisms in coopetitive innovation. We extend the RV to buyer-orchestrated coopetition, showing that the four relational rent mechanisms are channeled and constrained by orchestration mode. Our framework explains why high trust fails to unlock innovation under coercive orchestration – a counterintuitive finding that challenges assumptions in both the coopetition and trust literatures.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Physical Distribution & Logistics Management

papers.title: Where's the beef? Consumer stockpiling of fresh meat during and following a disruption
papers.abstract: Purpose Supply chains continue to be disrupted, leading to product scarcity. Consumers facing a product shortage often respond by stockpiling scarce products, which has implications across supply chain tiers (e.g. unavailability of goods, inflated prices). Thus, this research explores consumer stockpiling behavior of fresh meat items during and following a supply chain disruption to understand stockpiling of a category of perishable items. Design/methodology/approach We study this topic in the context of an exogenous shock whereby fresh meat production in the United States (U.S.) was curtailed due to COVID-19 outbreaks in meat packing plants from late April to early June 2020. We utilize data from NielsenIQ's Consumer Panel Dataset, the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, and the U.S. Census Bureau to employ a difference-in-differences design. Findings Consumers displayed behavior consistent with stockpiling of fresh meat products facing scarcity; this effect continued as the threat of the shortage was subsiding. Further, rural households displayed behavior consistent with stockpiling to a greater degree than urban households. Originality/value Literature surrounding stockpiling during disruptions mostly focuses on nonperishable products. Given the nature of perishable products, consumers may exhibit different stockpiling behavior. Thus, we expand this literature by exploring stockpiling of a type of perishable product: fresh meat. We further inform practice by focusing on the behavioral differences between urban versus rural consumers.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Physical Distribution & Logistics Management

papers.title: Financial market discipline and new business formation
papers.abstract: Abstract This study examines the effect of public disclosure of financial misconduct in the retail banking industry on the real economy. We propose that strengthened public disclosure of misconduct imposes disciplinary pressure which improves services and intermediation in the retail financial sector and that it ultimately benefits the local economy. Using a large dataset of public complaints about financial misconduct, we find a positive relationship between the intensity of public disclosure and new business formation in the local community. We also find such a market discipline avenue complements the role of social trust in improving the local entrepreneurial ecosystem.

papers.title: Moral legitimacy and market exit strategies: how home-country consumers evaluate firm responses to economic sanctions
papers.abstract: Economic sanctions are increasingly used as tools of international norm enforcement, yet little is known about how home-country consumers evaluate firms' strategic responses to such measures. This research examines how different market exit strategies from sanctioned host countries affect home-country consumers' legitimacy judgments and support for firms. Drawing on legitimacy theory and research in international business, we develop and test a framework to explain how home-country consumers respond to full, partial, and no-exit strategies. Across four studies using longitudinal secondary and experimental methods, we find that home-country consumers react more positively to firms that pursue full exit from a sanctioned market than to those that adopt partial or no exit strategies. Individual-level differences in susceptibility to normative influence, cognitive empathy, individualism, and ethical views on the use of sanctions shape these evaluations. The findings contribute to theories of legitimacy, international divestment, and moral stakeholder evaluation, and offer practical guidance to firms navigating the complexities of operating under economic sanctions.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence technology empowers firms’ export performance: does TMT human capital matter?
papers.abstract: Purpose Although the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) technology on firms’ strategic choices and performance has attracted considerable scholarly attention, how it influences firm export performance and how top management team (TMT) human capital moderates this relationship remain to be systematically explored. This study aims to integrate the competency-based view and upper echelons theory to address these critical research questions. Design/methodology/approach On the basis of the empirical data of Chinese listed companies from 2009 to 2023 (involving 1,404 listed companies and 7,580 years-firm observations), we empirically examine our theoretical viewpoints using the fixed effects model. Findings First, we find that AI technology enhances firms’ export performance. Second, both the overseas background and the digital background of the TMT strengthen the positive impact of AI technology on firms’ export performance. Surprisingly, but interestingly, the TMT’s education level has no moderating effect on this relationship. Originality/value This study introduces TMT human capital as a moderating variable to explore the relationship between AI technology and firms’ export performance in depth. From this perspective, we not only reveal the strategic significance of TMT human capital in the implementation of AI technology and its correlation with export performance but also provide an analytical framework that integrates technological capabilities and TMT characteristics in the field of international marketing.

papers.title: The Way Forward in Fashion e‐Commerce Returns: Enhancing Eco‐Efficiency
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT In fashion e‐commerce, about one in three orders is returned; however, firms keep offering free, fast returns driving these volumes even as they acknowledge the economic and environmental costs. Why do inefficient return practices persist? We argue that the answer is not a failure to optimize but a collective trap in which no single actor can afford to break away alone. Adopting a supply chain perspective and drawing on Extended Institutional Theory (EIT), through a qualitative multiple‐case study of Italian fashion e‐commerce firms, we examine how the interaction of legitimacy‐seeking and profit‐seeking logics across producers, retailers, and logistics and transport providers reproduces these practices. Upstream legitimacy‐driven decisions, aimed at maintaining high service levels, propagate downstream through contractual‐operational constraints, limiting the autonomy of logistics and transport providers. These interdependencies generate reinforcing decision‐making loops stabilizing dominant return practices, notwithstanding their inefficiencies. The study identifies outcome‐based imitation mechanisms, such as omnichannel return management, return consolidation, and differentiated return policies, as levers to disrupt these loops and enhance eco‐efficiency while maintaining legitimacy. The paper extends EIT to supply chain contexts and offers prescriptive insights. Practically, it highlights the need for sector‐based actions to rebalance legitimacy and profit motives for sustainable returns management.

papers.title: The protective role of sleep in tempering the impact of ICT ‐driven off‐hour interruptions on exhaustion at work
papers.abstract: Abstract Off‐hour work interruptions are prevalent in organizations that expect employee availability during off‐hours through information‐communication technologies (ICTs). We bring together domain switch theory and threaded cognition theory to argue that ICT availability demands increase off‐hour interruptions during periods intended for generating work‐relevant resources, resulting in exhaustion at work. We sought to identify how individuals could buffer this threat. While to date the literature has primarily examined sleep disruption as an outcome of ICT use or a means of restoring resources post‐stressor exposure, we extend the literature by exploring the protective power of sleep duration as a resource‐generating activity employees can leverage in ICT‐demanding work environments. Using multilevel data across a five‐day workweek from a sample of working adults (level 2: N = 176) with daily off‐hour interruption reports (level 1: N = 679), we found that sleep duration reduced the indirect effect of ICT availability demands on exhaustion via off‐hour interruptions, while controlling for sleep quality. These findings suggest that prioritizing sleep can help accrue resources needed for work, shifting the perspective from sleep as a reactive restorative process to a proactive protective mechanism. Results also underscore the potential value of organizational policies and leader behaviors that promote and enable sufficient off‐hours worker rest.

papers.title: The globalised dual banking system of Saudi Arabia and Islamic banks: a struggle for authenticity
papers.abstract: This study explores the divergence between Islamic banking’s ethical ideals and their implementation in Saudi Arabia, where global capitalist pressures and neo-imperial logics reshape local practices. Mobilising postcolonial theory, we extend its conventional focus on former colonies to a context never formally colonised. Saudi Arabia illustrates how coloniality persists beyond territorial conquest: through the adoption of Western regulatory frameworks, financial standards, and epistemic norms. Drawing on in-depth qualitative interviews with key stakeholders, we identify how international standards and local perceptions of Western superiority displace authentic Sharia-based financial practices, such as profit-and-loss sharing, in favour of debt-based products that mimic conventional banking. These dynamics institutionalise mimicry and erode the social and ethical distinctiveness of Islamic finance. Our analysis reveals displaced local practices to capture how indigenous modes of banking are marginalised within global financial architectures. The study contributes to the accounting and business ethics literature by demonstrating that postcolonial theorisation is analytically powerful even in non-colonised settings, and by highlighting the structural and ideological challenges that Islamic banks face in pursuing authenticity within a globalised financial system.

papers.title: Healer or Human? How Online Physician Reviews Guide Patient Choice
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Online reviews increasingly guide physician choice, yet it remains unclear whether content emphasizing a physician's competence (technical skills) or benevolence (prioritizing patients' welfare over self‐interest) more strongly influences patients' decisions. Integrating a field study of 12,351 physician reviews with two online experiments, we distinguish two dimensions of review effectiveness: how helpful readers find a review, and how confident they feel about the choice it informs. We show that competence‐ and benevolence‐focused content influences these outcomes through distinct mechanisms. Benevolence‐focused reviews receive higher helpfulness evaluations because caring behaviors are easier to describe in concrete, vivid language and because naturalistic review platforms reward such vividness through cumulative votes. However, when concreteness and evaluation context are held constant, competence‐focused reviews are perceived as more diagnostic. Competence‐focused content generates greater choice confidence because it directly signals clinical risk, the consideration central to high‐stakes decisions. These effects emerge primarily in negative reviews, whereas positive reviews show no differences. Together, the studies reveal a systematic gap between reviews that are perceived as “helpful” and those that shape patients' decisions, informing how platforms design ranking and voting systems, how physicians communicate both competence and care, and how patients weigh competence‐relevant content even when it attracts fewer endorsements.

papers.title: The place brand co-creation spectrum: dimensions, practices and resident roles
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to expand the boundaries of place brand co-creation going beyond the intentional and planned participation in structured co-creation activities. It responds to a need to clarify place brand co-creation and to a lack of theoretical clarity in how different forms of resident involvement and engagement with the brand shape brand meaning. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on two qualitative studies across five European cities, the research adopts a practice theory lens to examine both deliberate and unintentional forms of co-creation. Study 1 draws on interviews (n = 28), netnography and participant observation in Luton; Study 2 uses auto-driven photo-elicited interviews (n = 20) across London, Leicester, Oxford and Budapest. Findings Place brand co-creation occurs along three dimensions (structure, intentionality and temporality) that form the place brand co-creation spectrum. Four archetypes of place brand co-creation are identified along those dimensions based on the planned/unplanned and active/passive nature of resident involvement and in combination to seven identified resident roles. Research limitations/implications The place brand co-creation spectrum offers scholars and place managers a tool to understand and facilitate resident engagement, highlighting how even unintentional actions contribute to brand meaning. The findings are based on resident–municipality dynamics and do not explore other stakeholder perspectives (e.g. visitors, businesses) in broader stakeholder ecosystems. Originality/value The place brand co-creation spectrum offers a nuanced and dynamic conceptual model of place brand co-creation, extending existing theory by integrating unintentional and passive forms of co-creation and by applying practice theory to brand meaning formation.

papers.title: From influence to de-influence: exploring the impact of negative feedback by social media influencers
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to address the academic research gap on “de-influencing,” where influencers share negative feedback about brands. Specifically, the authors define de-influencing, explore its impact on consumers’ attitudes toward targeted brands (H1a and H1b) and examine its effect on engagement intentions (H2) via the underlying mechanism of consumers’ affective reactions (H3). The research contributes to the literature on influencer marketing, electronic word of mouth, negative advertising and affect-as-information in advertising. Design/methodology/approach Across three studies (n = 460), a pilot study using secondary data from TikTok, and a fourth study that appears in the Supplementary material, this research tests the proposed hypotheses using online panels and student samples. In the hypothesis-testing studies (Studies 1–3), the authors use employ between-subjects experimental designs in which the influencer’s endorsement strategy is manipulated (de-influencing, positive influencing) and consumers’ attitudes, engagement intentions, and affect are measured. Enhancing the robustness of their findings, the authors examine different product categories, both fictitious and real brands, and known and unknown influencers. Further, Study 2 employs a longitudinal design. Findings The findings show that de-influencing leads to more negative attitudes toward the brand and reduces consumers’ intention to engage with the posted content. Importantly, the impact of de-influencing on consumers’ attitudes was more pronounced (i.e. carries more weight) compared with positive influencing. In addition, consumers’ affective reactions was identified as the underlying mechanism explaining why de-influencing (vs. positive influencing) reduces engagement intentions. Finally, although de-influencing enhanced perceptions of helpfulness, these positive perceptions do not translate into improved attitudes toward the influencer or greater engagement intentions (i.e. did not benefit the influencer). Research limitations/implications The paper acknowledges several potential limitations and areas for future research. One limitation is that the findings may not apply to influencers whose personal brand is built on negativity or “honest reviews,” as consumers may more readily engage with their negative content. In addition, future research should examine how the language and tone used in expressing negative opinions shape consumer perceptions and engagement. Finally, future studies could investigate how brands can recover from negative endorsements and identify the conditions under which de-influencing may actually strengthen brand trust or credibility. Practical implications The research highlights significant implications for both influencers and brands. For influencers, de-influencing fails to bolster consumer engagement or improve consumer attitudes, suggesting they should address grievances privately with brands to avoid negative consequences. For brands, the study emphasizes the importance of monitoring influencer content, particularly in the context of de-influencing, as it can sway consumer perceptions of both familiar and unfamiliar brands. Brands should implement corrective actions, such as apologies or product replacements, to mitigate negative impacts. In addition, contracts with influencers should include clauses to manage negativity and protect brand reputation. Originality/value De-influencing is a novel persuasion strategy that has recently been adopted by influencers. Despite its growing popularity in influencer marketing and calls for research on de-influencing in the academic literature, de-influencing suffers from a lack of academic research and empirical investigation. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this research is among the first works to conceptually define this phenomenon, empirically investigate the outcomes of such negative strategies and address calls for research on the unexplored dark side of influencer marketing.

papers.title: Holding All the Cards from the Good Old Days: How Nostalgic Cues Enhance Artificial Intelligence Service Acceptance
papers.abstract: Although artificial intelligence (AI) has become deeply integrated into services, many customers exhibit low acceptance of AI-driven offerings. Identifying effective and efficient ways to enhance AI acceptance is both theoretically significant and practically valuable. Drawing on compensatory control theory, we propose that embedded nostalgic cues in AI services can increase customers’ acceptance of these services. The underlying mechanism is an enhanced, agent-specific sense of control: nostalgic cues reduce uncertainty associated with AI-mediated interactions and restore customers’ agent-specific sense of control over the AI service, thereby increasing their willingness to accept AI services. Moreover, the positive effect of nostalgic cues on AI acceptance is contingent upon moderators—AI role positioning and identity threat. We tested our proposed effect using field and online experiments. Our findings contribute theoretical insights into AI services and nostalgia while offering practical solutions for the service industry.

papers.title: The Governance Role of Quasi‐Official Shareholder Activism: Evidence From Firm–Investor Communication in China
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Research Question/Issue We investigate whether a quasi‐official minority shareholder, the China Securities Investor Services Center (CSISC), affects firms' investor relations management when it actively exercises its shareholder rights in listed firms. Research Findings/Insights We employ a machine learning–based algorithm to estimate response quality scores from over 4 million question‐and‐answer (Q&A) interactions involving all A‐share listed firms on the Shenzhen and Shanghai Stock Exchanges between 2009 and 2022. Using a staggered difference‐in‐differences research design, we find that the active exercise of shareholder rights by a quasi‐official shareholder enhances corporate communication with stakeholders and increases minority shareholder participation and attendance at annual shareholders' meetings. Cross‐sectional analyses further reveal that the effects are more pronounced among firms with lower board independence, those audited by smaller audit firms, and firms with limited analyst coverage. Theoretical/Academic Implications These findings contribute to the broader understanding of mechanisms that support minority shareholder protection and engagement in the governance of Chinese listed firms and highlight the potential of structured shareholder activism in amplifying minority voices and creating value in capital markets. Practitioner/Policy Implications The evidence indicates that CSISC's shareholder activism enhances corporate communication, fosters inclusive and transparent governance, and reduces information asymmetry, particularly benefiting minority shareholders. For managers and boards, high‐quality investor communication helps reduce the reputational and valuation costs associated with increased governance scrutiny.

papers.title: Putting Democratic Theory and Principles of Justice in the Right Place: Ethical Pluralism in Collaborative and Participatory Governance
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Participatory and collaborative governance (P&CG) is widely celebrated as an institutional vehicle for democratizing public decision‐making by inviting affected stakeholders into inclusive and deliberative policy processes. This essay argues that underlying appeals to democratic legitimacy in P&CG are tacit commitments to specific (and often ideologically bounded) conceptions of justice. Democracy, far from being normatively univocal, encompasses competing justice principles that yield divergent and sometimes incompatible design imperatives. In response, this essay calls for a shift from vague democratic invocations to a more precise theorization of justice as the operative normative currency in P&CG. To this end, the essay outlines an analytical framework that maps three core dimensions of governance design (input, process, and output) onto corresponding domains of justice: representational, procedural, and distributive. Systematically unpacking the plural and conflicting ethical principles within each domain shows how different principles of justice produce distinct governance dilemmas and trade‐offs.

papers.title: Citizens’ support for behavioural public policy and trust in government: evidence from two online experiments
papers.abstract: We explore citizens’ support for behavioral interventions by distinguishing interventions that exploit citizens’ bounded rationality through choice architecture (Nudge) from those that challenge bounded rationality by promoting reflection through deliberative forums (Think). We also examine the role of trust in government in shaping these preferences. Findings from two experiments involving 3,010 US participants show that citizens are more willing to support Think rather than Nudge. Whereas the adoption of Nudge, as compared to Think, does not seem to influence trust in government, encouraging higher levels of trust in government has a stronger effect on support for Nudge than for Think.

papers.title: Civic Embeddedness and Public Employment: How Institutional Proximity Structures Civic Participation
papers.abstract: Research on public service motivation consistently finds that public employees volunteer and contribute more than their private sector counterparts, yet less is known about how engagement varies across behavioral domains and institutional contexts. This study examines how civic engagement is structured among public employees compared to other citizens, with particular attention to variation across levels of government. Using the 2023 CPS Volunteering and Civic Life Supplement, the analysis constructs multidimensional measures across four domains: political participation, civic involvement, political expression, and social connectedness. Weighted regressions and propensity score matching show that public employees, especially at the local level, exhibit a distinct civic profile characterized by greater involvement in institutional forms of participation such as voting and volunteering, but lower engagement in informal activities such as political discussion and social interaction. These patterns persist after accounting for observable characteristics and suggest that public employment channels participation into specific forms rather than uniformly increasing overall engagement, with implications for how civil service reforms may alter the civic composition of local communities.

papers.title: How Front-Line Public Managers Become Institutional Entrepreneurs
papers.abstract: How do front-line public managers become institutional entrepreneurs? This article answers that question through a longitudinal single-case study of a large Norwegian municipality's healthcare services. Drawing on organizational institutionalism and public management scholarship, I first show how front-line public managers initiate divergent change by leveraging a sensing–legitimation nexus. They detect external and internal triggers, frame the need for change, and secure political, administrative, and professional support through direct negotiation and compelling operational narratives. They then act as co-creation catalysts, engaging residents and building cross-sector partnerships to adapt service designs and mobilize scarce resources. Finally, they institutionalize transformative public healthcare delivery by embedding routines in daily operations, formalizing interdisciplinary team structures, clarifying roles, and demonstrating performance gains. Evidence from two innovation projects shows that resource-constrained, non-heroic actors can disrupt entrenched practices and stabilize innovation as the new institutional arrangement. The study contributes to institutional entrepreneurship theory by positioning front-line public managers as credible entrepreneurial agents and by identifying co-creation as a core mechanism of public sector institutional change.

papers.title: Drug Discovery’s Blind Spot: Why Organoid–Artificial Intelligence Convergence Demands Integrated Governance
papers.abstract: Organoid-artificial intelligence (AI) platforms are increasingly central to drug discovery, yet they sit between two governance regimes. AI frameworks presume stable, well-characterized inputs, while organoid ethics focuses on donor consent, moral status, and tissue use, leaving downstream computational uses of organoid-derived data underregulated. This article argues that the convergence of living biological variability with algorithmic decision-making creates a governance vacuum in high-stakes preclinical contexts. The organoid-AI case is distinctive because two mature governance traditions, built on incompatible assumptions, intersect at a decision-critical point, and because organoid-derived biological states are transient and often irrecoverable. The article maps the structural causes of this gap, illustrates its practical consequences through three failure scenarios assessing likely probability and impact, and proposes an integrated two-pillar framework: graduated AI validation indexed to organoid functional complexity and tamper-resistant audit trails linking biological and algorithmic metadata. It concludes that proactive governance is morally preferable to delayed, crisis-driven regulation.

papers.title: Challenging Face-to-Face Communication in Clinical Ethics: Autism as an Illustrative Case
papers.abstract: This paper examines the ethical status of face-to-face communication in clinical practice, using autism as an illustrative case. Drawing on phenomenological accounts of embodiment and first-person descriptions of autistic experience, it argues that face-to-face interaction-characterized by immediacy, multimodality, and unpredictability-can impose significant perceptual and cognitive burdens on autistic patients. Digitally mediated communication, by contrast, provides greater temporal flexibility, semiotic stability, and user control, thereby reducing communicative pressure and supporting more accessible participation. Reframing communication through the principles of autonomy, non-maleficence, and relational care, the paper argues that communicative practices should be understood as context-sensitive and responsive to patients' perceptual conditions rather than governed by a default preference for face-to-face interaction. It concludes that presence should be reconceptualized as a relational achievement grounded in responsiveness rather than physical co-presence alone, with implications for how ethical communication in clinical care is understood.

papers.title: Leveraging limited testing data for early detection of emerging infectious disease outbreaks
papers.abstract: Early during emerging infectious disease outbreaks, case-based surveillance is constrained by limited test availability, diagnostic delays, and low clinical suspicion. Novel pathogens that mimic symptoms of established conditions may generate detectable outbreak signals in routine testing data, as infected individuals seek testing for known conditions and test negative. We developed analytic and simulation frameworks using Poisson and negative binomial models to evaluate whether total and negative testing volumes for a clinically similar ("mimicking") condition can provide timely outbreak warning. We systematically assessed detection performance across variations in baseline test counts, epidemic growth rates, testing fractions among cases, detection threshold stringency, and overdispersion. Detection thresholds based on negative tests consistently outperformed total test thresholds, achieving earlier detection with approximately one-third fewer cumulative cases while maintaining comparable false positive rates. However, reliable detection required stringent conditions: high testing fractions among epidemic cases, low baseline test volumes, and low overdispersion. When testing fractions fell below 5%, epidemic size estimates provided little practical information; above 30%, precision markedly improved. These findings support prioritizing access to disaggregated test result data but caution that this detection approach is best positioned as a resource-efficient complement within integrated surveillance portfolios rather than a standalone early warning system.

papers.title: Top, Bottom, or Versatile? Sexual Role Trends Across Generations and Regions on a Gay Dating App
papers.abstract: Understanding how men who have sex with men (MSM) identify with sexual role labels such as Top, Bottom, or Versatile offers descriptive insights into how sexuality, identity, and self-presentation intersect on dating platforms. Drawing on cross-sectional data from 141,156 active users of the global gay dating app Surge, this study describes age-based and regional differences in sexual role identification. We model user-reported role preferences using Poisson regression with interaction terms for age and continent, accounting for non-linear age effects and regional heterogeneity. Younger MSM were more likely to identify as Bottom or Versatile, while older users more often identified as Top. Across continents, Versatile was the most common identification in Europe and Oceania, whereas Bottom was most common in the Americas and Africa. These descriptive patterns are consistent with sexual role labels being context-dependent and may reflect age-related and cultural variation in how roles are communicated and perceived within MSM communities. The study highlights how platform-based data may help illuminate patterns of intimacy and self-presentation among MSM worldwide.

papers.title: Declining Investigations and Shifting Profiles: A 20-Year Analysis of Child Sexual Abuse Cases in Canadian Child Welfare
papers.abstract: This study examines 20-year trends in child sexual abuse (CSA) investigations within Canada's child welfare system, using data from the Canadian Incidence Study of Reported Child Abuse and Neglect (CIS) between 1998 and 2019. Data in the current study represent all Canadian provinces/territories except for Quebec. Findings indicate a substantial decline in both investigated and substantiated CSA cases, particularly among children aged 0-7 and cases involving non-parental perpetrators. Substantiated investigations among the youngest children fell by more than 80%, highlighting a marked shift in the age profile of cases coming to the attention of authorities. The overall reduction in CSA investigations may reflect genuine decreases in abuse for certain subgroups, but may also signal changing thresholds for reporting, professional hesitancy, and structural constraints within child welfare and law enforcement agencies. Notably, fewer substantiated cases in 2019 involved police intervention or ongoing services compared with 1998, raising concerns about unmet needs, diminished access to justice, and potential erosion of public confidence.

papers.title: Cumulative Incidence of Child Protective Services Involvement Among Indigenous and Nonindigenous Children: A Cross-National Analysis
papers.abstract: In settler-colonial societies, indigenous children exhibit elevated risk of CPS involvement, but little is known about the comparative dynamics of indigenous disadvantage. We calculated the cumulative incidence of CPS involvement before age 18 years among indigenous and nonindigenous children in Australia and the United States in 2019. We applied period life-table methods to linked administrative records. Among indigenous children, the cumulative incidences of maltreatment investigation and of out-of-home placement were higher in the U.S. than in Australia, but investigations confirming maltreatment were more common in Australia than in the U.S. Indigenous-nonindigenous disparities in CPS involvement were larger in Australia than in the U.S. In both countries, indigenous-nonindigenous disparities decreased with age and were larger at later stages of CPS involvement. Comparative findings contextualize indigenous children's CPS involvement in settler-colonial societies, informing research into its causes and prevention.

Designing farmer-centered extension programmes for low-carbon agriculture: evidence from a discrete choice experiment in China
papers.abstract: Low-carbon agricultural technologies (LCAT) are central to climate mitigation, yet their adoption remains low, including in emerging economies. While prior research has focused mainly on technology attributes and broad adoption barriers, less attention has been paid to how the design and delivery of organized LCAT extension programmes shape farmers’ willingness to engage. This study uses a discrete choice experiment to examine Chinese farmers’ preferences for organized LCAT extension programmes and focuses on four key attributes: organizing bodies, delivery agents, delivery formats, and participation costs. The findings show that the delivery format emerges as the most influential attribute, suggesting that policy-makers should prioritize it in programme design. Farmers place higher value on programmes organized by local agricultural bureaus and agricultural research institutions than on those organized by agricultural input suppliers, and they evaluate local extension personnel less favourably than the other delivery-agent categories. Participation cost remains an important constraint, and preferences vary systematically across farmer groups. In particular, older farmers, those operating larger farms, those in good health, and those with favourable attitudes towards agricultural technology exhibit greater willingness to participate. Welfare simulations further suggest that extension programmes combining public or research-based organization, formal technical delivery, and on-site field guidance generate the largest gains in farmer welfare. By quantifying farmers’ preferences for specific institutional and delivery configurations, our paper provides evidence for designing LCAT extension strategies that better reflect farmer priorities and for determining how programme components should be prioritized, sequenced, and supported under real-world budget and implementation constraints.

papers.title: Energy poverty: Seasonal variations, socioeconomic disparities and cumulative inequality
The fiscal and socioeconomic impact of the energy transition in the transport sector: The case of the Basque Country
papers.abstract: This paper analyses the fiscal challenges of the climate-neutral economy transition by 2050 in line with the European Green Deal's goals. It focuses on the regional level and examines the Basque Country, one of the sub-state entities with the greatest fiscal power in the European Union, and aims to quantify the implications of decarbonising the transport sector for public finances. To this end, it applies DERIO, a dynamic econometric New Keynesian Input-Output model, designed to evaluate the economic effects of scenarios and policies at regional level, particularly those related to energy and climate change. Our analysis indicates that transport electrification increases revenues from taxes on production, income, wealth, and corporate profits, as well as social-security contributions. However, it reduces receipts from taxes on products and yields an overall net decline in public revenues. The results highlight the complex, cross-sectoral transmission mechanisms at play during the transition and offer actionable insights for designing revenue-stable fiscal frameworks in the face of large structural changes.

papers.title: Machine learning for wind farm wake modeling: Output-driven taxonomy, architectural inductive biases, and benchmarking
papers.abstract: Accurate plant-scale wake modeling is essential for wind-farm design, control, and digital-twin operation, yet practical prediction remains constrained by the fidelity–deployability trade-off between fast engineering wake models and physics-rich computational fluid dynamics (CFD). Machine learning (ML) has expanded rapidly as a route to low-latency wake prediction and multi-fidelity correction, but existing studies remain difficult to compare because they differ in learned outputs, data provenance, and validation claims. This review reframes ML wake modeling around the predicted physical quantity rather than the algorithm alone. Four task families are distinguished: scalar response or key performance indicator (KPI) prediction, static wake-field or wake-state emulation, dynamic wake evolution, and turbine–turbine interaction-operator learning. For each family, we examine how representative architectures, including tabular surrogates, convolutional and recurrent models, graph neural networks, neural operators, reduced-order models, and physics-informed learning, embed inductive biases for spatial locality, temporal memory, directional coupling, coherent wake structure, and discretization-aware mapping. We further synthesize data regimes spanning engineering models, CFD, aero-servo-elastic simulation, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA), light detection and ranging (LiDAR), and wind-tunnel measurements, emphasizing how label fidelity, sample independence, operational confounding, and solver-specific assumptions shape the sim-to-real gap. Building on this taxonomy, we propose claim-driven benchmarking that aligns hold-out design, physics-aware diagnostics, uncertainty calibration, and deployment evidence across regime, layout, control-policy, site, discretization, and fidelity shifts. The review identifies where current ML wake models are mature, where validation remains weak, and how future work can support robust layout optimization, wake steering, load-aware control, and wind-farm digital twins.

DURABLE: A Workflow for Determining Corrosion-Driving and Protective Microbial Mechanisms
papers.abstract: Abstract Microbiologically influenced corrosion (MIC) threatens global infrastructure, causing billions of dollars in annual losses. Its persistence stems from unresolved mechanisms─particularly the metabolites produced by microorganisms that drive or inhibit corrosion─and the microbial community structures. Progress has been hindered by the absence of systematic workflows to rapidly and accurately identify MIC-relevant microorganisms and their functions. Here, we present DURABLE (Detection of Unique Corrosion Resistant or Accelerating Biologics in a Laboratory Environment), a pipeline that couples high-throughput microbial screening with genomic and metabolic workflows. We applied the DURABLE workflow to six diesel tank samples and revealed fuel-dependent microbial community structures, which showed greater diversity and evenness in bacterial communities than their fungal counterparts. The workflow used carbon steel beads to rapidly screen over 80 bacterial isolates for corrosive activity, reducing assay time to approximately 2 days compared with the conventional 30-day metal coupon test. More than 40 isolates were identified as corrosive. Further testing using mass spectrometry analysis revealed corrosion-associated metabolites, which were further validated using electrochemical assays. Thus, DURABLE achieved a ∼15-fold increase in screening speed and provided a scalable and mechanistic framework for dissecting MIC dynamics. We expect this advance will enable the development of precision mitigation strategies in hydrocarbon fuel infrastructure.

papers.title: A Review: Mechanisms, Processes and Design Principles of Recycling Spent Lithium-Ion Battery and Biomass
papers.abstract: Abstract End-of-life lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) and biomass wastes are usually studied in separate fields. This review shows that they should also be understood as complementary reaction systems. Biomass not only acts as a cheap carbon source but also provides reductive gases, biochar, organic acids, ligands, and redox-active organics to enable LIB recycling. Spent LIB-derived materials can serve as both a valuable resource and a catalyst to leverage biomass conversion. On this basis, this Review brings together three directions that are discussed in one framework: biomass-assisted thermochemical recycling, biomass-derived leaching systems, and LIB-enabled catalytic biomass valorization. This review identifies the common principles that control these processes, including oxygen potential, phase evolution, kinetics, coupled acid–redox–coordination chemistry, and catalyst design. We further compare process configurations, product pathways, and environmental trade-offs. Future work should focus on resolving coupled reaction mechanisms, defining composition and reactor design windows, integrating process-level assessment, and enabling data-driven optimization for scalable and low-impact corecycling systems.

papers.title: Production, Biodegradation, and Recalcitrance of Organic Carbon from Cultivated Saccharina latissima in Norway
papers.abstract: Abstract Particulate (POC) and dissolved (DOC) organic carbon released during macroalgae cultivation has been shown to lead to carbon burial and export to the open ocean and deep sea. The recalcitrant portion of the DOC (RDOC) is a critical contributor to carbon sequestration and a major knowledge gap. We investigate the production and bioavailability of DOC released from Saccharina latissima, a primary cultivar in Europe, with a focus on RDOC quantification. DOC release rates were 0.5–1.4 mg C g(dw)−1 h–1 within 24 h, and concentrations stabilized after 187 days of biodegradation, at 37–79% (mean 58%) from initial levels. The kelp released 920 (17%) unique compounds, including large quantities of sulfur-containing molecules (CHOS, CHONS). Increasing recalcitrance was observed in kelp and control treatments, despite small variations in CRAM molecules. Microbial biodegradation generated 1,805 (34%) new molecules, including 1,207 in the recalcitrant DOM fraction. Island of Stability (IOS) analysis revealed an intensity-weighted abundance of 0.2% RDOC in kelp treatments, with persistence on geological time scales. Beyond its biomass applications, macroalgae cultivation enables scalable CO2 sequestration in the oceans through RDOC production from continuous release and degradation of DOC and POC during grow-out, in itself a value-added product.
