Hotter days, smaller ranges: Air temperature constrains livestock movement and space use in Mediterranean rangelands
papers.abstract: Livestock has become the dominant large herbivore guild in most rangelands worldwide. Current climate adaptation frameworks emphasize extreme climatic events, although the extent to which these episodic drivers capture the environmental conditions shaping animal behaviour remains unclear. Rising temperatures and more frequent extreme climatic events (ECEs) are expected to influence animal behaviour, but the relative importance of daily climatic conditions versus discrete extreme events remains poorly quantified in managed grazing systems. Movement responses are especially informative as early-warning indicators of behavioural adjustments to environmental stress. We analysed GPS data from 26 sheep herds monitored in southern Spain between 2021 and 2022 (∼12,000 animals; 6464 monitoring days). Daily distance travelled, core area (50% kernel), and home range (95% kernel) were modelled against daily maximum air temperature, precipitation, pasture productivity (NDVI), distance to water sources, and the heat-wave indicator. Herds travelled shorter daily distances and used smaller core areas and home ranges as daily maximum air temperature increased, particularly during mid-summer. Across the annual cycle, all three responses showed nonlinear relationships with temperature, peaking at intermediate values, and were negatively related to NDVI. In contrast, precipitation and the heat-wave indicator were not retained in the best-supported models. Overall, daily maximum air temperature was consistently associated with all three movement and space-use metrics, whereas the heat-wave indicator was not retained in the best-supported models. As warming progresses, these contractions may reduce livestock movement, with potential consequences for vegetation dynamics and biodiversity. Anticipating such behavioural responses may help inform monitoring and management of Mediterranean grazing systems.

papers.title: Interpretable control rules derived from model predictive control for real-time control in stormwater management
papers.abstract: Real-time control of stormwater systems improves flood resilience, yet optimization-based methods, such as model predictive control (MPC), remain difficult to implement due to high computational demands and limited operational transparency. As a result, cities continue to rely on rule-based control (RBC), despite the lack of standardized approaches for deriving effective rule sets. This study introduces a framework that formulates interpretable, near-optimal control rules by learning directly from optimal behavior using regression decision trees. MPC is applied offline to generate optimal gate trajectories for 1158 historical rainfall events from 2007 to 2025, which are used to train decision-tree models that extract if-then rules reproducing optimal logic in real time without online optimization. The framework is applied on a basin where the objective is to maintain water levels between 14.8 m and 15.4 m to prevent overflows and preserve recreational activities. Results show that the derived RBC performs better than baseline static control and achieves performance comparable to MPC. In terms of safety, defined by the number of events during which the maximal water level was exceeded, RBC retained 86% of MPC performance, with a total exceedance duration 23% longer, and an increase of 21% in total overflow volume, while reducing gate movement by 57% and computational time by 88%. The extracted rules provided an interpretable representation of optimal control logic, enabling operator understanding, validation, and adjustment. By combining MPC optimization with the transparency and operational simplicity of RBC, this study offers a framework for implementing near-optimal real-time control in stormwater systems.

papers.title: Optimized design of ozone microbubble aeration reactor to enhance the removal of dissolved organic matter: A pilot-scale study on drinking water treatment
Economic competitiveness of separated dairy manure solids as a phosphorus fertilizer substitute
papers.abstract: Manure solid-liquid separation offers a potential pathway for redistributing nutrients from livestock-intensive, nutrient-surplus regions to cropland with fertilizer demand, but the competitiveness of separated manure products with synthetic phosphorus fertilizer depends on manure quality, acquisition price, and hauling distance. We developed a probabilistic techno-economic framework to evaluate separated dairy manure solids (SDMS) relative to synthetic phosphorus fertilizer under representative market and agronomic conditions and to identify transaction-level thresholds for competitive viability. The analysis combined Sobol global sensitivity analysis, Monte Carlo uncertainty propagation, deterministic scenario surfaces, and leverage analysis. SDMS acquisition price was the dominant driver of variance in net savings, followed by P 2 O 5 concentration and hauling distance. Competitiveness declined sharply with transport distance, with the 50% probability crossover occurring between 161 and 201 km and the most decision-sensitive range concentrated around 121-201 km under the modeled conditions. Scenario analysis showed that lower acquisition price and higher P 2 O 5 concentration substantially expanded the viable hauling radius, while moisture reduction also improved competitiveness but with different marginal returns across the quality surface. The leverage surface showed that the relative benefit of dewatering versus P 2 O 5 enrichment depends on the current product state; across much of the evaluated commercial range, a 1 percentage point reduction in moisture produced a greater gain in breakeven hauling distance than a 0.1 percentage point increase in P 2 O 5 concentration, although the reverse held at low P 2 O 5 concentrations combined with low moisture. The results also identified an acquisition-price ceiling beyond which additional processing no longer preserved competitiveness. These findings provide transaction-level economic criteria for manure redistribution and are implemented in NutrientChoice ( https://www.dairyconservation.org/NutrientChoice ), an open-source decision-support tool.

papers.title: Beyond Targeted Calibrations: Comprehensive Quantification of Oxygenated Organic Compounds in Urban Atmospheres
papers.abstract: Abstract Quantifying oxygenated volatile organic compounds (OVOCs) in the atmospheric gas phase remains a major challenge, particularly in urban environments where these compounds are important contributors to air quality and health impacts. Here, we present a collision-induced dissociation based voltage-scanning method to derive sensitivities for an ammonium-adduct chemical ionization mass spectrometer, enabling quantification of OVOCs beyond those available for direct calibration. The method was validated under laboratory conditions and applied during the 2023 AEROMMA airborne campaign and the 2024 SAPHIR-CHANEL chamber campaign. The approach extended quantification coverage to 98% of the total signal in chamber experiments and 78% in field measurements. Detected species spanned a wide volatility range, with chamber experiments allowing enhanced detection of more oxidized, higher-molecular-weight products compared to the more variable and diluted field observations. Although coverage decreased with increasing molecular size and oxidation state, the method consistently extended into these regimes, particularly under controlled chamber conditions. Sensitivity trends between chamber and field data showed strong agreement, supporting the use of chamber-derived calibrations for ambient quantification. Incorporating these additional quantified species increased estimates of OH reactivity and secondary organic aerosol formation potential by around 5% and around 62%, respectively, contributing to improved chemical closure in urban air.

papers.title: Photoinduced Intraparticle Chemistry Drives the Rapid Atmospheric Oxidation of Biomass Burning Organic Aerosol
papers.abstract: Abstract Biomass burning (BB) is the second largest global source of organic aerosol (OA), with its impact on climate and air quality expected to rise with global warming. Aircraft measurements of BB plumes show a rapid increase in the OA oxidation state, which could not be reproduced in simulation chambers based on gas-phase oxidation. Here, we investigate isolation key aging processes of BB emissions in controlled chamber experiments, including the effects of ultraviolet-A irradiation, OH-driven secondary OA formation, heterogeneous OH oxidation or ozonolysis, and evaporation. We find that ultraviolet-A irradiation can drive rapid intraparticle OA aging within hours, proceeding an order of magnitude faster than gas-phase oxidation. Other mechanisms were even slower in producing oxygenated OA (OOA). Based on our experiments, we estimate that this process proceeds with a quantum yield of ∼0.4%, meaning that four in every thousand photons absorbed by organic chromophores in BBOA generate radicals in the particle phase that rapidly oxidize the particulate organics. We further analyzed aircraft measurements of wildfire and prescribed burn plumes, showing that photoinduced processes can account for much of the rapid OOA formation. We estimate that, in BB-influenced regions, over half of OOA may originate from photo-oxidized primary OA within the first day. Our findings challenge the prevailing paradigm that gas-phase oxidation dominates BBOA aging and highlight a previously underappreciated, but dominant role of intraparticle photochemistry.

papers.title: Measuring Climate and Water Risk across the Bulk Power System
papers.abstract: Abstract As climate impacts increase and power systems transition to renewables, planners and operators need insights into climate risks to power generation and infrastructure to ensure reliable decision-making in the short and long-term. We present a standardized, consistent mechanism for utilities and system operators to evaluate the climate- and water-related risks of their current and future grid assets. Using a risk-based approach on the combined outcomes of high-fidelity climate drivers together with water and power system models, we examine the temperature and water availability impacts within the contiguous United States to power system assets at the water basin level in three different time periods and report resulting outcomes on lost capacity across different expansion scenarios and climate models. The results indicate that air temperature has the highest effect on derating. Changes in streamflow do not have a large impact on generation capacity at the national level. Electric sector buildout scenarios each have a unique regional risk profile, depending on the technology mix and total capacity, although risks from high temperatures are significant for both traditional and renewable energy generation. Stakeholders can use this approach to monitor effects of generation capacity losses and potential impacts as climate, generation mix, and infrastructure change.

papers.title: Rebuilding Greener? Green Building Diffusion after Extreme Weather Events
papers.abstract: Abstract As climate change intensifies, extreme weather events increasingly threaten communities and infrastructure. These shocks can act as a form of creative destruction, generating opportunities for sustainable reconstruction, while also reshaping risk perceptions and influencing investment in green technologies. This paper empirically examines how natural disasters and weather extremes affect the diffusion of green buildings across the United States. Using a panel data set of buildings certified under the U.S. Green Building Council’s Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) program at the city level from 2000 to 2020, we find that major flooding events increase the number of LEED-certified buildings within three to six years. Hurricanes initially reduce green building development, followed by a rebound in later years. We also find that extreme hot days are associated with increased green building adoption, whereas the effects of cold days and moderately hot days are limited and less consistent. These response patterns are driven primarily by private buildings rather than public properties. Overall, our findings highlight the heterogeneous and dynamic ways in which climate shocks shape green building adoption and provide insights for policymakers and planners seeking to promote sustainable urban development in a changing climate.

papers.title: Spatial Optimization of Multiscale Biorefinery Deployment for a Diversified Bioeconomy in the United States
papers.abstract: Abstract Strategic biorefinery siting is critical for a diversified bioeconomy, yet industry, policy, and research often focus on either large-scale biofuel plants or smaller-scale specialty bioproduct facilities, with limited coordination across scales. We address this gap by modeling biorefinery deployment spanning a 28-fold difference in capacity. We developed an open-source, spatially explicit framework integrating techno-economic analysis with logistics and refinery cost surrogate models to evaluate multiscale miscanthus-derived biorefineries across the rainfed U.S. for the production of ethanol, succinic acid, lactic acid, potassium sorbate, and acrylic acid. Overall costs change little as feedstock density increases, while transport distances decrease by ∼30 to 67% (∼100 km) and siting flexibility improves. Specifically, a 5-fold feedstock density increase (2% to 10% of suitable land) reduces minimum selling prices by <10% (e.g., 0.27 USD·gal–1 for ethanol). This limited economic sensitivity suggests dense planting is not required for competitive deployment, particularly for smaller-scale facilities. Representing collection areas as irregular rather than circular expands the feasible space under low-density scenarios. While large-scale refineries anchor regional supply chains, smaller facilities retain spatial flexibility even when large refineries are established. These findings highlight the importance of spatial representation and multiscale coordination for robust, regionally tailored biomanufacturing networks to advance renewable carbon integration without extensive land conversion.

papers.title: Collective Microbubble Interactions Drive Sulfur Transformation in Seawater
papers.abstract: Abstract Breaking waves, marine biological activity, and submarine geological processes continuously generate vast microbubble populations in seawater, yet the chemical consequences of bubble–bubble interactions remain poorly understood. Here, we address an apparent contradiction in saline interfacial chemistry: although high ionic strength suppresses oxidative responses at isolated bubble interfaces, dense microbubble swarms sustain transient photon emission and reactive oxygen species formation during bubbling. This contrast suggests that salinity weakens single-bubble interfacial reactivity, whereas collective bubble–bubble interactions create localized redox microenvironments through interfacial screening, conductivity effects, and repeated close interbubble encounters. The localized photon bursts observed during close bubble–bubble encounters, together with concurrent radical formation, are consistent with interbubble discharge-like events termed microlightning. Using dimethyl sulfide (DMS) as a representative marine organic sulfur compound, we further demonstrate that microbubble-mediated transformation redirects DMS toward inorganic sulfur species, including sulfate (SO42–) and reduced inorganic sulfur species. Electron spin resonance, oxidative fluorescence, spin-trapping mass spectrometry, and ion chromatography support a proposed branched radical-mediated network involving sulfur-centered activation, C–S fragmentation, oxygenation, and aqueous sulfur redox conversion. These findings reconcile salt-suppressed isolated-bubble reactivity with sustained swarm-level redox chemistry, identifying dense microbubble swarms as collective interfacial microreactors for aqueous sulfur transformation in seawater.

papers.title: Towards a circular economy for EV batteries in India: Spatiotemporal foresight of end-of-life material flows and reverse logistics stress (2030–2050)
Risk management externalities in agrifood supply chains
papers.abstract: Abstract Firms may under‐ or over‐invest in risk management from the social planner's perspective, resulting in a negative externality on other economic agents in the supply chain. The externality of risk management is particularly relevant for agrifood supply chains, which frequently experience disruptions and play a primary role in preventing major social losses from food insecurity. The magnitude of the externality depends on the structure of the supply chain. We build a theoretical model to characterize such externalities in US food supply chains where intermediary firms choose output quantities and investments in managing risks. The model allows for flexible market structures and interdependence of risk management among firms. Risk interdependence captures the unique feature of biotic hazards (e.g., animal and plant diseases) in agrifood supply chains, where the effectiveness of a firm's risk management depends on peer firms' behavior. We offer novel insights on the role of risk interdependence in driving the externality in risk management under different market structures. We show that private firms invest less than the socially optimal level under perfect competition, but risk interdependence and market power introduce complex incentives in risk‐reducing investment that shape the externality. In particular, when investments are complements across firms and firms possess strong market power in production but limited coordination in risk management, private investment may equal or even exceed the socially optimal level.

papers.title: The Impact of Homeless Encampments on Housing Prices
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT A topic of intense and heated discussion in urban America is the impact of homelessness, yet the quantitative evidence is limited. This study examines how proximity to a homeless encampment influences housing prices. Analyzing home sale transaction data in Seattle from 2017 to 2020, our hedonic models reveal that houses within 0.75 miles of an encampment sell for about 2.0% less (equivalent to an average impact of $17,445). Quantile regressions show that this negative effect persists across most market segments and is most pronounced in 2018–2019, when Seattle recorded the highest number of encampment removals. Results remain generally robust after adjusting for spatial autocorrelation.

papers.title: Are client ties pre‐entry resources? Performance implications of client tie diversification
papers.abstract: Abstract Research Summary This study investigates client tie diversification, where firms enter markets with existing clients. Recognizing the theoretical basis for both positive and negative performance implications, the paper adopts a question‐driven approach and discovers a strong negative correlation between client tie diversification and firm performance. Using data from the US federal lobbying industry during the creation of the Homeland Security issue market post‐9/11, I find that lobbying firms entering the new market with existing clients underperform compared to other firms. This underperformance is associated with over‐embeddedness with clients and agency costs from dispersed client tie ownership among lobbyists. These findings challenge the notion that client ties are readily fungible and highlight relational and agency‐related complexities that can lead firms to pursue value‐destroying diversification. Managerial Summary Do firms perform better when they diversify into new markets with their existing clients, or by pursuing new opportunities independently? This study found that firms that enter new markets alongside their current clients often underperform compared to those that do not. While it might seem beneficial to leverage existing client relationships, this approach can push firms into areas where they lack capabilities, create inefficiencies, and complicate relationships with other clients, leading to weaker performance. Managers should be cautious about letting client needs drive diversification decisions. Prioritizing current clients may offer short‐term gains but can limit the firm's ability to explore new markets and achieve long‐term growth. Strategic choices should balance client requests with the firm's own strengths and future prospects.

papers.title: Circular Transitions in Healthcare Waste Management in Vietnam: An Institutional Perspective
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Healthcare waste management (HCWM) is a growing environmental and public health concern. This study explores how the institutional pressures that shape HCWM practices evolve toward circularity through coercive, normative, and mimetic isomorphisms and how these mechanisms influence organisational behaviour in Vietnam, a complex, highly regulated setting. Data were collected through focus groups with representatives from hospitals and waste management firms in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City. Findings reveal that coercive pressures, such as state regulations, still have significant influence in Vietnam's complex administrative environment. However, normative pressures are increasingly embedding values of responsibility and competence, while mimetic pressures promote circular innovations and technologies through international benchmarking. This paper contributes to circular economy literature, particularly in emerging economies, by highlighting that circularity transitions are fundamentally institutional rather than completely technology dependent.

papers.title: Sustainability Certification Adoption in Small and Medium Enterprises' Food Supply Chains: Using a Complexity Approach to Build up Foundations
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Adopting certifications in food supply chains (FSCs) is a common practice for sustainable management, including among small and medium enterprises (SMEs). This study investigates how SMEs in FSCs navigate the complexities of certification adoption for sustainable supply chain management (SSCM). An interpretive case study methodology was used to capture the experiences of seven SMEs in Italy. Results reveal the foundational elements of certification adoption, highlighting the influence of varied complexity principles across decision‐making layers. The study provides a fresh perspective on SSCM by revealing strategies that enable SMEs to navigate those complexities and embrace certification as part of their sustainable trajectory. Unlike previous studies that acknowledge certifications as being complex without elaborating on that, this study applies complexity theory to disentangle this concept and uncover how SMEs can manage certification adoption. Differentiating between SMEs, the findings present practical initiatives to facilitate smoother certification adoption processes.

papers.title: Business Strategy for a Greener Future: How Entrepreneurial Cognition and Networks Drive Environmental Innovation Diffusion
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Despite growing recognition of environmental challenges to sustainability, the diffusion of green innovation within entrepreneurs' social networks remains uneven, and the mechanisms by which entrepreneurial decisions are disseminated within these networks have not received sufficient attention. Therefore, this research aims to fill a key gap in environmental strategy studies and to explore the dissemination of green innovation within the entrepreneurial ecosystem. Drawing on data from 570 entrepreneurs, we used Gephi to construct a diffusion network and compared its characteristics with those of random and scale‐free networks using a Python‐based simulation. Python simulations with node‐removal tests reveal that lower perceived uncertainty, recognition of green value and strong social norms speed up diffusion. By integrating entrepreneurial cognition, diffusion theory and social network analysis, this study has deepened the understanding of the formation and dissemination mechanisms of sustainable business strategies within entrepreneurial groups. Our research findings indicate that entrepreneurial cognition (particularly the reduction of uncertainty and value cognition) plays a much greater role in shaping the dissemination of environmental strategies than does the network structure. The research results provide practical insights for policymakers, incubators and ecosystem designers, helping them accelerate the transition to environmentally sustainable business models.

papers.title: Transparency in Supply Chain Service Design: Assessing the Impact of Country of Seller and Country of Fulfillment Information
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT To combat counterfeit or unsafe products in retail supply chains, regulations require large online retailers to disclose seller‐specific information including the country of seller (COS) and the country of order fulfillment (COF). This supply chain transparency aims to empower consumers to make more informed purchasing decisions. Yet, the impact of disclosing such supply chain information to consumers—particularly toward the policy goal of deterring counterfeit purchases by informing consumers—is unclear. Drawing on signaling theory, we conducted a scenario‐based experiment to examine how COS and COF disclosures impact consumer perceptions regarding the likelihood of receiving a counterfeit product and willingness to purchase. Our results reveal the benefits of disclosing COS or COF information in reducing consumer expectations of receiving a counterfeit product and increasing purchase intentions. Yet nuanced insights reveal that consumer perceptions of a country influence their interpretation of COS and COF information. Specifically, the presence of a country associated with low product quality as either COS or COF negates the positive effects of a high‐quality country affiliation.

papers.title: Gender Similarity in Hierarchical Work Relationships: A Meta‐Analysis
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Hierarchical work relationships, such as mentoring and supervisor relationships, provide access to key resources that promote employee well‐being and effectiveness. As such, scholars have investigated factors that enable relational success, with gender similarity being a key consideration. Despite abundant theoretical explanations for the importance of gender similarity in promoting high‐quality relationships and improved work outcomes, the empirical evidence is inconclusive. To add conceptual and empirical clarity to this literature, we meta‐analytically summarize the associations between gender similarity and a range of interpersonal (i.e., perceived similarity, relationship quality, and support) and work outcomes (i.e., work attitudes, performance, and turnover intentions). Moreover, we draw from social identity theory, as a basis for understanding when—or for whom—gender similarity in hierarchical work relationships is beneficial. Findings reveal that gender similarity promotes perceived similarity and relationship quality, but not work‐related outcomes. Moreover, junior women report higher perceived similarity and support in gender similar dyads than men. Finally, junior men report higher relationship quality in gender similar dyads, whereas junior women report comparable relationship quality across gender similar and dissimilar dyads. We discuss the implications for gender similarity and managing hierarchical work relationships.

papers.title: “Menopausal, Depleted, and Nostalgic”: The Bittersweet Effects of Menopause for Women Leaders
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Menopause is a natural but underexamined female experience in work settings, with significant implications for women in leadership positions. Drawing on self‐regulation perspectives, we develop a conceptual model examining how menopausal symptom severity shapes women leaders' experiences at work. We propose that severe menopausal symptoms act as a regulatory stressor that depletes leaders' psychological resources, triggering nostalgia for a premenopausal self. Nostalgia, in turn, can give rise to dual regulatory responses, enhancing empathy for subordinates on the one hand and fostering psychological withdrawal on the other. In Study 1 ( N = 341), using critical incidents, we found that menopausal symptom severity increased leader empathy and psychological withdrawal through a serial mediation of depletion and nostalgia. Study 2, employing a causal chain experiment with novel manipulations, supported the positive effects of (a) menopause severity on depletion (Study 2a, N = 203), (b) depletion on nostalgia (Study 2b, N = 132), and (c) nostalgia on empathy but not on psychological withdrawal (Study 2c, N = 115). We discuss implications for understanding women leaders' health and bodily experiences at work.

papers.title: Institutional Investor Impact Across Asset Classes: Exit, Voice, and/or Denial of Unconditional (Re)financing
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Research Question/Issue The Voice versus Exit debate among institutional investors dissatisfied with corporate issuers remains narrowly framed: Academic inquiry is de facto limited to listed equities. This overlooks the role of governance in corporate financing, which due to refinancing cycles, represents a key lever for investors aiming to influence issuers. We investigate which impact mechanisms institutional investors can use across asset classes in stand‐alone or mixed strategies to incentivize corporate transition towards aligning with the Paris Agreement. Research Findings/Insights We propose a new investor impact mechanism— Denial of Unconditional (Re)financing —and contrast it with the classic Voice and Exit choices. Denial is the investor action around the time of issuance, affecting realized demand in the book building of each issue. Conditional refinancing (sustainability‐linked debt with legally enforceable covenants) is its intended outcome. We argue that denial of unconditional (re)financing has a direct cash flow effect which is particularly strong when the company needs to repay existing debt at maturity. We provide clinical anecdotal evidence for the feasibility of both stages: (i) For the conditional refinancing outcome, we document the over $300bn self‐declared sustainability‐linked bond market based on Bloomberg data, demonstrating that an enforceable conditional instrument exists at scale (ii) with respect to the denial of unconditional refinancing, we show that bond issuance volumes in the segment with maturities over 20 years have declined even for the top credit‐rated fossil fuel majors, a pattern consistent with constrained access to long‐dated unconditional debt. Theoretical/Academic Implications We extend Hirschman's Exit versus Voice framework with a third investor impact mechanism and map all three across asset classes and the stages of the (re)financing cycle. The conditionality of refinancing warrants further consideration. More generally, the governance of corporate financing via sustainability‐related covenants (akin to financial covenants) appears to be a promising area for future corporate governance research beyond studying shareholders. Practitioner/Policy Implications Institutional investors can use corporate (re)financing pressures to lever their influence by withholding fresh cash unless Paris Alignment is ensured via legally binding sustainability‐linked covenants. Issuers can use bond contracts to credibly align their financing with their transition plans.

papers.title: Rethinking Top Public Management Through Relational Dynamics: A Systems‐Informed Study of Senior Executives
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The complex nature of top public managerial work is widely acknowledged in theory but rarely examined empirically. Existing research has mostly analyzed bivariate relationships among core components of top managerial work in government, including managers' attributes, practices, outcomes, and contexts. Drawing on a systems‐based framework, we investigate how effective top managerial work unfolds as a complex relational practice. We analyze seven cases of long‐serving, distinguished Chilean senior executives through a comprehensive and process‐oriented lens, based on 27 semi‐structured interviews with the managers and members of their personal and professional networks. Our findings indicate how the relational dynamics in which senior public executives engage shape their managerial attributes and practices. Specifically, strategizing, motivation building, and technical expertise are best understood as emerging primarily through interactions within agencies and with external sociopolitical environments. These results qualify perspectives that explain senior public management effectiveness by overemphasizing executives' individual attributes and views, and underscore the need for personnel policies and governance environments that equip managers with the capacities called for by a systems approach to top public management.

papers.title: When politics shapes technology adoption: a cross-national study of chatbot acceptance
papers.abstract: Existing literature on chatbot acceptance has largely relied on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) or Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), often neglecting the broader political, cultural, and attitudinal factors that shape user perceptions. Drawing on a cross-national survey conducted across four countries, we confirm the explanatory power of TAM/UTAUT indicators, while uncovering new determinants rooted in political values and cross-national perceptions. Specifically, participants are more likely to accept chatbots originating from countries toward which they hold positive sentiments — a country-of-origin effect linked to evaluations of political systems and technological advancement. Moreover, political ideology and technological openness significantly influence acceptance levels, but privacy concerns play a surprisingly minor role, except that German and American respondents' concern about excessive data collection hinders the acceptance of chatbots. These findings suggest that chatbot adoption is not merely a matter of technological functionality but also of political perception and cultural trust.

Swim Bladder Inflation in Fish: A Sensitive Endpoint for Risk Assessment and Mechanistic Research
papers.abstract: Abstract The swim bladder is a vital organ in many bony fish, playing an essential role in buoyancy regulation, position control in water and consequently survival. Ultimately, its potential malfunctioning may affect foraging efficiency, predator avoidance, and therefore population fitness. Nevertheless, proper swim bladder inflation is rarely systematically recorded as an endpoint in fish toxicity studies, regardless of the chemical class or mode of action under investigation. This represents a missed opportunity to detect sensitive sublethal effects and accumulate mechanistic evidence across studies. This paper therefore argues for the systematic inclusion of swim bladder inflation measurements in experimental designs that assess chemical exposure or manipulate neural and endocrine function. We highlight the biological basis of swim bladder development and inflation, summarize the growing body of evidence indicating its sensitivity to various chemical contaminants and pharmacological agents, and discuss its potential as an integrative indicator linking endocrine, metabolic, and neurobehavioral processes. We also identify key practical and methodological considerations for incorporating this endpoint into standardized tests, including timing, observation methods and species applicability. Incorporating this endpoint in studies ranging from ecotoxicological testing to neurodevelopmental and behavioral experiments could enhance the mechanistic interpretation of results, improve the detection of subtle sublethal effects and strengthen the ecological and physiological relevance of fish-based research.

papers.title: Machine-Learning-Assisted Auto-Fluorescence Cell-Sorting-Based Fast Differentiation and Quantification of Extracellular Polymeric Substances in the Microalgae and Bacteria Consortium
papers.abstract: Abstract Extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) are crucial in microalgae-bacteria consortia (MBC)-based wastewater treatment. Revealing the roles of EPS depends on reliable and accurate differentiation, extraction, and quantification of EPS from microalgae and bacteria in the MBC. Autofluorescence-based cell sorting (AFCS) coupled with thermal extraction can achieve the above goals, but it is time-consuming and costly, and invoves unignorable EPS loss (0.4–3.9%) during cell sorting. In this work, the raw data of microalgae (3.42 ± 0.14 mg/g TSS – 52.38 ± 0.47 mg/g TSS) and bacteria (2.95 ± 0.17 mg/g TSS – 48.94 ± 0.21 mg/g TSS) EPS from a series of MBC are obtained using AFCS with thermal extraction. Machine learning regression models are applied for microalgae and bacteria identification, and EPS concentration simulation and prediction. Results showed that, based on the total EPS concentrations and the fluorescence scattering characteristics (obtained from flow cytometry) of the MBC before and after heating, machine learning regression models enabled accurate prediction of EPS concentrations from microalgae (k-Nearest Neighbors, R2 = 0.975, P < 0.001) and bacteria (eXtreme Gradient Boosting, R2 = 0.953, P < 0.001) in the MBC, without cell sorting or EPS loss. This study provides an innovative method for rapid and accurate quantification of total EPS in microalgae and bacteria without requiring physical separation of the MBC, thereby laying a crucial foundation for in-depth analysis of EPS-based interaction mechanisms and functional regulation of microalgae and bacteria within the MBC during wastewater treatment.

Affective Polarization, Media Outlets, and Opinion Dynamics
papers.abstract: Abstract We study opinion dynamics in a social network consisting of two groups. Agents update their opinions by conforming to members of their own group while rejecting the views of the opposing group (affective polarization), and by listening to a media outlet that may provide biased information. We characterize the long-run opinions and identify when affective polarization and media bias lead to ideological polarization, persistent disagreement, or failures of learning. We also derive when information interventions or censorship improve the accuracy of average opinions} and reduce disagreement, and when they backfire: better information helps only under specific media bias configurations and when directed to the agents we identify as most effective at propagating it through the network.

papers.title: Local Shocks and Regional Dynamics in an Aging Economy
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies how population aging shapes regional adjustment to local shocks. I develop a dynamic spatial general equilibrium model that incorporates aggregate demographic change, life‐cycle variation in migration and employment choices, and forward‐looking investment in local capital. Applying the model to Japan, I find that aging can mitigate welfare losses from a negative local shock. Although older populations are less mobile, reduced outmigration sustains local capital demand and slows capital disinvestment, limiting declines in labor productivity. An extension illustrates the model's use for post‐disaster policy evaluation, highlighting a potential tradeoff between spatial equity and aggregate welfare.

papers.title: Does Digitalization Widen Labor Income Inequality?
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We develop a growth model that endogenizes the occupational choice of workers with different ability levels to study how digitalization affects labor income inequality. The framework incorporates digitalization's multifaceted effects on the economy: (i) it influences economic growth through automation, and (ii) it affects labor income inequality through labor productivity (demand side) and labor time modulation (supply side). We examine how these channels influence wage inequality between skilled and unskilled workers, within each skill group, and economy‐wide. The analysis reveals that digitalization's impact on labor income inequality—whether exacerbating or mitigating disparities—depends on the inequality metric employed.

papers.title: Assessing the Environmental, Economic and Social Impacts of a Greenhouse Gas Emission Tax in Swiss Agriculture
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Agriculture accounts for about one fifth of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, making mitigation a key policy priority. Although policymakers are increasingly considering market‐based approaches such as taxes, their broader impacts remain insufficiently assessed. This study examines the environmental, economic and social impacts of a GHG tax on Swiss agriculture. Using the agent‐based sector model SWISSland, representing 3077 farms and capturing heterogeneous responses to taxation and structural change, we simulate tax levels of 100, 200 and 300 CHF/tCO 2 eq for 2024–2030. We consider three mitigation pathways: technical measures, structural changes in land use and livestock numbers, and farm exits. We assess their impacts on GHG emissions, nitrogen surpluses, biodiversity, farm income, food production and food security. A GHG tax activates abatement mechanisms and induces dairy herd reductions, grassland extensification, shifts towards crop production for direct human consumption, and livestock farm exits. At 100 and 200 CHF/tCO 2 eq, emission reductions are mainly driven by technical measures, whereas at 300 CHF/tCO 2 eq they increasingly result from structural adjustment, including livestock farm exits and land reallocation to less emissions‐intensive production. A tax of 100 CHF/tCO 2 eq reduces emissions by 5%, while higher tax rates achieve greater reductions but increase sectoral income losses from 13% to 25%. Food self‐sufficiency and calorie production remain stable. The model also shows environmental co‐benefits, including lower nitrogen surpluses and increased biodiversity areas. These findings highlight synergies and trade‐offs across sustainability dimensions and suggest that redistributing tax revenues could mitigate adverse effects and improve policy outcomes, while enhancing the policy's social acceptability.

papers.title: Immigration and crimes against natives: the 2015 refugee crisis in Germany
Culture Promotion, Information Disclosure, and Firm Value: Evidence From Confucius Institutes
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Using the staggered establishment of Confucius Institutes in the United States, which promote underrepresented Chinese culture in local communities, we examine the nexus among culture promotion, information disclosure, and firm value. We find that the value of treatment firms (i.e., firms headquartered near a Confucius Institute) decreases significantly after the establishment. Our results are consistent with the argument that culture promotion in local communities impedes firm value by eroding local social capital. Moreover, firms with better information disclosure are resilient to the decline of firm value. We also observe a significant increase in nonmandatory disclosures, while mandatory disclosures remain unchanged. Our results are not likely driven by the change in local economic conditions.

papers.title: Choosing Startup Investors: Does Gender Matter?
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We investigate whether startups respond differently to male and female investors during outbound origination, a setting where female investors often report being marginalized by male founders. Using a randomized field experiment, we examine gender differences in startups' responses to investor outreach. Leveraging the rapid increase in outbound origination, our field experiment involves 40,572 startups sending identical unsolicited emails from fictitious male and female investors. Startups are substantially more likely to read emails from male investors, visit their websites, and attempt to make contact. This pattern is stronger for angel investors than for VC investors. Disclosing professional certifications increases a male investor's email's likelihood of being read but reduces the corresponding female investor's chances. A second experiment with 4836 recently incorporated startups reveals similar gender‐based choices. The findings provide large‐scale field evidence suggesting that gender‐based frictions in entrepreneurial finance may extend beyond founders' access to capital to investors' access to deal flow.

papers.title: Weathering hard times with bushmeat: rural household coping under rainfall shocks
papers.abstract: While bushmeat can be a crucial protein source for food insecure households, its consumption and trade raise significant concerns for both human health and wildlife conservation. Here we investigate how rainfall shocks influence rural households’ income from and reliance on bushmeat hunting. Drawing on data from nearly 8,000 rural households across 24 low- and middle-income countries, matched to gridded rainfall records and detailed agricultural season calendars, our study distinguishes between the effects of shocks depending on their type, intensity and timing of occurrence within the agricultural cycle. We mitigate endogeneity concerns faced in prior studies relying on self-reported shocks and cross-sectional data, by constructing a quarterly household panel survey integrated with objective, high-resolution data on climatic moisture stress. We find that dry conditions increase both bushmeat income and its share in total household income, particularly during critical agricultural periods. Conversely, wet conditions have the opposite effect, often decreasing hunting due to improved agricultural yields. However, these effects vary depending on the intensity of wet conditions. Additionally, we find heterogeneity in responses across socio-economic strata, as wealthier households tend to have higher bushmeat income during dry periods, likely due to better access to resources. The study increases our understanding of when and by whom climate stressors induce greater wildlife offtake, providing important insight for targeted development and conservation policy.

papers.title: The Effectiveness of Carbon Pricing: A Global Evaluation
papers.abstract: Abstract We estimate the effect of the staggered adoption of carbon pricing policies across the globe between 1990 and 2017 on per capita $$\text{CO}_2$$ emissions from fossil fuel combustion. We use recent econometric techniques robust to treatment effect heterogeneity. Our dynamic treatment effect estimations indicate gradual adjustments after implementation, resulting in a 19 to 23 percent decrease in $$\text{CO}_2$$ emissions after 10 years. These effects were primarily driven by resource substitution rather than improvements in energy efficiency and were not driven by short-term responses to carbon prices. Our results are robust to controlling for the potential effects of renewable energy policies. These results highlight the role of carbon pricing policies in steering medium-term expectations and complementing the climate policy mix.

papers.title: Effects of the New Revenue Recognition Standard (ASC 606) on the Informativeness of Earnings and Revenues
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We show that earnings announcements are accompanied by larger decreases in the bid–ask spread and the price impact of trades and a larger increase in price efficiency following the implementation of the new revenue recognition standard (Accounting Standards Codification 606 [ASC 606]). The implementation of ASC 606 is associated with a significant increase in the accuracy of analysts’ revenue and earnings forecasts and a decrease in the post‐earnings announcement drift (PEAD). These results indicate that ASC 606 has improved the informativeness of earnings and altered the effect of earnings announcements on the firm's information and trading environments.

papers.title: Medical Brain Drain: The Role of Job Attributes and Individual Traits
papers.abstract: Medical brain drain poses a major challenge for health systems, reducing physician supply and undermining public investment in medical training. Prior work examined migration flows and their macroeconomic determinants. This study uses a discrete choice experiment to assess how individual background and personality traits shape medical student intentions to migrate and whether job attributes are valued differently at home and abroad. We surveyed 527 senior medical students from 12 Italian universities between November 2020 and July 2021, using Italy as a pertinent case given high physician emigration and limited inflow of foreign-trained doctors. We find that students require compensation of around 30% of physicians' average starting salary to accept a job abroad rather than at home. Those from higher-quality schools or medical families, and those who are more altruistic, competitive, and risk-tolerant, require less compensation to migrate. Valuations of several job attributes also differ by location: at home, students value permanent contracts and professional development; abroad, they are willing to accept temporary contracts but reject under-skilling. These findings suggest that emigration may disproportionately involve the best-trained students. Policy simulations show that improving working conditions, job security, or professional development opportunities each substantially increases the predicted probability of choosing a domestic job, with salary increases having the largest effects.

papers.title: The promise and limits of industrial statecraft: the US response to China’s EV battery dominance
papers.abstract: In the literature on US-China techno-strategic rivalry, the semiconductor sector has received particular attention – a sector where the US is the incumbent leader. This paper shifts the focus to the EV battery sector to examine the rivalry when China is the emerging leader. In responding to China’s leapfrogging in EV batteries, the Biden administration pursued a strong industrial policy to build domestic capacity. While the US ‘industrial statecraft’ in the Biden era catalysed significant investment in battery cell production, project initiations in upstream segments, particularly in battery mineral processing, remained very limited. The relative success in cell production reflects an alignment between policy goals and corporate interests: subsidies make onshoring competitive and returns predictable. In upstream segments, by contrast, US policy largely remained ineffective at mitigating entry barriers and de-risking uncertain returns. In conceptualising the promise and limits of industrial statecraft, the paper argues that outcomes are mediated by a state-capital bargain, conditioned by macro-structural context and underlying sectoral dynamics.

papers.title: The language of leaving: Decoding defection via B2B customer language features
papers.abstract: Abstract Customer language data (e.g., online reviews, call transcripts) is widely available. Yet, research in B2B contexts is still in its early stages of analyzing a full range of customer language features to derive insight. Using an empirics-first approach, this research sequentially identifies robust and parsimonious language features in B2B customer data that are diagnostic of customer experiences and predictive of forthcoming purchasing decisions. The authors examine five categories of how business customers speak: sentiment, temporality, certainty, concreteness, and personal pronouns. Results reveal that sentiment and temporality consistently reflect customer experience and provide incremental predictive value of customer defections within request-for-proposal (RFP) decisions. The authors demonstrate this pattern across customers’ written (Study 1), spoken (Study 2), and pre-RFP (Study 3) language. These studies leverage empirical regularities to advance early-stage theorizing around psychological distance and language-based models of customer defection. Illustrating the managerial relevance of customer language features, findings show that in a customer’s collective communication prior to an RFP decision, a 1% increase in past focus raises the odds of a multimillion-dollar RFP defection by 8.4%. The research also equips practitioners to compute sentiment and temporality in customer language via large-language-model prompts and statistical code, facilitating resource allocation and prioritization of customer accounts.

papers.title: Leveling the Playing Field? Generative AI and Entrepreneurial Storytelling
papers.abstract: Cultural entrepreneurship research emphasizes the importance of storytelling and other cultural skills, yet recent work suggests that generative artificial intelligence (AI) levels the playing field for entrepreneurs lacking such skills. In this conceptual article, we challenge this view by outlining how the widespread use of AI tools likely leads to systematic changes in the institutional norms and expectations that shape entrepreneurial storytelling. Anchored in evidence-informed assumptions about average entrepreneurs’ use of AI, our theorization suggests that widespread AI adoption will lead to a homogenization in entrepreneurial storytelling—creating an evaluative environment that may require even greater cultural skills to navigate.

papers.title: The Benefits of Bundling Material Goods with Moderate Usage Complementarity
papers.abstract: Abstract Firms can bundle material goods together in various ways, including based on their usage complementarity (i.e., the likelihood that the goods are used together). While prior research has investigated the consequences of bundling products that are high (vs. low) in usage complementarity, the current research uncovers the benefits of bundling products that are moderate in usage complementarity (e.g., a coffee mug and a folding chair). Thirteen pre-registered experiments show that bundling products that are moderate in usage complementarity offers companies a unique advantage: Bundling these products prompts consumers to view them as relatively more experiential compared to bundling products that are low or high in usage complementarity and compared to their non-bundled components. This perceptual shift occurs because bundling products with moderate usage complementarity increases contextualization—the degree to which consumers consider the setting in which the products could be used rather than the use of the products themselves. It also changes consumer behavior in ways that can benefit firms (e.g., increasing purchase likelihood when seeking an experience). This research offers theoretical contributions to the bundling and material-experiential literatures and practical implications for companies interested in different bundling approaches and obtaining the advantages of heightened experiential perceptions for material goods.

papers.title: Media Review: Painted horses and floating signifiers: How China talked its way into capitalism
Integrated intelligence, autonomous operations, and trusted autonomy: AI-driven SCM performance in 2040
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI)-driven advancements may enhance supply chain management (SCM) performance across SCOR-DS processes by 2040, addressing the lack of systematic, long-horizon, cross-process evidence on AI-related performance effects. Design/methodology/approach A foresight-oriented real-time Delphi study assessed 13 projections developed from desk research and 12 semi-structured expert interviews, then refined in internal and expert workshops. Seventy experts rated each projection’s expected probability, impact and desirability, providing qualitative rationales. Results were analyzed using descriptive and consensus statistics, stakeholder comparisons, dissent diagnostics, qualitative coding and fuzzy c-means clustering, discussed through a complex adaptive systems lens. Findings Experts expect substantial AI-enabled SCM performance gains by 2040. Results indicate layered AI integration. Integrated intelligence emerges as the most plausible and impactful pathway, reflecting deeply embedded, predominantly assistive AI across planning, sourcing, fulfillment and returns. The autonomous operations pathway captures more selective, contested moves toward AI-led training, shared AI infrastructures, unmanned production and autonomous mass customization. Trusted autonomy is less directly impactful yet enables adoption by stabilizing data protection, contractual delegation and safety-related AI use. Assessments vary across SCOR-DS stakeholder groups, while country-based differences are negligible. Originality/value This study offers a SCOR-DS-wide, Delphi-based analysis of how AI-driven SCM performance enhancement is expected to unfold by 2040 as a layered, process-uneven configuration rather than a single linear trend. Through a complex adaptive systems lens, it shows that these trajectories operate through distinct mechanisms: schema and network-connectivity changes, shifts in agent composition and self-organization and governance-based boundary setting, thereby advancing theorizing on AI as an adaptive agent in supply networks.

Navigating Consumer Emotional Vulnerability in Services
papers.abstract: The growing awareness that consumer vulnerability extends beyond a person’s fixed status or identity is prompting concern to better understand the overlooked lived experiences of vulnerability that are under-theorized, poorly accommodated, and potentially harmful. We take the cascading mental health crises around the world as a critical impetus to conceptualize consumer emotional vulnerability (CEV) in service ecosystems and define it as psychological fragility that increases a person’s susceptibility to emotional harm in service exchange. We identify four dynamic tensions of CEV—invisibility, inescapability, uncertainty, and hypersensitivity that clarify its meaning and two dimensions (velocity and duration) that describe how it is organized. Our conceptual analysis embeds CEV within a network of antecedents, moderators, mediators, and consequences; derives a framework for service providers to implement CEV interventions; and synthesizes key theories related to intervention design. We propose new interventions grounded in the defining tensions of CEV and offer guidance for future service research seeking to promote consumer agency and reduce psychological strain. We contribute to service research by theorizing a pervasive yet overlooked form of vulnerability and offering actionable strategies to effectively support emotionally vulnerable consumers in service interactions and ecosystems.

papers.title: Managing Critical Frontline Agent–Customer Interactions: The Role of Service Recovery Explanations Across Artificial Intelligence and Human Agents
papers.abstract: Responding to service failures represents an acid test at organizational frontlines, where human service agents, alongside a growing share of artificial intelligence (AI)-powered service agents, engage in service recovery. Particularly when recovery outcomes are only partially favorable, customers may perceive these decisions as unclear or difficult to understand, potentially impairing their evaluation of the service encounter. This raises the question of whether explanations of service recovery decisions should be provided and, if so, how and by whom. Addressing this practical need and the related research gap, the article examines the effects of service recovery explanations on customers’ post-recovery reactions. Across three main studies and three supplementary studies spanning multiple service industries, the authors demonstrate that service recovery explanations can enhance customer satisfaction and choice by fostering perceptions of agent competence and warmth. These beneficial effects, however, depend on key contingencies: rationales outperform excuses and justifications, specific explanations tend to be more effective than general ones, and explanations provided by AI service agents can be more impactful than those delivered by human service agents. Overall, the article advances understanding of service recovery communication and offers actionable guidance for managing both AI- and human-mediated service recovery.

papers.title: Credit or Constraint: Postcolonial Feminist Ethics of Empowerment in Microfinance
papers.abstract: Abstract The microfinance industry has long been promoted as a “win-win” intervention in the Global South, producing both economic returns and social benefits. The industry disproportionately targets women as borrowers. In this paper, we argue that the ethical narrative of microfinance can fail to deliver—or actively obstruct—social gains for women by conflating the provision of credit with empowerment. Empowerment, we explain, cannot be reliably proxied via financialized metrics such as loan disbursement or repayment. Instead, it requires a connection between capital and agency that depends on women’s legitimacy as economic agents—a legitimacy shaped by cultural gender norms and, in postcolonial economies, by colonial legacies. By using a postcolonial feminist lens to critically analyze the contexts in which microfinance initiatives are enacted, scholars and practitioners can make visible the structural barriers which constrain women’s empowerment. We present a case study set in Ghana to demonstrate how capital, agency, and legitimacy can decouple. This project contributes to feminist business ethics by theorizing how structural and historical conditions mediate the relationship between credit and empowerment.

papers.title: Islamic Business Ethics, Muslim Feminism, and the Rhetorical Construction of Entrepreneurial Legitimacy: Evidence from Emirati Women
papers.abstract: Abstract Despite the United Arab Emirates’ state-led promotion of women’s entrepreneurship as central to national transformation, Emirati women entrepreneurs continue to face patriarchal norms that frame entrepreneurship as a masculine domain, rendering their entrepreneurial legitimacy both precarious and contested. Based on in-depth interviews, this study examines how women entrepreneurs construct entrepreneurial legitimacy within a patriarchal Muslim context, marked by a tension between empowerment rhetoric and gendered constraints. Drawing on Suddaby and Greenwood’s (2005) framework of rhetorical legitimation together with Islamic business ethics and Muslim feminism, we demonstrate how Emirati women entrepreneurs mobilise state-led empowerment and national transformation discourses to construct entrepreneurial legitimacy. We show how they align their entrepreneurship with national development goals through teleological strategies and with globalisation through cosmological strategies. We also reveal how they employ historical strategies that draw on both Emirati and Islamic history to legitimate their entrepreneurial pursuits. The analysis further reveals how Emirati, Muslim women entrepreneurs employ a Muslim feminist perspective, reinterpreting Islamic principles and business ethics to affirm their agency and inform their ontological and value-based strategies, thereby positioning their entrepreneurship as morally grounded and socially responsible. At the intersection of Islamic business ethics, Muslim feminism, and rhetorical legitimation, our analysis reveals how rhetorical legitimacy in patriarchal religious contexts depends on prior, often invisible, feminist ethical interpretation of religious texts, thereby positioning interpretative agency as a precondition for rhetorical legitimation. This study advances scholarship on women’s entrepreneurship, business ethics, and religion by demonstrating how legitimacy is constructed through interpretative work that reconciles ethical principles with rhetorical legitimation.

papers.title: Pricing on Carbon Transition Risks: Carbon Emission Trading and Stock Returns
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Relying on the phased rollout of the carbon emission trading (CET) pilot policy, we estimate a staggered difference‐in‐differences (DID) model to identify how transition risks induced by carbon pricing policies are priced in stock returns. Our results show that after CET implementation, stocks of CET‐covered firms command a significant carbon risk premium, providing empirical support for the carbon risk premium hypothesis. The premium arises from the market pricing of three distinct cash‐flow risks triggered by CET: operational uncertainty, credit deterioration, and information asymmetry. Meanwhile, divestment by rational investors serves as a key transmission channel for the premium. Dynamic analysis reveals pronounced time variation in the premium: it is significant during the initial period, persists for two years after implementation, then gradually attenuates, and reappears after the national CET launch. We further find that exposure to these risks is partially captured by established market factors (size/ SMB , value/ HML , profitability/ RMW ), indicating that carbon risk itself does not constitute a standalone pricing factor. Third‐party verified environmental ratings account for a substantial fraction of the cross‐sectional variation, whereas self‐disclosed environmental information by firms has limited explanatory power, indicating that information asymmetry constrains the market's ability to price carbon transition risks. This study provides microlevel evidence on how carbon policies are transmitted through capital markets.

papers.title: Cultural Theory, Political Ideology, and Burden Tolerance: The Role of Core Beliefs in Shaping Support for Administrative Burdens
papers.abstract: Administrative burdens embedded within many public policies are often politically contentious, such that core values and belief systems can drive either support or opposition. In this paper, we use survey data from US respondents to replicate and extend previous research on the public acceptance of administrative burdens in general. First, we confirm the measure's validity by examining its effects on beliefs across policies that range from highly polarized to less politically contentious. Second, we test the relationship between tolerance of administrative burden and cultural theory (CT) variables that tap into worldview orientations related to hierarchy, egalitarianism, individualism, and fatalism, which previous research has found predictive of policy preferences across a wide range of domains, even after accounting for political ideology and partisanship. We hypothesize that egalitarians and individualists will generally be less tolerant of burdens, while hierarchs will be more accepting of burdensome requirements. However, this effect varies depending on the nature of the burdens and how they relate to perceived threats for each worldview.

papers.title: Does Gender Budgeting Improve Women's Well‐Being, Equality, and Empowerment?
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The United Nations' fifth Sustainable Development Goal calls for gender equality and empowerment. Gender budgeting (GB) has been proposed as a potential mechanism to reduce gender disparities. This is a novel approach to budgeting that considers the impact of public spending on women and other underrepresented groups. Despite its growing popularity, spreading to over 80 countries since its launch in the 1980s, the effectiveness of GB remains less understood. This study tests whether GB has led to tangible improvements in women's well‐being, equality, and empowerment. We use an event study research design with staggered adoption to analyze data across 47 countries from 2000 to 2023. Our analyses of average and heterogeneous treatment effects reveal short‐ and long‐term impacts; notably, we find significant reductions in maternal mortality ratios and adolescent birth rates, as well as improvements in women's political empowerment.

papers.title: Improving Dietary Data Quality in Nutrition Studies: Development and Validation of an Explainable, Reproducible, Open Machine Learning-Assisted Framework for Outlier Detection in 24-Hour Recalls
papers.abstract: Twenty-four-hour dietary recalls (24HRs) are widely used in nutritional epidemiology, but repeated administration is required to capture within-person variability, introducing temporal dependence and challenges for data cleaning. Existing outlier detection approaches are largely static, manual, and based on adult-centric thresholds, limiting reproducibility and scalability. We developed and validated an explainable, reproducible machine learning (ML)-assisted framework to detect and evaluate implausible intake values in cross-sectional and longitudinal 24HRs and to generate AI-ready dietary datasets. The open pipeline integrates automated statistical detection using digitized National Cancer Institute 5th-95th percentile intake ranges, longitudinal interquartile range-based flagging, and ML-based rule explainability for outlier detection. Validation was conducted using the Microbiota, Growth, and Diet (MiGrowD) study in Ontario, Canada (126 children aged 8-12 years), and data from the 2015 Canadian Community Health Survey-Nutrition, a nationally representative sample of Canadian children and adults with repeated 24HRs (n = 15 216). Across energy intake and seven nutrients, 75 recalls containing at least one potentially implausible value were identified. In longitudinal data, the framework achieved > 77% sensitivity, 97% specificity, and 88% precision, outperforming the static method. This explainable data-driven framework improves data quality, transparency, and reproducibility, supporting scalable epidemiologic analyses using AI-ready dietary data.

papers.title: Early-life and Adulthood Eviction and Risk of Depressive Symptoms in Black Reproductive Age Women: Social Epidemiology to Combat Unjust Residential Evictions (SECURE) Study
papers.abstract: Residential evictions and chronic depression are worsening public health issues that disproportionately affect Black communities, though few studies have examined their association. Using qualitative and quantitative data from the (ANONYMIZED FOR REVIEW); 2021-2024; n = 1428). We used Poisson regression to estimate risk of high depressive symptoms (Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression (CESD) score 16+; Cronbach's alpha: 0.91) associated with 5 measures of eviction, by type, recency, and life-stage. We also used a content analysis methodology to mix responses to an open-ended survey question about the impact of childhood eviction (n = 349) with quantitative data to provide a deeper contextual understanding of the findings. Fifty-four percent (n = 775) of participants had CESD scores indicating they were at risk for clinical depression. We observed between 14-17% higher risk of high depressive symptoms among those who reported childhood eviction and recent and lifetime court-ordered eviction, compared to those who did not, in adjusted models (95% confidence interval range: 1.01-1.28). Qualitative data suggests that childhood eviction may be associated with risk of clinical depression through 5 novel potential mechanisms. The 20-item depressive symptom scale completely aligned with the qualitative themes. Future research, mental health interventions and policy solutions are warranted to achieve health equity goals.

Who Pays the Piper Calls the Tune: Funding Sources and Earnings Management in Charities
papers.abstract: This study examines how funding structures shape earnings management behaviour in charities and, in doing so, contributes to the nonprofit accountability literature. Drawing on resource dependence theory, we argue that funding sources create distinct accountability environments that influence managers’ incentives and opportunities to manage reported financial performance. Using a large panel of U.K. charities from 2007 to 2023, we investigate both accrual-based and real earnings management around a zero-surplus benchmark. The findings indicate that charities employ discretionary accruals as well as adjustments to fundraising and support costs to influence reported outcomes. However, these behaviours vary systematically across funding structures. Charities funded by sophisticated funders and those more reliant on donations exhibit lower levels of accrual-based earnings management, whereas service-oriented charities exhibit higher levels. The findings suggest that donor monitoring, fund restrictions, and accountability pressures play an important role in constraining financial reporting discretion and strengthening financial integrity within charitable organisations. papers.title: Pulse-based state-of-charge and state-of-health estimation of randomly retired lithium-ion batteries for second-life applications
papers.abstract: Retired lithium-ion batteries are an important resource for second-life energy storage, but their practical reuse requires rapid and efficient state assessment under unknown usage histories. To address this problem, we develop a pulse-based framework for joint state-of-health (SOH) and state-of-charge (SOC) estimation of randomly retired lithium-ion battery cells. A set of voltage-response features is extracted from short bipolar pulse tests and used as diagnostic descriptors. Based on these features, two machine learning models, extremely randomized trees (ExtraTrees) and a tabular prior-data fitted network (TabPFN), are employed for battery state estimation and evaluated using data from 270 retired cells that cover three chemistry types and four capacity classes. The results show that TabPFN clearly outperforms ExtraTrees and achieves mean absolute errors ranging from 0.0076 to 0.0306 for SOH estimation and below 0.01 for SOC estimation across all cell groups. To reduce the testing burden, a subset of SOC-dependent pulse tests is removed, and the missing feature points are reconstructed using interpolation methods. The reduced-test results show that near-baseline estimation accuracy can be retained even after removing 40%–70% of SOC-dependent pulse tests, depending on the target state and accuracy requirements. These results demonstrate a practical route toward faster, lower-cost, and scalable state assessment for second-life battery applications.

papers.title: Why Japan’s sovereign climate finance took a transition-bond form: bureaucratic mediation in an eco-developmental state
papers.abstract: This article explains why Japan organized its Green Transformation (GX) sovereign borrowing programme around a transition-labelled use-of-proceeds instrument despite its prior green-finance infrastructure and the international prevalence of sovereign green bonds. It develops a political economy account of instrument choice within an eco-developmental state. The article introduces accommodative instrument design as a process through which bureaucratic actors translate incumbent sectors’ conditional support for decarbonization into an instrument that combines a formal climate objective with gradual adjustment. The analysis draws on documentary evidence and process tracing of policy developments from 2017 through February 2024, including 21 semi-structured interview sessions with 18 participants. It finds that an alignment between the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry and transition-exposed industries helped shape eligible sectors and transition pathways. Environmental actors exerted less influence in the venues where the GX programme and its eligible uses were designed. The article contributes to distributive climate politics and policy-instrument scholarship by showing how mandate-differentiated agencies convert sectoral bargains into the rules of sovereign finance.
