papers.abstract: Abstract We experimentally study decentralized one-to-one matching markets with transfers. We vary the information available to participants, complete or incomplete, and the surplus structure, supermodular or submodular. Several insights emerge. First, while markets often culminate in efficient matchings, stability is more elusive, reflecting the difficulty of arranging attendant transfers. Second, incomplete information and submodularity present hurdles to efficiency and especially stability; their combination drastically diminishes stability's likelihood. Third, matchings form ``from the top down'' in complete-information supermodular markets, but exhibit many more and less-obviously ordered offers otherwise. Last, participants' market positions matter far more than their dynamic bargaining styles for outcomes.

papers.title: Why Veil? Religious Headscarves and the Economic Role of Women
papers.abstract: Abstract We show that the emergence of new economic opportunities that draw women away from their traditional domestic roles has significantly influenced the adoption of religious veiling. We measure the prevalence of veiling among young women across Indonesia's districts for more than two decades by hand-coding around a quarter million photographs attached to Indonesia's public high school registers. To establish causality, we exploit exogenous variation generated by international demand for Indonesia's products, interacted with the gender and sectoral composition of local industries. Districts exposed to stronger positive economic shocks---and thus greater economic opportunities for women---exhibit higher rates of veiling adoption. Our findings suggest that veiling facilitates young women's participation in formal labor markets while safeguarding their personal and social image in society.

papers.title: Labor Supply and the Pension Contribution-Benefit Link
Early-Career Discrimination: Spiraling or Self-Correcting?
The Market for ESG Ratings
Labor Associations: The Blue Wall of Silence
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We present a model showing that when the demand for labor services is inelastic and individual behavior is imperfectly monitored, a firm's employees may prefer to protect its shirkers and conceal information about peers' performance from the firm.

papers.title: Short‐Term Temperature Differences and Analyst Forecasts: Empirical Evidence From Chinese Financial Analysts
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether short‐term temperature differences experienced by financial analysts during corporate site visits impair their forecasting performance. Using a large sample of analyst site visits to Chinese listed firms, we find that larger short‐term temperature differentials significantly reduce forecast accuracy. This effect is stronger among less experienced analysts, who are more vulnerable to cognitive impairment, and during visits with limited temperature control, when physical discomfort is likely to be more severe. We further find that analysts exposed to larger short‐term temperature differences issue less optimistic forecasts, and that the temperature effect is stronger when visiting analysts come from the same institution but weaker when they come from different institutions. Overall, our study highlights the broader influence of short‐term temperature differences on analysts’ forecasting behavior.

papers.title: The Effect of Tick Size on Price Clustering: Evidence From the 2016 US Tick Size Pilot Program
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We examine the price clustering anomaly around the SEC's Tick Size Pilot Program (TSPP), which raised the minimum tick size from $0.01 to $0.05 for a group of small‐cap stocks. We find a significant decline in abnormal price clustering for treatment stocks relative to control stocks following the implementation of the TSPP. Importantly, upon the conclusion of the program, abnormal price clustering in treatment stocks rebounds to the levels observed in control stocks. Cross‐sectional tests show that the decline is most pronounced among tick‐unconstrained stocks (those with already wide pre‐TSPP spreads), as well as stocks with smaller market capitalization and limited analyst coverage. These patterns are broadly consistent with an attention‐based explanation and less supportive of liquidity‐based price uncertainty or negotiation mechanisms. Our findings inform ongoing debates on tick size policy and market design.

papers.title: The ontological dimensions of coastal mangrove reserve conflicts——insights from China
papers.abstract: In the context of escalating anthropogenic pressures on coastal ecosystems, this article employs a case study of one of China’s southeastern coastal mangrove reserves to interrogate the interplay between local communities and state authorities in natural resource governance from an ontological perspective. Through qualitative research involving 30 semi-structured interviews conducted between 2019 and 2023, we reveal how state, market, and community actors operate from fundamentally different – and often incompatible – understandings of mangroves. We trace a historical shift from a community ontology, where mangroves were perceived as socio-ecological commons buffering against flooding, to a market ontology through which mangroves were seen as barriers to marketized aquaculture development. While state intervention later curtailed market overexploitation, its regulatory, ecological ontology clashed with both the eroded community framework and the persistent market logic. Consequently, state governance, though justified by ecologically necessity, proved ontologically irreconcilable with the community’s original, relational approach. This study demonstrates that environmental governance conflicts are not merely about resource distribution but are rooted in conflicting ontologies and clashes between divergent world-making practices. It thus contributes a novel analytical lens for understanding governance conflicts in socio-ecological systems under competing state and market pressures, revealing that effective and just governance requires recognizing and navigating deep ontological divides, not just negotiating resource claims.

papers.title: Environmental conditions and the conversion of economic and relational resources into subjective well-being in China
From colonial extraction to structural adjustment: sectoral policy and unequal exchange in Sub-Saharan Africa
papers.abstract: Structural adjustment programs (SAPs) and their developmental impacts have been extensively studied. Literatures on neo-colonialism and unequal exchange suggest that SAPs represented a continuation or resumption of extractive colonial strategies, promoting the transfer of physical resources and value from post-colonial countries to developed countries. However, there has been little systematic analysis (1) exploring measurable similarities between colonial and SAP policies and (2) tying those similarities to patterns of neo-colonial exploitation and unequal exchange. This paper contributes to this gap by measuring similarities in agricultural, extractive and industrial sector policies between the colonial and SAP eras in ten Sub-Saharan African countries. I construct ‘sector focus’ indicators measuring the degree to which each sector was prioritised by policymakers in each period. I then assess (1) whether sectoral focus was similar across the two periods and (2) whether the observed patterns suggest that sectoral policies may have been used to promote unequal exchange by prioritising agricultural and natural resource extraction for world markets. While mixed, the results lend some support to theories of neo-colonialism and unequal exchange, with sectoral policies in both periods generally favouring agricultural and natural resource extraction for export and under-prioritising industrial sector activities relative to primary sector activities.

papers.title: Women, work and political economy: the Langham Place group’s use of the “dismal science” to advance middle-class female employment
papers.abstract: In the late 19th century, the Langham Place group, composed of middle-class women, advocated for social changes, especially in women’s work. They primarily demanded better education and greater access to professions at the time closed to women. This paper explores their use of political economy to address issues of limited labour market access for women, particular women of their social class, and to advocate for change.
papers.journal_name: The European Journal of the History of Economic Thought

papers.title: Resonance, Consonance, Dissonance: Explaining Divergent Responses to Entrepreneurial Setbacks
A Process Model of Managerial Phronesis in the Age of Generative AI
papers.abstract: Managerial phronesis involves first-hand experience that helps managers make moral and context-specific judgments at work in pursuit of the common good. Yet, as managers increasingly rely on generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) at work, many of these first-hand experiences are replaced by synthetic outputs. While past research has investigated how human–AI interactions alter managerial agency, we do not know why, how, and under which conditions GenAI affects the development of managerial phronesis. Answering these questions is important because phronesis underpins much of knowledge use in organizations. Consequently, we develop a baseline model that advances our understanding of how phronesis emerges in the absence of GenAI, introducing conceptual innovations that explain how new experiences are generated. We then extend this model by explaining why and how GenAI shapes the development of phronesis. Specifically, we theorize how GenAI can shift the development of phronesis toward what we term epistemic de-skilling, when conditions of perceived time pressure prompt cognitive offloading of tasks, and toward epistemic up-skilling, when conditions of accountability activate managerial reflexivity. We discuss the theoretical and practical implications of our model, and articulate an agenda for future research.

papers.title: Governing cross-border innovation: how country-specific director experience enables board-level boundary spanning in MNEs
papers.abstract: Abstract The internationalization of innovation is critical for multinational enterprises (MNEs), yet foreign subsidiaries often struggle to gain headquarters support for their innovations, while knowledge from subsidiary-country contexts remains underused in headquarters’ R&D. This study examines how directors with professional experience in a subsidiary country help boards govern these challenges. Drawing on boundary-spanning theory, we argue that such directors improve headquarters’ evaluation of subsidiary innovations and expand the scope of knowledge that headquarters draws upon. Using 8,264 firm-country-year observations for U.S.-headquartered MNEs from 2000 to 2021, we find that headquarters-based directors with experience in subsidiary countries are positively associated with both subsidiary innovations patented in the home market and headquarters’ use of subsidiary–country knowledge reflected in patent citations. Both relationships are amplified by knowledge distance, the divergence between home and subsidiary-country innovation systems, because directors are most consequential when headquarters’ cognitive frameworks are most misaligned with the subsidiary context. The findings contribute to international business, corporate governance, and innovation research by showing how board composition shapes where innovation is supported and which foreign knowledge enters headquarters-led R&D. Practically, MNEs can improve global innovation governance by matching directors’ international experience to the countries in which their subsidiaries operate.

papers.title: Spatial (In)equality and Entrepreneurial Ecosystem Policy: A Historical Analysis of the Scottish Highlands
papers.abstract: We built a theory on how entrepreneurial ecosystem policy benefits some places within rural regions while leaving others behind. In a historical analysis of the Scottish Highlands and Islands, 1965 to 1990, we compared policies that attract external resources from outside the region with those that embed resources within local communities. We found that resource-attracting policies not only generated higher economic output but also concentrated opportunity, drained peripheral areas, and increased regional fragility. Resource-embedding policies produced lower aggregate output but greater spatial inclusion and resilience. Our historical analysis identifies spatial draining, disempowerment, and empowerment as mechanisms through which policy shapes ecosystem outcomes over time.

papers.title: The impact of generative artificial intelligence on innovation: Evidence from software products
papers.abstract: Abstract Research Summary We study the impact of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) tools on product‐level innovation outcomes in the context of software products. Specifically, we illustrate how GAI can alter the direction of innovation by shifting the activities of developers away from generational innovation and toward original innovation, which may be new to the market but not necessarily more novel than previous innovations. We argue that this shift is driven by GAI's ability to facilitate tasks in both the ideation and implementation of software products, which enables some developers to create software products that were previously beyond their reach, while allowing others to reallocate their effort with respect to different activities. Our analyses in the context of browser add‐ons provide empirical evidence for these arguments. We discuss implications for innovation research and the generalizability of our findings to other domains. Managerial Summary Generative AI tools are changing how organizations innovate. Studying the Firefox browser add‐on ecosystem, we find that after ChatGPT's release, the number of new add‐ons increased by 34%, driven by both existing and first‐time developers. However, developers simultaneously reduced improvements to their existing add‐ons by 20%, redirecting effort toward new projects. While new add‐ons drew on a broader set of knowledge domains, they were not substantially different from what already existed. This suggests that generative AI helps developers efficiently combine existing knowledge rather than produce truly novel ideas. For platform managers and business leaders, these findings highlight that although Generative AI can democratize product creation and accelerate new product launches, it may require new strategies to maintain product quality and encourage genuine novelty.

papers.title: The Role of Rivals in Resource Picking from Factor Markets
papers.abstract: Abstract While we know that rivals' activities in product markets are an important source of information, we know little about how firms set expectations and react to information emerging from competitors in strategic factor markets. Our theoretical framework examines this question and explains how rivals' actions in factor markets shape a firm's own resource‐picking decisions. We consider that rivals can utilize a factor of production for different applications and distinguish three distinct rival actions that lead to strategic responses, which are explained by the mechanism of herding. Further, we consider that rivals' actions beyond information also convey competitive pressure that firms react to. We show that considering both informational and competitive cues determines whether firms respond by picking resources from factor markets or by building internal capabilities. The theoretical framework, hence, helps understand the role of rivals when firms decide to pursue new strategic factors and how they obtain such factors. We test our predictions using a fine‐grained dataset of new product development of global bio‐pharmaceutical firms from 1993 to 2018. Overall, the paper provides an important step towards a better understanding of how rivals shape firms' expectations in strategic factor markets.

papers.title: Taxes and Investment: Evidence from the “Halloween Massacre” of 2006
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the relation between taxes and business investment using the setting of an unexpected and economically significant federal corporate income tax rate increase in Canada known colloquially as the Halloween Massacre of 2006. This tax increase only applies to firms organized as income trusts, but not corporations. Using a difference‐in‐differences design, we find that investment by income trusts decreases about 0.67% for each 1 percentage point increase in the tax rate, translating into over $10 billion in reduced aggregate investment. In decomposing total investment, our results reveal that capital expenditures exhibit an immediate decrease while there is a delayed decrease in acquisition activity. Our results are concentrated in high‐investment income trusts that are most sensitive to the link between investment and taxes. Our study helps resolve conflicting prior results by providing robust evidence that tax increases have an economically significant and negative causal effect on business investment.

papers.title: Regulatory Balancing Acts: Lobbying and Medical Device Approval
papers.abstract: Lobbying is one of the primary nonmarket strategies firms use to shape regulatory outcomes, yet it is often treated as either an informational input that helps regulators make better decisions or a distortionary influence that undermines bureaucratic judgment. We develop a reputation-based theory of how regulators interpret lobbying under uncertainty. Because agencies are evaluated for both acting too quickly and acting too slowly, regulators use discretion over decision time to manage reputational risk. From this perspective, lobbying matters less as persuasion and more as sustained engagement that affects regulators’ confidence that foreseeable risks have been identified and addressed. We argue that the effects of lobbying depend on firm-level reputational cues that influence how regulators interpret lobbying activity, ultimately affecting the speed at which agencies grant regulatory approval. Using a novel dataset of FDA medical device approvals from 2002 to 2021, we find that lobbying is associated with faster approval on average. However, following product recalls this effect can reverse, suggesting that regulators treat interaction as misplaced confidence and increase scrutiny to reduce exposure to decisions that may become reputationally costly. By contrast, innovation reputation signals strengthen the approval-accelerating effect of lobbying by making timely approval more defensible to external audiences. Our theory suggests that the success of lobbying depends on how regulators interpret it in light of firm reputational cues, providing a reputation-based explanation for prior mixed findings on lobbying effectiveness.

papers.title: Staffing Leverage at the Audit Office and Audit Quality
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The PCAOB posits that audit partner and manager involvement, primarily through greater supervision and review (“oversight”) of audit engagements, is an important determinant and indicator of audit quality. We test this notion by empirically examining the link between staffing leverage, as measured by an office's ratio of audit partners and managers to audit employees, and audit outcomes from 2008 to 2022. We find staffing leverage is associated with lower rates of client misstatements, comment letters, and PCAOB inspection deficiencies, suggesting higher audit quality. When disaggregated, the association pertains to both partners and nonpartner managers. This relation is stronger for more complex clients and for offices with better management. We also find that staffing leverage measured at the firm level predicts audit quality, and that both office‐ and firm‐level staffing leverage are incrementally informative of audit quality, suggesting disclosing audit oversight metrics at multiple levels could be beneficial. However, the association between firm‐level staffing leverage and audit quality is statistically detected only within Big 4 audits. These findings suggest that audit committees, investors, and regulators can use audit‐office partner‐staffing and manager‐staffing leverage as an informative indicator of audit quality, particularly for complex engagements.

papers.title: A Bourdieusian perspective on internal activism and professional careers
papers.abstract: Professionals increasingly seek to use their careers to advance social and environmental change, yet we know little about how professional rules and career norms shape the forms that activism takes and its career consequences. Drawing on Bourdieu’s theoretical ideas, this study explores how professionals navigate internal activism around climate issues inside professional service firms (PSFs). Based on 58 interviews with mainly management consultants involved in internal climate activist groups, we identify three practice configurations: integrating activism for career progression, leveraging activism through career leadership and separating activism from organisational career for societal purpose . These configurations are shaped by field-level norms and by professionals’ dispositions, and are underpinned by two mechanisms, namely capital accumulation and capital conversion , through which professionals build and translate activism-related career capital. We demonstrate how the PSF field rewards commercially compatible forms of activism, while more resistant forms remain unrecognised in career terms. In doing so, we develop career-based mechanisms that explain why internal activism is commonly channelled into incremental rather than transformative forms, and highlight how, when pursued as an individual career project rather than collective action, internal activism is vulnerable to co-optation and can reinforce the very field structures it seeks to challenge.

papers.title: How Strategic Dialogue Enables Inclusive Execution
papers.abstract: Digital strategizing fails if organizations do not address a fundamental tension: inclusion creates buy-in but risks paralysis, while rapid decision-making enables execution but triggers resistance. Current open strategy research acknowledges this tension but provides no operational guidance for managing it. What is needed is a framework that operationalizes how organizations move between opening and closing in strategizing. This article identifies four dialogue forms and four orchestration approaches that enable strategists to balance stakeholder inclusion with strategy execution, rather than relying on intuition.

papers.title: Making Inclusion Work: Managing Engagement in Open Strategy
papers.abstract: Open Strategy’s promise of collective intelligence hinges on moving beyond inviting a broader set of actors into strategy-making to enabling and sustaining their engagement over time. This paper introduces the Engagement Matrix, a diagnostic framework that describes four contribution profiles in Open Strategy work, and traces how actors move across profiles as process conditions change. The analysis shows how these changing conditions produce broader and narrower engagement patterns across the process. The article explains how ability, motivation, and opportunity shape these movements and derives four design principles for managers and facilitators seeking to sustain meaningful inclusion throughout the process.

papers.title: The employee share ownership participation decision: An integrative review and agenda for future research
papers.abstract: Broad-based employee share ownership (ESO) plans are a widely used form of employee compensation. Past reviews have focused on employee attitudes and organizational performance, offering limited insight into why employees participate or the duration of their participation. Further, ESO is rarely considered as a dynamic phenomenon despite most plans being a continuing form of employee compensation. These omissions impede theoretical developments and advice to practitioners. In a review of 48 publications, across multiple disciplines, we propose an integrative framework that identifies the antecedents and mechanisms of three interrelated ESO participation decisions (i.e., buy, contributions, and holdings) within the context of employee stock purchase (and similar) plans. Building on this integrative framework, we propose an agenda for future research that we believe to be most promising for theory development and practice: the temporal dynamics of ESO participation, the influence of contextual (i.e., organizational-level) factors, and methodological innovations.

papers.title: The invisible presence of migrant women in tourism: labour at the intersection of gender, class and migration
papers.abstract: Purpose Although the tourism sector increasingly relies on migrant female labour for operational sustainability, this form of labour is frequently entrapped within a spiral of structural exploitation and invisibility. In this context, the purpose of this study is to examine the forms of invisibility of Asian migrant female labour in the spa units of hospitality establishments at the intersection of gender, class and migration, through the lens of precariat and intersectionality theories. Design/methodology/approach Designed as a qualitative case study, the research reached 31 Asian migrant women in Nevsehir using the criterion and snowball sampling techniques. Data collected via vignette-based interviews were analysed using content and descriptive analysis techniques with the support of MAXQDA software; findings were systematised using a code-sub-code-theory model. Findings The analysis identified 5 main themes, 22 sub-themes and 415 codes. The most frequently recurring findings were wage exploitation, communicative isolation, customer-induced harassment, compulsory emotional labour and status fragility. The research reveals that these elements confine women within a grip of “shadow presence”. Research limitations/implications Theoretically, this study advances the literature by synthesising precariat and intersectionality theories to decode how structural identities systematically marginalise migrant female labour. Practically, the study recommends that businesses adopt transparent policies against wage exploitation, provide language courses to address communicative isolation, offer psychological support/job rotation to address emotional labour burdens and enforce a “zero tolerance” policy regarding harassment. For policymakers, regulations that prevent informality and ensure legal integration are advised. Originality/value This research possesses methodological originality through the vignette technique, which facilitates access to sensitive data, and theoretical originality through the concepts of “shadow presence” and “parallax invisibility”, introduced to the literature via the synthesis of precariat and intersectionality theories.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

papers.title: Doubling Down on Brand Activism: A Multilayered Framing Contest Following Brand-Initiated Provocation
papers.abstract: While brands are often drawn into social controversies, the public debates that follow brand‑initiated provocations remain understudied. We examine how public debate evolves when activist brands engage in conflict framing—intentionally casting an issue as a conflict of frames. Based on a frame analysis of a public debate that followed a brand’s attempt to provoke deliberation about entrenched societal practices with significant climate impacts, we develop a model of brand activism as a multilayered debate. The model shows, on one hand, stakeholder reactions that criticize the brand activism campaign across multiple layers of frames and, on the other hand, the brand’s steadfast commitment to foreground its conflict frame—milk as an environmental and sociopolitical issue. We advance theorizations of framing and engagement strategies in contested contexts by showing how brand–stakeholder interactions change following conflict framing grounded in defiance, and we identify four doubling-down tactics: rebutting , retaliating , redirecting , and rebelling .

papers.title: “Caste at Work”: Caste Work and Reflexivity to Maintain and Resist Caste in Organizations
papers.abstract: Despite growing scholarly attention to caste within management and organization studies, an understanding of how caste is maintained and resisted in organizations is limited. We theorize caste as a social-symbolic object defined by purity—hierarchical, ritualistic, and boundary purity. Using social-symbolic work, we theorize caste work and its three forms at multiple levels: purity work, dehumanizing work, and caste defiance work. Building on this, we develop a typology of caste actors that illuminates the underexamined role of reflexivity in the maintenance and resistance of caste in organizations across the globe. Through such theorizing, we contribute to existing scholarship on social-symbolic work by providing a conceptual expansion beyond previously identified forms and highlighting broader implications in how other forms of social-symbolic work can be conceptualized. We also contribute to the literature on inequality by offering insights on work that resists and challenges caste, which has implications for more inclusive organizational practices.

papers.title: Goodwill Bubbles in Emerging Markets: Can Clan Culture Serve as an Informal Circuit Breaker?
papers.abstract: This paper takes Chinese A-share listed companies from 2012 to 2024 as the research sample to examine the governance effect of clan culture, a local informal institution, on excess goodwill from mergers and acquisitions (M&As). The study finds that enterprises located in regions with a stronger clan culture have a significantly lower level of excess goodwill generated in M&As. Mechanism tests reveal that clan culture operates through two channels: by easing financing constraints, it curbs managers’ incentive to signal growth via high-premium acquisitions, thereby reducing M&A premiums; and by attracting analyst coverage and improving information transparency, it mitigates managerial opportunism in M&A pricing. The moderating effect test shows that digital transformation amplifies the governance role of clan culture by improving the enforceability of reputation-based constraints, while family control weakens this effect by alienating clan networks and turning them into instruments for private benefit heterogeneity analysis reveals that the mitigating effect is more pronounced for non-state-owned enterprises, firms with lower audit quality, M&As with performance commitments, non-green M&A transactions, firms with limited M&A experience, firms in the decline stage of their life cycle, and firms located in southern China. Economic consequence tests demonstrate that by suppressing excess goodwill, clan culture significantly enhances firms’ long-term market value, improves future performance stability, reduces financial distress risk, and promotes stronger social responsibility performance.

papers.title: Modifying the Corporate Objective to Improve Social Welfare: The Case of Employee Layoffs
papers.abstract: This article defends the notion that the appropriate moral foundation of economic systems is the improvement of social welfare, a prescription based on utilitarian moral philosophy. It further demonstrates that, in the case of employee layoffs, the widely accepted corporate objective – shareholder wealth maximization (SWM) – does not reliably lead to improved social welfare. For many of the large and important firms in the corporate economy, adoption of a version of SWM, modified to include compensation for laid-off employees in company shares in amounts determined through negotiations , would virtually guarantee shareholder gains while (at minimum) holding employees harmless, resulting in a Pareto Improvement in social welfare. The article concludes with a “roadmap” for extending the application of the modified objective to other stakeholders and, in the process, developing a corporate objective that would lead to improved social welfare overall.

papers.title: Navigating the gray rhino: The impact of technological path heterogeneity on profitability
Environmental management accounting and sustainability context in the management commitment–performance relationship: a meta-analysis
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines the relationship between management commitment and organizational performance and assesses whether this relationship varies across contextual and organizational conditions. In particular, the study evaluates the potential moderating roles of national sustainability, environmental management accounting (EMA), performance type (environmental versus non-environmental) and firm size. Design/methodology/approach A meta-analysis was conducted using 47 independent samples comprising 14,163 observations drawn from empirical studies across multiple industries and countries. Effect sizes were aggregated to estimate the overall relationship between management commitment and organizational performance. Subgroup analyses were then performed to test whether this relationship differs across sustainability contexts, EMA-related study groupings, performance types and firm size categories. National sustainability was operationalized using a sustainability index derived from the World Economic Forum's Future of Growth Report (2024). Findings The results reveal a significant positive overall association between management commitment and organizational performance. However, subgroup analyses indicate that this relationship remains broadly consistent across high- and low-sustainability contexts, environmental versus non-environmental performance outcomes, SMEs versus large firms and EMA-related study groupings. None of the examined factors shows statistically significant moderating effects, suggesting that the positive influence of management commitment on performance may be relatively stable across these contexts. Practical implications The findings highlight the importance of management commitment as a broadly effective driver of organizational performance across diverse contexts. While sustainability-oriented practices and EMA remain important managerial tools, the results suggest that strengthening managerial commitment itself may be a more universally reliable mechanism for improving organizational outcomes. Originality/value This study provides the first comprehensive meta-analytic synthesis of the relationship between management commitment and organizational performance while systematically examining the potential moderating roles of sustainability context, EMA, performance type and firm size. By integrating evidence across prior empirical studies, the findings offer a robust pooled estimate of this relationship and challenge assumptions that contextual factors necessarily strengthen or weaken the commitment–performance link.

papers.title: The Effects of Prosocial CEOs on Auditors’ Risk Assessments: Evidence from Audit Pricing
papers.abstract: Synopsis The research problem The study explores whether auditors adjust their audit fees in response to the presence of prosocial CEOs. The research aims to understand how the ethical traits of CEOs influence auditors’ risk perceptions and, consequently, audit pricing. Motivation or theoretical reasoning The study is motivated by the broader discussion of ethical leadership and its impact on corporate governance. Leveraging upper echelon theory, which suggests that the personal characteristics of top executives can profoundly influence organizational outcomes, the research examines how these traits affect auditors’ perceptions and actions. Test hypothesis The study tests the hypothesis that prosocial CEOs are associated with lower audit fees, as auditors perceive them to have lower business and audit risks. Target population The study analyzes a sample of S&P 1500 firms over the period from 2004 to 2016, excluding financial firms due to their unique accounting practices. Adopted methodology The methodology involves statistical and econometric analyses of audit fees against a range of control variables, such as firm size, operational complexity, and CEO traits. Prosocial CEOs are identified based on their consistent personal charitable donations throughout their tenure. Analyses Empirical analyses include regression models to estimate the impact of prosocial CEOs on audit fees, controlling for various firm and executive characteristics. Findings The findings reveal that firms led by prosocial CEOs tend to pay audit fees that are approximately 5% lower on average, equating to significant cost savings. Further analyses suggest that these reduced fees are driven by prosocial CEOs’ abilities to mitigate agency issues and reduce firm-specific business and audit risks. In addition, the negative relationship between prosocial CEOs and audit fees is particularly pronounced in controversial and socially sensitive industries, where environmental, social, and governance (ESG) risks significantly impact earnings uncertainty.

papers.title: Aspirations in duality: how upward social cohesion shapes the social fabric of the bottom of the pyramid consumers
Don’t treat me like a child! The influence of over-attentive service on adult identity-associated consumption choices
Tail-driven asymmetries in sustainable finance: SMEs, ESG, and energy innovation under market stress
When p=0: Governance failure and pure social diffusion in rivalrous technology adoption
Public procurement for social innovation: Building a collaboration logic through interactive spaces
papers.abstract: Public procurement of innovation is increasingly expected to address complex societal challenges, yet research has focused mainly on technological and environmental innovation, paying limited attention to social problems and innovations. Less is known about how public procurement can support social innovation in service settings where solutions cannot be specified in advance and innovation depends on reconfiguring cross-sectoral relations, roles, and practices. This study examines how public procurement can support social innovation through the organisation of interactive spaces that enable institutional work and the development of a collaboration logic. Drawing on institutional theory, we analyse a longitudinal case study of the Tesoma Wellbeing Centre in Tampere, Finland, where public, private, and third-sector actors jointly developed an integrated social and healthcare service model. The findings show how procurers deliberately orchestrated different forms of interaction over the procurement process, enabling actors to question established arrangements, develop shared goals and practices, and anchor them in governance and service delivery. Through this process, an impact-driven collaboration logic gradually emerged and became partially stabilised, reshaping actor relations, perceptions, and practices. We contribute to the research on public procurement and social innovation by explaining how the sequencing of interactive spaces across procurement phases can support social innovation in complex service settings.

papers.title: Customers’ disposition towards loyalty program engagement
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how customers’ inherent tendencies and capacity to engage with loyalty programmes (LPs) shape their actual engagement, and how this subsequently influences their engagement with and loyalty to retailers. Design/methodology/approach In Study 1, the components of loyalty programme engagement (LPE) are validated using data collected from 250 Australian supermarket retail customers. In Study 2, using data from 820 Australian supermarket retail customers the proposed research model is tested. Both symmetrical partial least squares structural equation modelling and asymmetric fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) are used to enhance the rigour of the findings. Findings Results show that customers’ disposition towards LP engagement, in the form of internal tendencies and capacity, are important drivers of LP engagement. In addition, results also show that LP engagement leads to retailer engagement and customer loyalty (both attitudinal and behavioural loyalty). fsQCA results show that combination of trust, commitment and perceived benefits is the key configuration whose presence or absence determines the enhancement or impediment of LP engagement. Research limitations/implications These findings will help retailers design LPs based on a better understanding of the factors (i.e. trust, commitment, perceived benefits and temporal and spatial price searches) influencing customers’ LPE. Practical implications Retailers should consider customers’ internal tendencies and capacity to engage with LPs. Importantly, retailers must aim to focus on a combination of perceived benefits, trust and commitment towards LPs when designing these. Originality/value The central role played by customers’ disposition towards LPE as a key driver of both LP engagement and customer loyalty represents an important contribution to the existing LP literature. In addition, providing the recipe for designing effective LPs provides another valuable and original contribution to the LP research.

papers.title: Coupled supply and demand forecasting in platform accommodation markets
papers.abstract: Tourism demand forecasting is methodologically mature, but it usually treats accommodation supply as fixed, exogenous, or slow-moving. This Progress in Tourism Management article develops a narrated, conceptually focused review of forecasting in platform-mediated short-term rental markets, where supply is elastic, decision-driven, and jointly shaped with demand through pricing, information design, host participation, and policy intervention. The article reframes realized booked nights as a constrained outcome generated by latent demand, effective supply, and matching frictions. It synthesizes tourism forecasting, revenue management, two-sided market economics, causal inference, and compositional time-series methods; articulates a three-layer coupling framework spanning intervention, behavioral, and informational channels; and uses a stylized model experiment to illustrate one supply-shock failure mode. The contribution is a theoretical and methodological map: where platform accommodation forecasting has developed, what remains under-specified, and how future work can validate coupled supply–demand forecasting. It does not attempt a completed comparative empirical evaluation.

papers.title: Orchestrating Sustainable Service Ecosystems
papers.abstract: Achieving and maintaining sustainability in complex service ecosystems is a pressing challenge for service firms. Yet, many sustainability efforts, like compliance-driven measures, remain incremental and fall short in the face of accelerating global crises. To create meaningful impact, service firms are called upon to act as change agents within their ecosystems and have been given a mandate to drive systemic sustainability transformation. However, many struggle to operationalize such a shift. We argue this is due largely to a lack of conceptual clarity of what sustainability in service looks like, how service firms can advance sustainability objectives, as well as how service firms should enable ecosystem-wide transformation. To address these questions, we conduct an integrative review of 467 empirical and conceptual studies published between 2018 and 2024 that explore sustainability in service. We introduce the concept of sustainable service ecosystem orchestration and provide a novel typology of four sustainable service orchestration ideal types. In doing so, we position sustainable service orchestration as a foundational concept to advance theoretical understanding of sustainable service ecosystems, guide future research, and offer practical pathways for service firms through a managerial roadmap of sustainable service ecosystem orchestration.

papers.title: Beyond Greenwashing: Governing Sustainable AI for the Common Good Through a Virtue Ethics and Human-Centered AI Framework
papers.abstract: Abstract As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes deeply embedded in human and organizational life, debates about Sustainable AI demand renewed ethical reflection. Current approaches often remain fragmented—separating AI for Sustainability, such as climate-mitigation applications, from the Sustainability of AI, including the intensive resource use and discriminatory effects of AI systems themselves—and lack a coherent moral foundation. This article addresses Sustainable AI as an integrated ethical concept, rather than focusing narrowly on either strand, and reframes it through the lens of virtue ethics, emphasizing human flourishing, moral agency, and the pursuit of the common good. Complementing this perspective with the Human-Centered AI (HCAI) paradigm, we develop an integrated governance framework that incorporates MacIntyrean categories of practices, institutions, and traditions while explicitly addressing the environmental, socio-cultural, economic, and organizational dimensions of the common good. In this framework, these four dimensions identify the substantive goods that Sustainable AI should protect and promote, while the micro (practices), meso (organizational and governance structures), and macro (cultural-historical traditions) levels specify the constructive conditions through which such goods are discerned, coordinated, and sustained over time. The framework illustrates how virtues can guide the responsible design, deployment, use, and oversight of AI systems. Our contribution is threefold: we advance Sustainable AI ethics by grounding it in virtue ethics and the common good; we extend business ethics by introducing a virtue–HCAI approach to governance; and we bridge theory and practice through a multi-level model that offers conceptual clarity and ethical orientation for long-term human flourishing.

papers.title: Social Practice Involvement and Its Impact on Social-Emotional Competencies: Evidence from Primary and Secondary School Students in Four Northwest Chinese Counties
Effects of Country Governance, Market-Oriented Institutional Quality, and Financial Development on Climate Action: Evidence from MENA Countries
papers.abstract: This study investigates the effects of country governance, market-oriented institutional quality, and financial development on climate change adaptation and mitigation, using data from fifteen MENA countries spanning 2002 to 2022. Results indicate that country governance improves both adaptation and mitigation across the board. However, high market-oriented institutional quality hinders both, suggesting that economic freedom reinforces fossil fuel dependence. Financial development yields mixed results. It undermines adaptation in low-income countries but aids both adaptation and mitigation in high-income countries. These results help policymakers tailor climate strategies by income level and guide the financial and institutional reforms required for MENA’s low-carbon transition.

papers.title: Innovative Leading Role of Chain Masters Along the Supply Chain
papers.abstract: This article examines how Chain Masters drive supply chain innovation. We argue that Chain Masters internalize innovation externalities through governance and resource channels, thereby mitigating vertical partners’ agency conflicts and resource constraints. Findings show that: (i) Chain Masters’ innovation significantly increases vertical partners’ innovation. (ii) Chain Masters play an innovative leading role in the supply chain through improving internal control quality, alleviating financial constraints, and increasing innovation efficiency. (iii) This leadership effect is weaker when Chain Masters are located upstream. Moreover, Chain Masters’ innovation increases vertical partners’ total factor productivity by encouraging incremental innovation.

papers.title: Income Inequality and Household Default Risk in China: Measurement and Empirical Evidence
papers.abstract: Rising income inequality and household debt burdens increasingly threaten financial stability in emerging markets. Yet how income inequality affects household default risk remains underexplored, and existing measures of default risk often neglect asset returns, volatility, and portfolio composition. Using data from the CHFS, we apply the Merton model to estimate household default risk based on household asset allocation, returns, and volatility. The results show that household default risk ranged from approximately 3% to 5% between 2015 and 2019. Income inequality significantly increases household default risk. Mechanism analyses show that income inequality raises default risk by tightening credit constraints, increasing asset portfolio risk, and deepening social fragmentation. Heterogeneity analyses indicate that the effect is more pronounced among rural, low-income, and middle-aged households, as well as male-headed households. Further analysis suggests that digital financial inclusion can serve as an effective tool for mitigating the risk-enhancing effect of income inequality.

papers.title: How Does Digitalization Empower Tourism Development? Evidence from Digital Governance and Financial Accessibility
papers.abstract: With the continued digital transformation of the service sector, the digital economy has become an important force reshaping tourism development. Based on balanced provincial panel data from China for the period 2011–2024, this study examines the impact of digital economy development on tourism development and its underlying mechanisms. The results show that the digital economy significantly increases tourism revenue, expands tourist arrivals, and improves high-quality tourism development. Mechanism tests indicate that the digital economy promotes tourism development by enhancing government digital governance capacity and improving financial accessibility. Further analysis shows that tourism development plays a transmission role in the process through which the digital economy promotes consumption structure upgrading. By measuring tourism development from the dimensions of tourism revenue, tourist arrivals, and high-quality tourism development, and by integrating government digital governance, financial accessibility, and consumption structure upgrading into a unified framework, this study provides empirical evidence for understanding how the digital economy empowers high-quality tourism development.

papers.title: Financial Resource Allocation Efficiency and Internal Pay Gap
papers.abstract: Using panel data of Chinese A-share listed enterprises spanning 2010–2022, this paper examines the relationship between financial resource allocation efficiency and internal pay gaps. The results reveal several principal findings. Firstly, improvements in financial resource allocation efficiency significantly widen internal pay gaps. The research findings remain robust when concerns about endogeneity are addressed and multiple robustness tests are conducted. Secondly, mechanism analysis suggests that enhanced financial allocation efficiency primarily widens internal pay gaps by improving firm performance and strengthening management bargaining power. Thirdly, the heterogeneity analysis indicates that financial resource allocation efficiency exerts a stronger influence on firms with a lower degree of green transformation, higher external financing dependence, and non-state ownership, especially in the manufacturing sector and among capital- and technology-intensive enterprises. Fourthly, extension analysis shows that improving financial resource allocation efficiency only increases reasonable internal pay gaps without affecting excessive pay disparities. Consequently, it contributes to productivity improvements without exacerbating internal income inequality, thereby achieving a balance between efficiency and equity. Furthermore, the relationship between financial resource allocation efficiency and reasonable pay gaps is positively moderated by a combination of green policy tools, while individual policy instruments fail to yield significant moderating effects.

papers.title: How Does Regional Climate-Friendly Technology Innovation Affect Corporate Cash Holdings? Evidence from Chinese Listed Companies
papers.abstract: Regional climate-friendly technology innovation (RCFTI) can reduce carbon emissions and lower the carbon risks faced by enterprises. This study investigates whether and how RCFTI influences corporate cash holdings. Using panel data on Chinese cities and A-share listed enterprises from 2008 to 2022, we find that RCFTI significantly reduces corporate cash holdings. RCFTI indirectly affects corporate cash holdings by reducing agency costs and increasing long-term real investment. Furthermore, the reduction is more pronounced among enterprises with high short-term debt and those located in financially underdeveloped regions.

papers.title: Green Supply Chain Management’s Restraining Effect on Corporate Greenwashing
papers.abstract: Using a sample of China’s A-share non-financial listed companies from 2015 to 2023, this article empirically explores how green supply chain management (GSCM) constrains corporate greenwashing. Baseline results confirm GSCM exerts significant governance effects on greenwashing. Mechanism tests show GSCM restrains greenwashing by lifting environmental disclosure quality, boosting substantive green innovation and tightening internal and external supervision. Such an inhibitory effect is stronger for firms with higher supply chain concentration, greater supply chain resilience, dominant market status and better reputation. Further economic consequence analysis finds that GSCM-induced greenwashing reduction improves ESG performance, narrows ESG divergence, eases financing constraints, cuts supply chain risks and fosters new quality productivity. This article supplements relevant literature and offers empirical evidence for green industrial chain governance and high-quality economic development.

papers.title: The Effect of Public Pension Contribution Rate Reductions on Employee Wages: Evidence from China
papers.abstract: China’s 2019 reform cut the employer public pension contribution rate from 20% to 16%. Using a difference-in-differences design on panel data from A-share listed firms over 2014–2023, we examined whether these savings translated into employee wage gains. Estimates showed that the reform raised average wages by approximately 2%, implying a pass-through of about 24.7% of the employer cost saving and roughly half the advanced-economy benchmark. Mechanism evidence is consistent with two channels: a distributional channel operating through within-firm pay restructuring and a growth channel operating through eased financing constraints. Wage effects were concentrated among private, labor-intensive, and high-human-capital firms.

papers.title: Trade Uncertainty Under Geopolitical Risks: A Cross-Country Analysis of Mechanisms and Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: In recent years, geopolitical conflicts, economic sanctions, and strategic competition among major powers have continued to intensify, making geopolitical risk (GPR) an important external shock affecting global trade stability. However, existing studies mainly focus on trade policy uncertainty (TPU) or changes in trade flows, while systematic cross-country empirical evidence remains limited on whether and how GPR affects a country’s overall trade uncertainty (TU). To this end, this paper systematically examines important practical issues, including the mechanisms through which GPR affects TU, the moderating role of external openness, and cross-country heterogeneity. The results suggest that higher levels of GPR are associated with higher TU, potentially through increased economic policy uncertainty (EPU), reduced cross-border capital inflows, and greater exchange rate volatility. Further analysis indicates that higher levels of economic openness tend to mitigate the relationship between GPR and TU, whereas greater financial openness may amplify this uncertainty. Moreover, the relationship between GPR and TU varies across countries depending on their level of economic development, degree of regional integration, and industrial structure, with the association appearing particularly pronounced in developing countries, non-EU member states, and countries with more advanced industrial structures. These findings provide useful insights for maintaining the stable development of global trade and economic systems.

papers.title: Provincial Climate Resilience in China: Measurement, Spatiotemporal Evolution, and Obstacle Factors
papers.abstract: Using panel data for 30 province-level regions in mainland China from 2010 to 2022, this study distinguishes baseline climate-resilience capacity (CRI), observed climate pressure (CP), and pressure-adjusted resilience performance (AdjCRI). CRI and AdjCRI improved, while CP declined overall and regional disparities narrowed but persisted. AdjCRI exhibits positive spatial dependence, strong state persistence, and favorable neighborhood effects on upward transitions. Major capacity bottlenecks concern innovation conversion, environmental and resource governance, fiscal capacity, government implementation, and water-related infrastructure. The findings show that capacity-only measures may misrepresent realized resilience under heterogeneous climate pressure and support differentiated, spatially coordinated adaptation policies.

papers.title: Intermediary Institutions’ Collaborative Governance and Post-IPO Performance Change
papers.abstract: Based on Chinese A-share IPOs from February 1, 2004, to December 31, 2023, this paper examines whether intermediary institutions’ collaborative governance mitigates post-initial public offering (IPO) performance deterioration. To capture the collaborative governance mechanism, we construct an intermediary collaborative network and examine the impact of network centrality, which represents an intermediary’s structural position within the network, on post-IPO performance. Results indicate higher network centrality significantly mitigates post-IPO performance deterioration for issuer firms, and this effect is primarily driven by cross-intermediary collaboration. The governance effect arises from reputational discipline, enhanced independence, and information advantages. Moreover, firms engaging more central intermediaries exhibit lower pre-IPO earnings management, reduced prospectus complexity, and fewer disclosure violations. Finally, the effect is more pronounced in firms with weaker internal governance, those listed under the registration system, those with higher analyst coverage, and state-owned enterprises. These findings highlight the role of intermediary collaborative networks in IPO governance in an emerging market.

papers.title: Occupational AI Substitution Risk, Skill Mismatch, and Individual Income Inequality: Evidence from China
papers.abstract: This study examines how occupational exposure to artificial intelligence substitution risk is associated with individual income inequality in China. Using China Family Panel Studies data matched with occupation-level AI substitution risk and O*NET skill-demand information, we decompose income inequality into overall, within-occupation, and between-occupation components based on Kakwani’s relative deprivation framework. The results reveal a dual distributional effect. AI substitution risk is negatively associated with within-occupation inequality, suggesting that AI-related task standardization may compress income differences among workers in similar occupations. However, it is positively associated with between-occupation inequality and overall inequality, indicating that AI substitution risk may widen income gaps across occupational groups. Mechanism tests show that AI substitution risk is associated with lower skill shortage but higher skill surplus, suggesting that skill adjustment under technological pressure may generate both better within-occupation matching and broader human-capital underutilization. Heterogeneity analysis further shows that older workers and flexible workers are more vulnerable to the inequality-enhancing effects of AI substitution risk. These findings suggest that AI does not reshape income inequality in a uniform direction, but reorganizes labor-market inequality through occupational structure, skill mismatch, and worker vulnerability.

papers.title: AI Development and Corporate Capital Allocation–Evidence from Shadow Banking
papers.abstract: AI as a key driver of the new wave of technological revolution, is fundamentally reshaping corporate resource allocation. This study finds that AI development significantly promotes corporate shadow banking. Second, mechanism analysis shows that AI development increases corporate shadow banking by promoting data assetization and enhancing firms’ risk-taking. Third, heterogeneity analysis indicates that this positive effect is more pronounced among firms with higher ownership concentration, non-state-owned enterprises, high-tech firms, and labor-intensive firms. This study provides policy implications for improving AI governance and preventing systemic financial risks.

papers.title: The Land–Debt Feedback Loop: Land Finance Contraction, Endogenous Collateral, and Macroeconomic Amplification in China
papers.abstract: Whether falling asset prices and public debt risk can form a self-reinforcing feedback loop is a central question in macro-finance. China’s land finance model, under which local governments fund public expenditure through land conveyances and land-collateralized borrowing, has contracted sharply since 2021, offering a relatively clear institutional setting for examining this mechanism. Standard models let collateral values move with asset prices but fix the loan-to-value (LTV) ratio, precluding endogenous feedback between borrowing capacity and asset prices. We develop a DSGE model in which a local government’s effective LTV responds endogenously to land-price deviations through a confidence multiplier, so that a land-price decline simultaneously erodes collateral value and tightens financing capacity, compressing fiscal expenditure and real activity and further weakening land demand. Calibrated to Chinese institutional data for 2010–2024, the model yields three findings. First, the endogenous collateral constraint substantially amplifies the cumulative macroeconomic effects of adverse shocks, supporting the existence of the feedback loop. Second, feedback strength is convex: beyond a threshold, risk accelerates disproportionately. Third, policies that directly weaken the feedback chain, namely land-price stabilization and reaffirming implicit guarantees, dampen macroeconomic volatility more effectively than fiscal expansion alone, which can set a floor under output but leaves the feedback chain intact.

papers.title: Regulation by Rating: Can Market-Based Rating Improve Corporate Non-Financial Performance?
papers.abstract: Corporate non-financial performance is increasingly attracting global attention. This study examines whether inclusion in SynTao Green Finance’s ESG rating system affects the non-financial performance of Chinese listed companies. Employing a staggered difference-in-differences framework over the period 2009–2020, we find that market-based ratings significantly improve corporate non-financial performance, a result that holds across a range of robustness checks. The effect operates through a sequence of market responses, ratings raise media attention to rated corporations, which lowers their financing costs and motivates green innovation, thereby aligning economic and social value. In addition, the effect is stronger for corporations in regions with higher marketization and greater fiscal spending on science and technology, and for state-owned enterprises. These findings show how market-based ESG ratings can function as an informal governance mechanism that enhances corporate non-financial performance in emerging markets.

papers.title: Factor Risk Spillovers in a Policy-Sensitive Market: The Role of EPU in China
papers.abstract: This study examines risk spillovers in China’s equity market from a factor-network perspective by constructing a TVP-VAR connectedness system that links six pricing factors with four disaggregated economic policy uncertainty (EPU) indices. The baseline 2005–2021 analysis identifies a structural break around 2014–2015, after which HML replaces RMW as the leading net transmitter in the factor network. On the EPU side, monetary policy uncertainty (MPU) and exchange-rate policy uncertainty (ERPU) emerge as the most persistent net transmitters. Further evidence shows that MPU is more closely associated with changes in the total spillover index (TSI), whereas ERPU is more closely related to changes in factor-level transmitter–receiver roles. A supplementary aggregate-EPU extension through 2024 serves as a factor-side check for the post-2021 period.

papers.title: Interaction and Transition Between Administrative and Market-Based Policies in Corporate Low-Carbon Transformation: An Evolutionary Game Analysis
papers.abstract: This study examines how administrative regulation and market-based mechanisms jointly shape corporate low-carbon transformation in emerging markets. A tripartite evolutionary game model involving the government, high-carbon firms, and low-carbon firms is developed to analyze evolutionary paths and stable equilibria under different policy combinations. The model is calibrated using power-sector data from China’s national emission trading system and environmental regulation. Analytical results show that policy choice is cost-driven: administrative regulation dominates when enforcement costs are lower than carbon market costs, while declining market costs promote a transformation to market-based governance. For high-carbon firms, higher inspection probability is more effective than stringent penalties in inducing early transformation, whereas market mechanisms later encourage proactive transformation. Low-carbon firms’ expansion is more strongly influenced by transaction frictions and benchmark carbon intensity than by carbon prices. Simulation results based on calibrated parameters indicate that administratively driven and high-carbon transformation-driven pathways are more stable than market-driven pathways. These findings suggest that emerging markets should adopt a stage-based balance between administrative oversight and carbon market institutions.

papers.title: Common Shareholders Along the Supply Chain and Suppliers’ Working Capital Management: Evidence from China
papers.abstract: Using a sample of Chinese non-financial A-share listed companies from 2007 to 2023, this study investigates how common shareholders along the supply chain (CSSC) influence suppliers’ working capital management. The empirical results show that CSSC significantly reduce suppliers’ capital tied up in inventory and accounts receivable. Mechanism tests indicate that CSSC enhance working capital management mainly by improving supply–demand matching accuracy and customer relationship stability. Heterogeneity analyses show that the effect is more pronounced in periods of high economic policy uncertainty, among suppliers with weaker internal controls, and among non-state-owned enterprises. Moreover, the effects are mainly concentrated among controlling, institutional, and strategic CSSC. The economic consequences analysis indicates that improvements in suppliers’ working capital management are associated with higher supply chain value. Overall, this study extends research on common ownership and working capital management by showing how vertical equity linkages in supply chains can serve as a governance and coordination mechanism.

papers.title: Examining the Dynamics of FDI and Total Factor Productivity in Selected South Asian Countries
papers.abstract: This article examines the relationship between Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) and Total Factor Productivity (TFP) in Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka from 1982 to 2022. Using Vector Error Correction Models and Johansen cointegration on annual time‑series data, we find that FDI positively affects TFP in all four countries, with trade openness, government expenditure, and education serving as significant transmission channels. However, human capital negatively impacts TFP in Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, suggesting labor-market mismatches in these transitioning economies. The speed of error correction varies significantly: Pakistan adjusts fastest while Bangladesh adjusts slowest. Disaggregating FDI reveals that greenfield investment drives TFP gains more than cross-border M&A. Robustness checks using alternative TFP measures, instrumental variables, and panel ARDL confirm the baseline findings. Policy implications include country-specific strategies: vocational training prioritization in Sri Lanka, regulatory simplification in Pakistan, and FDI source diversification across the region.

papers.title: Does Social Trust Affect Workforce Stability? Evidence from China
Academic CEOs as Stewards of Corporate ESG: Evidence from China
papers.abstract: Drawing on imprinting and stewardship theories, this study examines how CEOs with academic backgrounds influence corporate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance. Using a sample of Chinese listed firms from 2011 to 2024, the study finds that firms led by academic CEOs exhibit significantly higher ESG performance. Mediation analyses reveal that this effect operates through stewardship behavior, as manifested in the CEO’s long-term and stakeholder orientations. Additionally, the study provides evidence supporting stewardship over agency theory by showing that the positive ESG effect of academic CEOs is significantly attenuated by managerial ownership, consistent with the stewardship prediction that extrinsic ownership incentives crowd out intrinsically motivated stewardship behavior. The findings provide a theoretically grounded account of how academic socialization translates into corporate sustainability and have concrete implications for CEO selection and policy frameworks that promote ESG-oriented corporate behavior.

papers.title: ESG Performance and Supply Chain Concentration
papers.abstract: We assess whether firms’ Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) performance is reflected in their supply chain concentration. Drawing on Chinese A-share listed firms over 2018–2022, we show that higher ESG scores correspond to lower supply chain concentration, with the pattern arising mainly on the supplier side. Additional analyses indicate that corporate reputation, financing constraints, and internal control quality are plausible channels. The relation is stronger for non-state-owned enterprises, pollution-intensive firms, and firms in less economically developed regions. Further profitability tests show that lower reliance on major trading partners is associated with higher profitability, suggesting that this ESG-related difference in supply chain concentration has economic relevance. Overall, the findings show that ESG performance is connected not only with capital-market assessment but also with firms’ operating ties with suppliers and customers.

papers.title: The Effects of Digital Finance Use on Rural Households’ Entrepreneurial Choices—From the Perspective of Capital Endowment
papers.abstract: From the perspective of capital endowment, this study adopts three rounds of panel data from the China Household Finance Survey (CHFS) covering 2015, 2017, and 2019, and employs the staggered difference-in-differences model (Staggered DID) to examine the impact of digital finance use on rural households’ entrepreneurial decisions. Propensity Score Matching combined with Difference-in-Differences (PSM-DID) and the instrumental variable (IV) approach are utilized to address endogeneity concerns. The empirical results reveal that the adoption of digital finance significantly raises the likelihood of entrepreneurship among rural households. Heterogeneity analysis demonstrates that digital lending exerts the strongest promotional effect, and digital finance imposes a far more pronounced influence on non-agricultural and opportunity-driven entrepreneurship than on agricultural and survival-driven entrepreneurship. In terms of impact mechanisms, digital finance indirectly boosts rural households’ entrepreneurial probability by accumulating social capital, improving human capital, and fostering psychological capital. Accordingly, to advance the high-quality development of rural entrepreneurship, it is essential to design credit products compatible with agricultural production cycles, optimize digital financial services, and activate multi-dimensional capital endowments, so as to systematically stimulate innovation and entrepreneurship vitality in rural areas.

papers.title: Invisible Digital Barriers: Digital Trade Barriers and Export Product Quality Upgrading
papers.abstract: Data localization mandates, cross-border data flow curbs, and digital service licensing rules have spawned new trade frictions distinct from traditional tariffs and non-tariff barriers. This article investigates how such digital trade barriers affect the export product quality of Chinese listed firms. Using the OECD Digital Services Trade Restrictiveness Index and a shift‑share approach, we construct an exogenous firm-level exposure index by matching national regulatory intensity with preset provincial-industry input structures and firm cost profiles. Two-way fixed-effect regressions, validated by instrumental variable tests and multiple robustness checks, reveal that higher digital trade barrier exposure significantly reduces firms’ export technological sophistication. Two underlying mechanisms are verified: suppressed value-added intensity and distorted internal resource allocation. The adverse impact is more pronounced for non-state-owned and non-overseas-cross-listed firms, which lack institutional and informational buffers. Dynamic analysis further shows the negative effect peaks in the policy enforcement year and dissipates within 3 years, allowing room for prompt policy intervention. Overall, this study highlights digital trade regulations as an overlooked key factor of export competitiveness and proposes coordinating international digital trade rule-making and boosting domestic digital infrastructure as countermeasures.

papers.title: Climate Risks and Household Debt: Evidence from China
Policy Signaling of Carbon Tariffs and Export Competitiveness: Evidence from China
papers.abstract: Although carbon tariffs were substantively implemented only in 2026, their anticipated introduction by developed economies has generated policy signaling effects that reshape government behavior and trade expectations in emerging markets. This paper examines how carbon tariff policy signals affect China’s export competitiveness by identifying external carbon tariff signaling shocks across provinces. Using panel data from 30 Chinese provinces during 2006–2024, we find that stronger carbon tariff signals significantly reduce export competitiveness, particularly in central, non-coastal, and ETS pilot regions. Mechanism analyses show that policy signals generate positive effects through technological innovation and stricter environmental constraints, but these effects are outweighed by negative direct effects arising from trade policy uncertainty. The findings demonstrate that anticipated carbon tariffs have already influenced local policy priorities and export structures through signaling and expectation channels before formal implementation, highlighting how international climate-related trade policies reshape domestic competitiveness.

papers.title: Identifying Green Bond Greenwashing Behavior Using Large Language Models: Evidence from China
papers.abstract: Green bonds, as an important financing tool for promoting the transition to a low-carbon economy, warrant attention to their actual environmental benefits. The existence of greenwashing behavior not only harms the interests of investors but may also undermine the credibility of the green financial market. This study takes the Chinese green bond market from 2016 to 2024 as the research object, introduces the BERT artificial intelligence model into the field of greenwashing behavior identification, and constructs a greenwashing identification framework covering two dimensions of selective disclosure and expressive manipulation with six sub-indicators. The study finds: (1) Compared with traditional bag-of-words methods and machine learning methods, the BERT artificial intelligence model has significant advantages in identifying greenwashing behavior; (2) With the improvement of regulatory policies, the greenwashing strategies of bond issuers show dynamic evolution characteristics, the space for selective disclosure is compressed, and expressive manipulation becomes the more dominant form of greenwashing; (3) Bond issuers with greenwashing behavior are more likely to engage in strategic green innovation in the future, and their future financial performance and sustainability are significantly weaker than non-greenwashing entities, and this situation exists in both bond issuers with selective disclosure and expressive manipulation. This study provides a new technical path for the automatic identification of greenwashing behavior in green bonds and provides empirical evidence for regulatory agencies to improve the information disclosure system.
