Asthma in some boys stops at puberty: mouse results hint at why
The Impact of Unions on Nonunion Wage Setting: Threats and Bargaining
Longevity, Health, and Housing Risk Management in Retirement
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Annuities, long‐term care insurance, and reverse mortgages remain puzzlingly unpopular to manage post‐retirement longevity, health, and housing price risks. We use a flexible life‐cycle model structurally estimated with a unique stated‐preference survey experiment of Canadian households to understand why. Key factors include high risk aversion, concern over long‐run risks, strong discounting of valuation in disability states, imperfect housing substitutability, and bequest motives. The remaining disinterest is accounted for by information frictions and inertia. We also document evidence of public insurance crowding out, spousal co‐insurance, and responsiveness to product bundling.

papers.title: Macroprudential regulation and banks’ supply of liquidity services
Revealed Social Networks
papers.abstract: The linear-in-means model is the standard empirical model of peer effects and asks that an agent’s choice or outcome is a combination of their ideal point and the mean outcome of their group. Using choice data and exogenous group variation, we develop a revealed preference style test for the linear-in-means model. This test is formulated as a linear program and can be interpreted as a condition about differentiating the behaviour of each agent in a consistent manner. We then study the identification properties of the linear-in-means model. A key takeaway from our analysis is the close relationship between the dimension of the outcome variable and identification. When the outcome variable is one-dimensional, failures of identification are generic. When the outcome variable is multidimensional, we provide natural conditions under which identification is generic.

papers.title: Life, Death, and Migration in the Early Modern City: The Urban Historical Demography of WürzburgJandeVries, (Cambridge University Press, 2026. Pp. 304. ISBN 9781009641517. Hbk £95)
papers.abstract: This book addresses Allan Sharlin's well-known thesis about the role of migration in early modern urban demography.Sharlin's original article, which was published in Past and Present in 1978, challenged traditional interpretations of the reasons for the slow growth of towns and cities in this period.The conventional view regarded these cities as 'urban graveyards' which only succeeded in sustaining themselves as a result of in-migration.Sharlin argued that the characterization of early modern cities as 'urban graveyards' was exaggerated and that their slow growth was actually caused by the barriers faced by temporary migrants in the marriage market.This meant that migrants faced the same mortality risks as the 'native' population without having the same opportunity to contribute to birth rates.In 1981, he responded to criticism of this argument by proposing a detailed analysis of the demographic history of the German city of Würzburg, but he died before he could undertake this.Jan de Vries was originally asked to take over responsibility for Sharlin's project but 'the rich data yielded by Sharlin's research design enabled the writing of a demographic analysis that comprehended his thesis but went beyond it' (p.xviii).This delayed completion of the project but led to the publication of this study.The book starts by providing a detailed account of Würzburg's history before giving an introduction to its records and the questions to which they lend themselves.These can be set out as follows: (1) how family demography varied by social class; (2) whether chronic high mortality in excess of fertility prevailed in Würzburg; (3) whether pre-industrial life generated a distinctive urban fertility regime; and (4) what role migration played in either supporting or limiting population growth.As De Vries explains, Würzburg was not necessarily an ideal test of Sharlin's original hypothesis.It was the Residenzstaat, or administrative capital, of the Prince-Bishopric of Würzburg.All rights reserved, including rights for text and data mining and training of artificial intelligence technologies or similar technologies.

papers.title: Transport mode and the geography of exchange rate pass-through
Distributional Effect of Insurer Competition on Premiums: Evidence From the Employer‐Sponsored Health Insurance Market
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We study how insurer competition affects premiums for fully‐insured plans in the employer‐sponsored health insurance market. By utilizing quasi‐experimental variations induced by mergers among national insurers, we show that increased insurer concentration leads to higher premiums, but there exists substantial heterogeneity. In particular, we find that a increase in insurer concentration increases premiums for mid‐sized firms by but reduces premiums for large firms by . We explore additional sources of heterogeneity to shed light on the underlying mechanisms and conclude by discussing policy implications.

papers.title: Platform Fulfilment and Seller Reputation: Evidence From Amazon's Marketplace
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT In 2006, Amazon launched the Fulfilment by Amazon (FBA) program, providing support to third‐party sellers for a fee. While the program has the potential to enhance sellers' reputations, evidence regarding its effectiveness is limited. This study estimates the association between FBA usage and seller reputation, measured by the average star rating a seller receives. Using fixed effects and staggered difference‐in‐differences estimation approaches as well as 26 weeks of panel data from Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States, three key findings emerge. First, using FBA is significantly and positively associated with a seller's reputation, leading to higher average ratings in the short term than in the long term. This improvement is mainly due to FBA's competitive advantages, such as eligibility for Amazon Prime, standardised fulfilment quality and excellent customer service. Second, although the correlation between FBA and reputation is positive in every country, we find cross‐country heterogeneity in effect sizes and significance levels, with the largest effects in Canada. Third, we show that large sellers have the best reputation, and all sellers benefit from the FBA program. However, medium‐sized sellers benefit the most from the program. This trend can be attributed to how the benefits of the FBA program accrue optimally to sellers based on their operational scale. These results suggest that the FBA program is indeed effective in enhancing seller reputation, with implications for third‐party sellers, Amazon and regulators.

papers.title: Enhancing financial inclusion measurements: A comparative analysis using unsupervised machine learning methods across Mexican municipalities
Farmers' preferences for the design of an agglomeration bonus in the context of peatland restoration
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how the specific design of an agglomeration bonus affects farmers' willingness to participate in a stylised peatland restoration scheme. The analysis is based on a discrete choice experiment with 110 farmers from peatland regions in northwest Germany. The results suggest that, relative to the scheme's land-use restrictions, the agglomeration bonus plays a minor role in the decision to participate in the scheme. The bonus had no statistically significant effect in the mixed logit estimations and was mostly ignored in the decision-making process. Only when preferences are adjusted for attribute non-attendance does the bonus enhance willingness to participate and the scheme's cost-effectiveness. Respondents who did not ignore the attributes of bonus design preferred a lump sum payment at the start of the scheme to an annual disbursement of the bonus, and an area-based bonus to a neighbourhood bonus. More generally, the results suggest that only mediocre levels of commitment on the part of farmers can be achieved through a voluntary approach. More ambitious peatland restoration, which may be necessary to achieve the reduction targets in the LULUCF sector, will need to combine incentive systems with regulatory or planning instruments.

papers.title: Borrower‐lender political homophily and loan characteristics
papers.abstract: Abstract This study investigates political homophily between the top executives of borrowers and lenders. We observe a high level of political homophily between borrowers' and lenders' management teams, with a one‐standard‐deviation increase in homophily associated with an increase in spreads of approximately 126 basis points. However, greater political homophily is associated with less covenant intensity and fewer collateral requirements. These associations are stronger among borrowers with high information asymmetry and weaker governance. These findings are consistent with political homophily reflecting relational contracting and borrowers' preferences for contractual flexibility.

papers.title: Exploring the Effects of Corporate Digital Transformation: A Bibliometric Analysis and Future Research Agenda
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study uses a hybrid methodology of bibliometric analysis and systematic review to critically review the existing research on corporate digital transformation (CDT) effects published between 2018 and 2025. Descriptive analysis shows that this research field was still in its infancy before 2022 and experienced an explosive growth period thereafter. China takes the lead in publication volume, while Finance Research Letters emerges as the most prolific journal and research results are predominantly concentrated in domains such as finance and economics. Keyword and thematic analysis indicate that “digital transformation” is the core keyword, and research themes have gradually expanded from basic dimensions like firm performance to diverse areas including ESG, supply chain management, and risk management. The evolution of CDT effects research proceeds along the lines of technological determinism, organizational adaptation, and social construction. This study advances a systematic understanding of the CDT effects by developing a bibliometric overview of relevant research and illustrating the field's conceptual framework and thematic interconnections. The findings offer empirical insights to guide managers in formulating differentiated digital strategies and assist policymakers in constructing supportive ecosystems for digital transformation.

papers.title: Data Envelopment Analysis in Business and Economics: Methods, Trends, and Research Frontiers
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) has become an important multidimensional research method and is now widely used in business and economics. This study adopts a scoping‐review approach and uses Natural Language Processing (NLP), a data‐driven machine‐learning technique, to analyze 12,686 relevant studies and classify the literature into major research themes and categories. Specifically, we identify three DEA‐related themes, CoreDEA (11,167 studies), StatDEA (1266 studies), and DecisionDEA (253 studies), which can be further divided into 15 categories, including Dynamic DEA, Undesirable DEA, Bootstrap DEA, and ANP/AHP DEA. The findings show that traditional DEA methods, especially those within CoreDEA, continue to develop actively. At the same time, the growing prominence of sustainability‐related research suggests that SBM DEA and hybrid models incorporating bootstrap, meta‐frontier, and network DEA may represent an important direction for future research.

papers.title: The Livelihood Resilience of Smallholder Farmers: A Review
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The livelihood resilience of smallholder farmers has become an important issue affecting food security and rural development. This paper presents a systematic review of 135 important publications on smallholders’ livelihood resilience from 2009 to 2025, covering the framework and methods of measurement, influencing factors, and strategies and practices. We find that the authors studying smallholders’ livelihood resilience mainly come from China, and the research topics are strongly related to macro policies. Second, the major frameworks of measurement include sustainable livelihoods framework, socio‐ecological system resilience framework, household livelihood resilience approach, vulnerability framework and resilience index measurement and analysis framework. The research methods include quantitative, qualitative, and mixed approaches. Third, the livelihood resilience of smallholder farmers is influenced by multidimensional factors, such as livelihood capital, household geographic characteristics, market and value chain, climate change. Fourth, there are many strategies and practices for enhancing livelihood resilience of smallholder farmers, including agroecological and technological system innovation, livelihood diversification and capacity building, institutional strengthening and empowerment, knowledge systems and innovation support. Finally, the existing research is marked by inconsistent measurement frameworks, insufficient longitudinal data, and limited policy universality. Future research should identify resilience thresholds, target vulnerable groups, and develop actionable monitoring tools for policymakers.

papers.title: Legitimacy and green innovation: the mediating role of green alliance partners
Strategising AI innovation: boosting firm productivity through discontinuous jumps between exploration and exploitation
papers.abstract: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) has largely emphasised its productivity-enhancing potential, yet far less is known about how firms can strategically manage the tension between exploration and exploitation during the AI innovation process. Drawing on the literature on sequential ambidexterity, this study examines how discontinuous jumps between exploration and exploitation during AI innovation affect firm productivity. Using panel data on Chinese listed firms, we find that such discontinuous jumps significantly enhance firm productivity. This positive effect is stronger in more munificent industries but weaker when competitive intensity is higher. By providing large-scale empirical evidence on the productivity outcomes of discontinuous jumps during AI innovation and identifying their boundary conditions, this study advances understanding of how firms can temporally organize exploration and exploitation in AI innovation and offers practical insights for managing AI innovation more effectively to enhance productivity.

papers.title: Cleaner Domestic Growth from a Globalization-Oriented Big Push: Evidence from China’s Belt and Road Initiative
Making climate change manageable in an uninsurable world: the complex environmentalism of global reinsurers
papers.abstract: In the political economy literature on business and climate change, fossil fuel interests have drawn more attention than climate-constructive business actors. We contend that the climate-related corporate strategies, political preferences and communication approaches pursued by ‘good’ business actors are key to enhancing our understanding of climate politics. Drawing on literatures in management and organisation studies that emphasise corporate contradictions, we argue that even corporate actors who stand to benefit from climate change engage in complex environmentalism. Focusing on the reinsurance sector with the two biggest players Swiss Re and Munich Re as key climate actors, we triangulate internal documents, expert interviews and quantitative text data. We find that reinsurers never feared the limits to insurability that climate change might impose, but embrace the business opportunities it presents. While guarding profitable markets from state intervention, they encourage governments to generate new markets. Their communication cautiously warns against manmade climate change but also optimistically emphasises the manageability of climate change. These results underscore the importance of a broader perspective on corporate environmentalism to understand how market economies absorb climate change.

papers.title: Unequal exchange between France and Africa’s CFA zone: monetary dependency and imperialist appropriation
papers.abstract: The material prosperity of the global North relies on the appropriation of labour and resources from the global South through unequal exchange. While recent empirical research demonstrates this general pattern, little has been done to assess how it operates in the case of specific neocolonial arrangements. Here we focus on Françafrique, the long-standing neocolonial relationship between France and its former colonies in the African CFA zone. Using the environmentally extended multi-regional input-output model Eora, we quantify the flows of embodied energy, materials, labour, land and water between France and the CFA zone over the period 1990-2015. Our findings reveal clear patterns of unequal exchange, with France appropriating large quantities of resources from the CFA zone, particularly land, water and materials. We discuss the extent to which this appropriation may be enabled by France’s control over currency and monetary policy in Africa through the CFA system. Finally, we find that other major Eurozone economies also net-appropriate large quantities from the CFA zone, more intensely than the UK, US and other core states outside the Eurozone do, apparently benefitting from the Françafrique arrangement. By contrast, China and India have much lower appropriation from, and a more reciprocal relationship with, the CFA zone.

papers.title: Introducing the special issue on influencer marketing with extension into synthetic word of mouth: How AI shapes the future of influencer marketing
papers.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming word of mouth (WOM) and influencer marketing. This development gives rise to synthetic WOM, a form of WOM in which AI participates in creating, mediating, evaluating, and/or acting on the consumption-related communication. Despite its growing prevalence, existing research has not fully conceptualized synthetic WOM or explained how consumers perceive varying degrees of machine involvement in WOM content. This article addresses these gaps by developing a conceptual framework that integrates AI into the core WOM elements of source, message, channel, and receiver. This article also introduces the notion of degree of syntheticity, defined as consumers’ perceptions of the extent to which WOM reflects machine-driven rather than human-driven processes, and conceptualizes it as a multidimensional construct encompassing narrative, voice, appearance, and consumption syntheticity. Building on this framework, this article outlines key directions for future research, including the role of AI agents as communicators and receivers, AI-to-AI WOM environments, and the potential dark and regulatory implications of synthetic WOM. This work advances understanding of how AI reshapes WOM and offers a foundation for future theory and research.
papers.journal_name: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

papers.title: National identity rhetoric under bilateral geopolitical tensions: evidence from Taiwanese MNEs
papers.abstract: Abstract When geopolitical tensions pit home and host audiences against each other, how do multinational enterprises (MNEs) respond? We examine MNEs’ organizational identity work directed at external audiences under bilateral geopolitical tensions, where efforts to gain acceptance from one side may provoke backlash from the other. Focusing on MNEs’ national identity rhetoric—how firms use language to emphasize or downplay national affiliation—we analyze longitudinal data (2001–2020) from the public communications of two Taiwan-originated MNEs, Foxconn and TSMC, which operate amid the geopolitical dynamics of the Taiwan Strait. Our analysis identifies four rhetorical strategies—augmenting-localizing, augmenting-globalizing, ambiguating, and affirming—through which MNEs manage tensions associated with the expression of national affiliation. We theorize how the deployment of these strategies varies according to two key contingencies: the level of bilateral geopolitical tension and the MNE’s resource dependence on the host economy. We find that rising geopolitical tensions increase pressure on firms to actively calibrate their home identity, while host-country resource dependence shapes the extent to which firms accommodate host audiences. By highlighting rhetoric as a mechanism through which MNEs strategically manage national identity, this research contributes to the literature on MNEs’ responses to increasingly polarized geopolitical environments.

papers.title: Public institutions, governance capability, and platform internationalization: institutional substitution at home and abroad
papers.abstract: Abstract Digital platforms often expand internationally faster than public institutions can evolve, raising the question of how they sustain operations in weak institutional environments. I theorize governance capability, defined as the firm-level ability to design, implement, and enforce rules regulating participant behavior, as a dual institutional substitute. When home-country institutions are weak, platforms develop governance capability to fill domestic institutional voids (substitution at home), establishing order and trust where public enforcement is limited. Once developed, this capability becomes transferable across borders, enabling platforms to navigate weak host-country institutions during internationalization (substitution abroad). Its effect is conditional: it is stronger when home country institutions are stronger than those of the host country, and for broker platforms whose governance routines can be replicated globally at lower cost. Using a longitudinal sample of 50 digital platforms from China and the United States entering 61 host countries between 1996 and 2023, I find support for these predictions. These results position governance capability as a portable institutional infrastructure, offering a capability-based alternative to structural responses such as diversification in institutionally weak contexts, and highlighting its role as a supply-side driver of platform internationalization that complements demand-side forces such as network effects.

papers.title: AI Presents Both Problems and Opportunities for Minorities
papers.abstract: Abstract The recent Point article by Wu (2026) calls for a better understanding of factors that could lead to the development of AI systems that are likely to perpetuate social inequality. The Point article introduces the idea that computational beliefs interact with computational inequalities in a more systematic manner that develops AI systems which perpetuate biases. We present our counterpoint and show where we agree with Wu (2026) but also present areas that are not accounted for in the Point article. Specifically, using cases from financial services and HR systems, we highlight how algorithmic transparency driven by organizational governance and regulatory intervention can mitigate many of the issues, leading to the development of AI systems that could potentially be bias free.

papers.title: Decomposing venture evaluation: Learning about belief formation
papers.abstract: Abstract Research Summary Evaluating early‐stage ventures is difficult because observable signals of future quality are weak and noisy. How closely are evaluators' assessments related to venture quality, and do their subjective judgments add to the information already available about a venture? Using more than 1600 screening decisions from a venture incubator, we examine how judges use application information to evaluate ventures by rating them on a set of 14 criteria and providing an overall recommendation. Judges' beliefs as recorded in the grades of the criteria explain their recommendations well, but they are only weakly associated with venture quality. We document some systematic miscalibration in how criteria are weighted, though the miscalibrations largely even out when examining the correlation between recommendations and quality. Within the models we estimate, beliefs and recommendations predict venture quality no better than ventures' observable attributes. Experienced judges are more selective but identify high‐quality ventures only slightly better than novice ones. Managerial Summary Accelerators and incubators rely on expert judges to screen early‐stage ventures, but how much does this expertise add? Using more than 1600 screening decisions at a venture incubator, we assess how well judges identify high‐quality ventures and where their judgment falls short. We find that judges' recommendations are only modestly accurate. Judges form a recommendation from venture information by first rating a set of 14 criteria, but the beliefs formed are themselves only weakly tied to venture quality. Judges also misweight the evidence: several characteristics that matter most for quality carry little weight in their recommendation, while others sway decisions despite mattering little. Experience helps at the margin; seasoned judges are more selective and better at filtering out weak ventures, but they don't spot winners better than novices. A simple model using only the objective data that ventures report in their applications predicts quality as well as the judges do.

papers.title: The Debt Market Role of Asset Valuation Uncertainty
Managing Perishable Inventory Systems with Positive Lead Times: Inventory Position vs. Projected Inventory Level
papers.abstract: We study periodic review perishable inventory systems with a fixed product lifetime, positive replenishment lead times, and a general issuance policy under the average cost criterion. The optimal replenishment policy for such systems is notoriously complex and computationally intractable because of the curse of dimensionality. To address this challenge, we propose a class of projected inventory level (PIL) policies, which maintain a constant expected on-hand inventory level, and compare them with conventional base-stock (BS) policies that maintain a constant inventory position. For both backlogging and lost-sales systems, we show that the best PIL policy is asymptotically optimal with large unit penalty costs for a broad class of unbounded demand distributions. When demand is bounded and the unit penalty cost is sufficiently large, we prove that the best BS policy is optimal under first-in-first-out issuance, whereas the best PIL policy is optimal under last-in-first-out issuance (under certain conditions). Furthermore, we show that both policies are asymptotically optimal as the demand population size grows large, and their optimality gaps diminish exponentially fast in backlogging systems under a broad range of issuance policies. To facilitate computation, we introduce a class of approximate PIL (APIL) policies and extend most theoretical results for PIL to the APIL policy. Numerical results show that both PIL and APIL policies perform very close to optimal and significantly outperform BS policies. This paper was accepted by Jeannette Song, operations management. Funding: X. Gong and H. Yin were partially supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72425008] and the Hong Kong Research Grants Council General Research Fund [Grant CUHK14500120]. J. Bu was partially supported by the Hong Kong Research Grants Council General Research Fund [Grant PolyU15504525]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03801 .

papers.title: Centralization vs. Decentralization: First Evidence from the Laboratory
papers.abstract: The future architecture of financial systems is a subject of contention, with centralized and decentralized governance proponents. Here, we ask the following question. Would the architecture affect the quality of decision making? We propose a game where financial network participants demarcate the ownership of claims to income. This governance task can be decentralized (shared authority), centralized (single authority), or hybrid (alternating authority). Without communication, all architectures supported poor outcomes. With communication, decentralization ensured good governance and maximum profits, whereas centralization did not—lowering communication’s potency in promoting socially optimal decisions. This indicates that there is scope for decentralization in innovating financial institutions. This paper has been accepted by Camelia Kuhnen for the Virtual Special Issue on Digital Finance. Funding: N. Chemaya acknowledges partial financial support from the NET Institute. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02314 .

papers.title: Rejected Applicant Reactions to Artificial Intelligence/Human Manager‐Based Recruitment
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in job recruitment has transformed recruitment practices. Little is known, however, about how applicants react to AI‐based rejection. Drawing on appraisal theory, we propose that applicants rejected by AI tend to appraise the rejection as others' responsibility, leading to negative emotions and adverse reactions against the organization. Using a person‐centered approach and mixed‐methods design in two studies, we identify four distinct profiles based on the combination of outward‐focused negative emotions (OFNE) and inward‐focused negative emotions (IFNE). Specifically, we argue and test that introducing a human manager to review AI‐based rejection can soothe rejected applicants. Our findings show that involving human touch can shift applicants' profiles, leading to better reactions toward the organization. Theoretical and practical implications for rejected applicant reactions in the context of AI‐based recruitment processes are discussed.

papers.title: Green Innovation and the Nonlinear Productivity Value of Supply Chain Finance
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Although supply chain finance is often presented as a productivity‐enhancing financial arrangement, limited evidence examines whether its benefits persist as supply chain finance increases and whether green innovation transmits them. This study examines the nonlinear relationship between supply chain finance and total factor productivity using 34,785 firm‐year observations from 3386 Chinese A‐share‐listed firms from 2009 to 2024. Two‐way fixed‐effects estimations reveal an inverted U‐shaped relationship between supply chain finance and total factor productivity, with an inflection point at 0.296. A similar inverted U‐shaped relationship governs the relationship between supply chain finance and green innovation, peaking at 0.249. Green innovation is positively associated with total factor productivity and partially mediates the indirect effects of supply chain finance. The findings persist across alternative measures, 1‐ and 2‐year lags, additional fixed effects, placebo analysis and instrumental‐variable sensitivity tests. The productivity curve differs significantly between heavy‐polluting and nonheavy‐polluting industries.

papers.title: Green Organizational System and Organizational Identification: The Roles of Career Ecological Fit and Environmental Concern
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how a green organizational system (GOS) shapes employees' organizational identification. Drawing on person‐environment fit theory and organizational identification research, we conceptualize GOS as a distinct system‐level construct comprising aligned green leadership, culture, and HRM practices. We argue that GOS provides coherent environmental cues that make sustainability commitments visible, credible, and relevant to employees' longer‐term career judgments. Accordingly, career ecological fit is the key psychological mechanism linking GOS to identification, and employees' environmental concern weakens this relationship because highly concerned employees rely more on internalized standards than organizational cues. Using a two‐wave, multi‐source survey of 366 matched employee–supervisor dyads across 55 subsidiaries of multinational enterprises in China, we find support for the hypothesized mediation and moderated effects. The study contributes by introducing GOS as a system‐level green management construct, identifying career ecological fit as its key mechanism, and specifying when these effects weaken.

papers.title: Cultural Drivers of Circular Economy Performance: Examining When Green Supply Chain Integration and Organizational Culture Become Necessary
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Achieving circular economy performance (CEP) in resource‐constrained economies depends on the combined influence of organisational culture and green supply chain integration (GSCI). Although both have received increasing attention in the sustainability literature, little is known about how different organisational culture types interact with GSCI to enhance CEP. This study addresses this gap using the competing values framework (CVF) and analysing survey data collected from 311 managers of manufacturing SMEs. Partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS‐SEM) was used to examine the hypothesized relationships; necessary condition analysis (NCA) was employed to identify conditions that are essential for achieving CEP; and importance‐performance map analysis (IPMA) was conducted to identify improvement priorities. The findings reveal that apart from rational culture, the three cultural dimensions (developmental, group and hierarchical) significantly enhance CEP, with the model explaining 54.7% of CEP variance. Green internal integration and green customer integration also have significant positive effects on CEP, whereas green supplier integration does not. Furthermore, green internal integration significantly mediates the relationships between all four organisational culture types and CEP. The NCA results further identify developmental culture (d = 0.275), rational culture (d = 0.191), hierarchical culture (d = 0.160) and green internal integration (d = 0.146) as necessary conditions for achieving CEP. This study extends the application of the CVF to CE contexts in Sub‐Saharan Africa where empirical evidence is scarce. The study provides both theoretical understanding and practical guidance for improving circular economy performance among manufacturing SMEs.

papers.title: Environmental Management System (ISO 14001) and Total‐Factor Carbon Emission Performance: A Two‐Stage Malmquist Data Envelopment Analysis
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT As global decarbonization goals become more urgent, it is vital to understand that decoupling carbon from growth is not a purely mechanical process of adopting green machines; it is a socio‐technical transition. Understanding carbon productivity requires analyzing the synergy between voluntary standards and strict regulation, demonstrating that technology only drives societal change when embedded in a robust institutional framework that prevents mere compliance. Therefore, this cross‐country panel study examines whether the diffusion of Environmental Management System (EMS) ISO 14001 is associated with improvements in total‐factor carbon emission performance in 15 countries with the highest ISO 14001 adoption intensity over 2010–2024, yielding a balanced panel of 210 country‐year observations. Using a two‐stage Malmquist Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) model, we decompose change in carbon performance into two critical vectors: change in efficiency (catch‐up effect) and technological change (frontier shift). The decomposition results indicate that, for most countries, 24% in carbon performance observed gains were more closely associated with efficiency catch‐up than with frontier‐shifting technological change. Meanwhile, Germany shows consistently shifted the carbon‐efficiency frontier during the study period. Moreover, panel regression analysis indicates that ISO 14001 adoption intensity remains conditionally associated with these improvements after controlling for energy intensity and industrial structure. This study contributes to the literature by demonstrating that management systems act as technology absorption mechanisms, enabling lagging nations to reach the frontier of existing best practices. Finally, the findings provide a forward‐looking basis suggesting that, without an acceleration in radical technological innovation (frontier‐shift), current efficiency efforts based on voluntary standards will be insufficient to achieve net‐zero emissions goals.

papers.title: Environmental Regulation, Green Innovation, and Firm Competitiveness: A Conditional Innovation Pathway From Selected MENA Manufacturing
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Environmental regulation is increasingly viewed as a catalyst for innovation and strategic upgrading, yet its effectiveness in emerging economies remains uncertain. This study examines the association between environmental regulation, green innovation, and firm competitiveness in the manufacturing sectors of five selected Middle East and North Africa (MENA) economies between 2010 and 2023. Building on the Porter hypothesis, institutional theory, and the resource‐based view, the analysis develops an integrated conditional innovation framework linking environmental regulation, green innovation, and firm competitiveness under varying levels of institutional quality and firm‐level innovation capability. Using fixed‐effects and dynamic common correlated effects mean group (DCCE–MG) estimators, the results indicate that environmental regulation is positively associated with green innovation, while green innovation is positively associated with firm competitiveness. Mediation analysis suggests that green innovation represents the principal pathway linking environmental regulation and firm performance, while firm‐level innovation capability and institutional quality strengthen this relationship. Quantile estimates further reveal that these associations are more pronounced among innovation‐intensive firms, suggesting heterogeneous and capability‐dependent responses across the firm distribution. Overall, the findings suggest that well‐designed and credibly enforced environmental regulation is associated with stronger innovation and competitiveness outcomes within supportive institutional environments. Given the observational nature of the data, these findings should be interpreted as conditional empirical associations rather than conclusive evidence of causal effects. The study contributes to the literature by extending the Porter mechanism to resource‐dependent and institutionally diverse settings and offers policy‐relevant insights that may inform low‐carbon industrial transformation strategies in selected MENA economies.

papers.title: Strategic Silence? Mandatory Sustainability Disclosure and the Discipline of Corporate Over‐Claiming Under the European Union Non‐Financial Reporting Directive
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines whether mandatory sustainability disclosure under the European Union Non‐Financial Reporting Directive (NFRD) reduces corporate greenwashing among listed European firms, with a focus on the 500‐employee compliance threshold. We conceptualise greenwashing as strategic decoupling between sustainability communication (talk) and environmental performance (walk). Using merged LSEG Workspace and Orbis data, we estimate a local sharp regression discontinuity design around a predetermined 2016 employment baseline, focusing on 2019–2025 when the key variables are sufficiently observed. Crossing the threshold is associated with a robust decline in a residual‐based excess‐talk measure. Evidence for a standardised talk–walk gap is directionally similar but less precise. Decomposition tests show that the discontinuity sits on the communication side: firms above the threshold reduce sustainability claims, while emissions‐related performance does not exhibit a comparable short‐run shift. We do not detect significant local moderation by external monitoring or organisational complexity, nor statistically significant short‐horizon discontinuities in ESG controversies, valuation, or cost of capital. The evidence is consistent with a sequencing effect in which disclosure pressure disciplines over‐claiming before it produces observable operational change or downstream market consequences.

papers.title: Resolving the Carbon—Performance Paradox: Global Evidence on Stakeholder Engagement, Risk and Institutions
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how greenhouse gas emissions influence corporate performance and explains why prior evidence on the carbon–performance relationship has remained inconsistent. Drawing on institutional, stakeholder and slack resource perspectives, the study investigates the direct effects of carbon intensity and emissions reduction (efficiency) on return on capital employed, return on assets and Tobin's Q, while assessing the moderating roles of stakeholder engagement and idiosyncratic risk. Using a global panel of 3070 publicly listed firms from Europe, North America, Asia‐Pacific and Africa between 2014 and 2023, the analysis employs dynamic System GMM to address endogeneity, persistence and firm‐level heterogeneity. The findings show that carbon intensity is positively associated with market valuation and capital efficiency in capital‐intensive contexts, whereas emissions reduction tends to generate short‐term performance costs. Stakeholder engagement and firm‐specific risk significantly shape these relationships, revealing that the financial consequences of decarbonisation depend on credibility, risk exposure and institutional context. Cross‐regional analyses confirm that the valuation of carbon performance varies systematically across regulatory and market environments. The study contributes to the literature by identifying boundary conditions that explain divergent findings on carbon performance and offers practical implications for managers, investors and policymakers seeking to align decarbonisation strategies with long‐term value creation.

papers.title: Does ESG reduce hospitality firms’ cost of debt? Roles of information asymmetric and internal control quality
How digital human capital investment drives AI innovation in tourism and hospitality firms: The roles of data assets and TMT stability
From benevolent leadership to environmental citizenship in the hospitality sector: an affective commitment mediated pathway
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aimed to propose and test a research model that investigated the nexus between benevolent leadership (BL), affective commitment (AC) and organizational citizenship behavior for the environment (OCBE) in the hospitality sector. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 372 hotel employees in Poland via a computer-assisted Web interview technique. The hypothesized relationships were gauged using the partial least squares structural equation modeling. Findings BL boosted AC, which subsequently predicted OCBE. BL affected OCBE via affective internalization of employees’ emotional attachment to the organization instead of through direct behavioral modeling. Originality/value This study adds to the leadership–sustainability research by demonstrating that BL, a non-environmental leadership style, relates to OCBE through employees’ AC, rather than through a direct link. The results underscore AC as a significant internalization mechanism that connects moral leadership with context-specific environmental citizenship rather than direct behavioral relationship.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

papers.title: The Influence of Brand–Game Congruity in the Promotional Phase of Advergames: The Role of Perceived Legitimacy
papers.abstract: Advergames—video games created by brands to convey their message—are continuously used in advertising. As voluntary entertainment experiences, their success depends on both in-game engagement and pre-play promotion. This research examines how brand–game congruity influences consumer responses in the promotional phase. Three experimental studies explore the role of three types of brand–game congruity: advertising, image, and lifestyle congruity. The combined findings establish that high congruity strengthens perceived legitimacy, leading to more favorable attitudes and behavioral responses to both the brand and the game, prior to the game experience. These insights offer relevant managerial implications for optimizing both advergame promotions and advertising effectiveness.

papers.title: Moonlighting and the transition to full-time entrepreneurship
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper examines the transition from moonlighting to full-time self-employment using panel data from the Survey of Income and Program Participation. Motivations for moonlighting vary—from financial necessity to entrepreneurial experimentation—and these motivations shape the likelihood of transitioning. The paper finds moonlighters with higher moonlighting income and weaker attachment to their primary job are more likely to become self-employed. Access to employer-provided health insurance inhibits transition, and marriage allows for risk-sharing which promotes entry. Understanding the nuanced pathways from moonlighting to self-employment offers critical insight for designing policies that lower barriers and support entrepreneurial growth.

papers.title: Boredom and psychological well-being among the self-employed
papers.abstract: Abstract Individuals not only seek a happy and meaningful life, but an interesting rather than a boring one. In this paper, we analyze data from 19,000 individuals across 25 European countries to demonstrate that self-employment is associated with modestly lower boredom on average—a relationship that is not captured by traditional measures of hedonic or eudaimonic well-being. The negative association between self-employment and boredom is small but robust across broad sectors, significantly stronger among those with ten or more employees, and similar in size to the associations between self-employment and life satisfaction or meaning in life. While this association is not restricted to low-income individuals, the data do not allow strong conclusions about whether this association generalizes to high-income employees. We replicate our main findings in a separate sample of 1000 US participants. Using this sample, we also show that our main results are not driven by individuals with lower boredom proneness self-selecting into self-employment. Taken together, our results suggest that prior research has overlooked an important dimension of the relationship between self-employment and well-being.

papers.title: Adolescents’ entrepreneurial or employment intention for individualistic and communal business purposes
papers.abstract: Abstract Adolescents today are increasingly more agentic and more communal than prior cohorts and want social and environmental change. When contemplating an occupation to provide them with income and self-actualization, they face a concurrent choice between employment and self-employed entrepreneurship and between individualistic (profit and work satisfaction) and communalistic (social impact and environmental restoration) business purposes. Employment choices may be restricted by high local unemployment, automation, and artificial intelligence. Noting that entrepreneurial behavior can be pursued independently or as an employee, their occupational choices include starting a firm or joining a firm as an employee (and acting entrepreneurially or not). We study the determinants of their occupational intentions and find bespoke configurations of their personal and parental characteristics that culminate in their occupational intention and their preferred combination of business purposes. Interestingly, most of the sampled adolescents did not exhibit traditional gender role expectations, males were mostly communalistic in their preferred business purposes, and no group of females sought profit as their primary business purpose. This paper contributes to the literatures on entrepreneurial intention, adolescent development, and parental influence on adolescent choice with implications for policy, education, and research.

papers.title: Subsidy for the first hires and firm performance
From approval to routine use: the two-stage technology transfer of new drugs in U.S. clinical practice
Fostering managers’ trust in performance measurement systems through business intelligence: a longitudinal case study
papers.abstract: This paper explores whether and how the adoption of business intelligence solutions promotes managers’ trust in performance measurement systems by enhancing the use of the information these systems provide. The analysis was conducted through a longitudinal case study of an Italian company, using empirical material collected via non-participant observation, document analysis, and interviews with managers. The findings were interpreted using a theoretical framework that combines three studies on organisational trust. This approach enabled a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between business intelligence solutions and managers’ trust in performance measurement systems, focusing not only on outcomes but also on antecedents and the processes through which trust develops. The results show that business intelligence solutions can play a pivotal role in structuring and mobilising trust relationships between managers and performance measurement systems. However, such relationships do not emerge automatically as a result of adopting more advanced technological tools. The technical advancements associated with business intelligence solutions are not, in themselves, sufficient to stimulate the degree of perceived ability, benevolence, and integrity that is essential for structuring a trust relationship between managers and performance measurement systems. Rather, the case study shows that trust unfolds as the outcome of a multidimensional, gradual, and dynamic process in which technical advancements must be combined with organisational and individual factors. These factors collectively encourage managers to accept vulnerability and engage in risk-taking behaviours, such as relying on information provided by systems they previously did not trust.

papers.title: Signal or Solution? Unlocking the Power of Dividends in Mitigating Corporate Default Risk in China
papers.abstract: The relationship between dividend policy and corporate risk has attracted significant attention. We extend this literature by examining how cash dividend distribution affects debt default risk through its role in mitigating agency conflicts. We find that both the presence of cash dividends and higher payout ratios significantly reduce corporate debt default risk, with signalling and internal governance serving as the key mediating mechanisms. Further analyses reveal that this risk‐reduction effect strengthens with macroeconomic uncertainty, operational risk, weak managerial incentives, a high interest‐bearing debt ratio, and among non‐mature firms. Moreover, the interaction between cash dividend distribution and debt default risk significantly promotes a shift toward a longer‐term debt maturity structure. We further demonstrate that the strategic choice of dividend policy has significant implications for corporate risk management and firm value.

papers.title: Do auditors care about firms’ engagement in blockchain? Evidence from auditors’ responses
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how auditors respond to firms' disclosed blockchain engagement. While the technology offers potential efficiency gains, it also introduces new risks and complexity. We investigate whether and how auditors use audit pricing and auditor resignation as their strategies to manage blockchain-related risks. Design/methodology/approach This study uses a large sample of Chinese A-share listed companies spanning 2016 to 2022. We extract data regarding corporate blockchain engagement by conducting textual analysis on firms’ publicly disclosed reports. Regression analysis is applied to verify the research hypotheses, followed by a series of robustness tests. In addition, we carry out cross-sectional tests and examine auditors’ responses to distinct categories of blockchain-related activities. We further investigate the relative priority of auditors’ risk management strategies and identify potential channels. Findings There is a positive relation between firms’ disclosed blockchain engagement and audit fees. This relation is more pronounced among larger audit firms, auditors without an information technology (IT) background and those with shorter tenures. Both audit effort and audit risk serve as two plausible channels linking companies’ engagement in blockchain to increased audit fees. Firms engaging in blockchain to facilitate management processes, rather than provide blockchain-related products or services, are associated with elevated audit fees. Although blockchain engagement is also related to a higher likelihood of auditor resignation, we observe a hierarchical pattern in auditor responses, with fee adjustments being the more prevalent initial reaction relative to resignation. Research limitations/implications Our disclosure-based measure may not fully distinguish the depth of adoption, investor-facing signaling or strategic narrative because doing so would require obtaining in-depth blockchain data from the sample firms. This is highly challenging as such data are not subject to mandatory disclosure by regulators and may constitute corporate confidential information. Our findings should be interpreted as auditors’ responses to “perceived blockchain-related risks” rather than a direct response to “the adoption of blockchain technology.” Practical implications First, for audit firms, our results underscore the importance of investing in technological training and developing firm-level expertise in emerging technologies such as blockchain. The finding that the fee premium is concentrated among auditors without IT backgrounds suggests that audit firms that proactively build technological competence may be better positioned to serve clients engaging with new technologies while managing their own costs. Second, for corporate managers, our findings alert them that public blockchain engagement, even when disclosed for strategic signaling purposes, may carry tangible costs in the form of higher audit fees, particularly when blockchain is deployed for internal management processes. This cost should be factored into firms’ cost–benefit analyses when making blockchain investment decisions. Third, for regulators and standard-setters, the heterogeneity in auditor responses documented in our study highlights the need for clearer accounting and auditing guidance for blockchain-based transactions, which would reduce the uncertainty that currently drives elevated audit pricing. Originality/value This study provides evidence consistent with auditors strategically adapting to technological disruptions in their risk management practices. The study offers timely and practical insights for auditors, regulators and corporate managers as blockchain applications continue to proliferate.

papers.title: Understanding cross-platform dynamics in digital music consumption: A panel VAR approach
The social cost of free: service robots, anticipatory indebtedness, and free-trial acceptance
Building brand awareness or driving sales? How influencers’ campaign intent shapes consumer engagement with sponsored posts
Driverless, not thoughtless? Automated vehicle regulation, the dilemma of control, and the prospect of dual corrigibility
papers.abstract: When regulating emerging technologies, authorities must balance available knowledge, means for control, and desirable directions of development. The article asks which normative orientation guides Norway's automated vehicle regulation, how the regulation is configured, and whether this regulatory strategy aligns with the underpinning normative orientation. To answer these questions, the article analyses the policy-making process preceding Norway's Act Relating to Testing of Self-Driving Vehicles, the content of the finalised Act, and interview data from the first automated vehicle trial conducted after the Act's effectuation. The article shows that Norway pursues a two-stage regulatory strategy. During the first stage, interested parties may organise automated vehicle trials; during the second stage, the state will establish a permanent regulation for automated vehicles. This two-stage strategy builds upon the untenable assumption that practical concerns regarding a technology's functioning can be addressed separately from normative concerns. Drawing upon David Collingridge's writings on the dilemma of control, the article argues that practical and normative concerns must be processed in parallel and suggests dual corrigibility – corrigibility of decisions and corrigibility of orientation – as a guiding principle for regulating emerging technologies.

papers.title: Campaign success and activity-system contradictions in livestream influencer marketing
papers.abstract: Purpose Livestream influencer marketing (LSIM) differs from traditional influencer marketing in its real-time selling format, team-based operations and sales-driven integration with e-commerce. Despite LSIM’s rapid growth and importance for e-commerce, emerging research has generally favoured consumer perspectives. The purpose of this paper is to respond to calls for supply-side research by examining the LSIM operational environment, campaign success factors as perceived by livestream influencers (LSIs) and multi-channel network (MCN) team members, and contradictions within LSI–MCN collaborative operations. Design/methodology/approach This mixed-method study draws on activity theory. Sixty-five in-depth interviews were conducted primarily with LSIs and MCN team members; supplementary interviews with five brand sponsors, three platform providers and five viewers enabled triangulation. Survey responses from 112 LSIs and 100 MCN team members engaged with China’s four leading LSIM platforms were also analysed. Findings Results reveal a dynamic LSIM activity system involving interactions among LSIs, MCN team members, tools, culture and policies. Prominent factors in LSIM campaign success, from LSIs’ and MCN team members’ perspectives, include influencer capabilities, LSI–MCN coordination and platform strategies. A two-phase design (2021 and 2024) shows how LSIs and MCN team members respond to activity-system contradictions through adaptive strategies. Research limitations/implications Future research should confirm this study’s results across diverse contexts (e.g. platforms, brand categories and countries). Practical implications Findings offer strategic recommendations for LSIs and MCN teams with respect to capability development, collaboration models and policy implementation. These recommendations can promote sustainable industry performance while addressing inherent contradictions. Originality/value Addressing limited supply-side LSIM research, this study explores LSIs’ and MCN team members’ perspectives on LSIM campaign success factors and how contradictions are managed through adaptive strategies.

papers.title: When Managing Time Comes at a Cost: A Cross‐Role Resource Tradeoff Perspective on Team Temporal Leadership
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT While team temporal leadership (TL) has been widely regarded as beneficial for team functioning, existing research has largely overlooked the potential resource costs underlying these benefits. Drawing on conservation of resources theory, we conceptualize TL as a form of leader resource investment that may create a cross‐role resource tradeoff between leader costs and follower benefits. Using two multiwave, multisource field studies, we examine how TL shapes resource dynamics that ultimately influence the task performance of both leaders and followers. Study 1 indicates that TL increases leaders' emotional exhaustion while reducing followers' emotional exhaustion, thereby shaping their respective task performance. Moreover, the beneficial effects of TL on follower outcomes are stronger under higher team task complexity. To unpack this tradeoff, we further theorize mental effort and process clarity as two micromechanisms. Study 2 shows that team task complexity does not moderate the effect of TL on leaders' mental effort but strengthens the effect of TL on leaders' process clarity, with downstream implications for their emotional exhaustion and performance. Team task complexity also strengthens TL's effects in reducing followers' mental effort and enhancing their process clarity. Overall, these findings suggest that team task complexity primarily amplifies the benefits rather than the costs of TL, making TL a more favorable resource investment when team tasks are more complex. This study advances TL research by uncovering its underlying resource tradeoff and clarifying how it is shaped by cognitive processes and contextual demands.

papers.title: Rules in the light, voices in the dark: exploring pressures and exploitation disclosure behaviour in ready-made garment suppliers
papers.abstract: Purpose The study aims to examine how macro-level pressures drive the adoption of modern slavery prevention mechanisms (MSPMs), how meso-level organisational contextual factors shape their effectiveness, and how MSPMs, in turn, influence micro-level (non)disclosure behaviour of workers at ready-made garment suppliers in Bangladesh. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative research design and an abductive approach were employed in this study. Data were collected through 45 semi-structured interviews with workers, managers, trade union representatives, lawyers, and non-governmental organisation officers, and were complemented by secondary sources. The analysis drew on institutional theory and the theory of planned behaviour to explore macro-level pressures, meso-level organisational contextual factors, and micro-level workers' exploitation (non)disclosure behaviour. Findings The study shows that macro-level pressures such as market access, professional legitimacy, and competitiveness drive suppliers to adopt MSPMs, including grievance and preventive policies, digitalised systems, and training programmes. However, meso-level organisational contextual factors (weak management commitment, cost and time pressures, and fragmented control across supply chains) undermine their effectiveness, resulting in symbolic implementation of MSPMs. At the micro-level, these symbolic MSPMs shape workers' socio-psychological conditions, manifested in negative attitudes, unsupportive social norms, and low perceived behavioural control, leading to non-disclosure behaviour of exploitation. Originality/value This study develops a multi-level framework and empirical explanation of MSPMs by demonstrating how symbolic implementation at the meso-level translates macro-level pressures into micro-level non-disclosure behaviour through workers' socio-psychological conditions. In doing so, it extends the focus of both research and practice from the adoption of MSPMs to their effectiveness in supply chains.
