An Empirical Investigation of New and Existing Non-GAAP Exclusion Quality Indicators
Public Enforcement and Initial Public Offering Reporting Quality in Weak Institutional Environments: Evidence from a Random Experiment in China
papers.abstract: Using China’s randomized pre-initial public offering on-site inspection program, we examine the causal effects of proactive public enforcement on the financial reporting quality of initial public offering applicants. Our analysis shows that the program enhances the reporting quality of selected applicants by screening out firms with questionable financial disclosures. More importantly, it generates a significant deterrence effect, discouraging future applicants from submitting low-quality financial reports. However, we also find that public enforcement can lead to the rejection of some firms that may otherwise merit approval. These findings highlight both the benefits and costs of employing public enforcement to improve financial reporting in settings with weak institutional oversight. This paper was accepted by Eric So, accounting. Funding: K. Guo acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72302146 and 72132006], the Shanghai Pujiang Program, and the National Social Science Fund of China [Grant 22AZD034]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05042 .

papers.title: Harmonizing Safety and Speed: A Human-Algorithm Approach to Enhance the FDA’s Medical Device Clearance Policy
papers.abstract: The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA)’s 510(k) pathway allows manufacturers to gain medical device approval by demonstrating substantial equivalence to a legally marketed device. However, the inherent ambiguity of this regulatory procedure has been associated with high recall among many devices cleared through this pathway, raising significant safety concerns. In this paper, we develop a combined human-algorithm approach to assist the FDA in improving its 510(k) medical device clearance process by reducing recall risk and regulatory workload. We first develop machine learning methods to estimate the risk of recall of 510(k) medical devices based on the information available at the time of submission. We then propose a data-driven clearance policy that recommends acceptance, rejection, or deferral to FDA’s committees for in-depth evaluation. We conduct an empirical study using a unique data set of over 31,000 submissions that we assembled based on data sources from the FDA and Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Compared to the FDA’s current practice, which has a recall rate of 10.3% and a normalized workload measure of 100%, a conservative evaluation of our policy shows a 32.9% improvement in the recall rate and a 40.5% reduction in the workload. Our analyses further suggest annual cost savings of approximately $1.7 billion for the healthcare system driven by avoided replacement costs, which is equivalent to 1.1% of the entire United States annual medical device expenditure. Our findings highlight the value of a holistic and data-driven approach to improve the FDA’s current 510(k) pathway. This paper was accepted by Stefan Scholtes, healthcare management. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06477 .

papers.title: The Digital Visibility‐Belonging Paradox: Digital Cohesion and Control in Contemporary Organizational Management
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Digital visibility has become a central organizing condition in digitally mediated work, reshaping how employees are recognized, evaluated, and connected. In this conceptual paper, we theorize digital visibility as a sociomaterial HRM condition that simultaneously enables recognition and generates performative pressures. Anchored in relational cohesion theory, we develop the Digital Visibility–Belonging Paradox concept to explain why the same visibility infrastructures that make employees more observable may also weaken the relational foundations of belonging. We distinguish between authentic belonging and simulated belonging to show how digital visibility can simultaneously support felt recognition and relational connection while encouraging employees to display connection, availability, and engagement through digitally visible cues. We further identify cognitive, emotional, and structural mechanisms through which visibility shapes these divergent trajectories, as well as organizational and system‐level boundary conditions that influence whether visibility supports relational connection or intensifies performative availability. The paper contributes to HRM scholarship by repositioning visibility governance as a relational and humanistic responsibility in digitally mediated work.

papers.title: Competing creditor claims and loan recoverability: evidence from anti-recharacterization laws
papers.abstract: Abstract Anti-recharacterization laws significantly increase the rights of securitization creditors by allowing the buyers of securitized assets to exclusively and immediately seize collateral in bankruptcy. However, strengthening the rights of securitization creditors can limit other creditors’ ability to recover loans. We find that, after a state adopts an anti-recharacterization law, local banks operating in the same state accrue more loan loss provisions, tighten their loan contracts, and incur higher future loan charge-offs. These findings are consistent with the argument that a safe harbor for securitization transactions advantages Wall Street-style structured finance at the expense of Main Street-style lending.

papers.title: Removing sludge: How rating system design affects the informativeness of crowd-based performance measures
Urban Climate Risk and Corporate Collaborative Innovation: An Inverted U‐Shaped Relationship
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Against the backdrop of the growing impacts of climate risk on regional economic and financial stability, enhancing climate resilience through collaborative innovation has emerged as a critical issue for enterprises and is a key focus of academic research. Drawing on resource dependence theory and the attention‐based view, this study examines the impact of urban climate risk on corporate collaborative innovation using a sample of Chinese A‐share listed companies on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges from 2009 to 2023. The findings reveal a significant inverted U‐shaped relationship between urban climate risk and corporate collaborative innovation, a conclusion that remains robust after a series of endogeneity and robustness checks. Moderation analysis indicates that in contexts where urban openness is high and corporate collaborative culture is strong, the downward slope of the inverted U‐shaped relationship between urban climate risk and corporate collaborative innovation becomes flatter. Heterogeneity analysis based on the technology–organization–environment (TOE) framework reveals that the inverted U‐shaped relationship is more pronounced among firms with lower levels of digitalization, firms with lower levels of slack resources, and firms located in cities with lower ecological resilience. By revealing this nonlinear relationship, our study provides theoretical foundations and practical insights for enterprises to optimize collaborative innovation strategies in response to physical climate shocks and for governments to design more effective climate adaptation policies.

papers.title: Perceived Strategic Green Marketing Orientation and Buyer–Supplier Relational Outcomes: Evidence From Small‐ and Medium‐Sized Enterprises
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT As sustainability becomes increasingly central to business relationships, firms are under growing pressure to demonstrate credible environmental commitment. This study examines how perceived strategic green marketing orientation (PSGMO) relates to buyer–supplier relational outcomes among small‐ and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs). Drawing on trust–commitment theory, we propose that PSGMO is associated with willingness to pay (WTP), positive word‐of‐mouth (WOM) and propensity to stay through trust and commitment. Using cross‐sectional survey data from 388 US‐based SME owner–managers and moderated mediation analyses via Hayes PROCESS models, we find that PSGMO is directly associated with WTP and WOM, while its relationship with propensity to stay is mediated by trust and commitment. Further, commitment‐based indirect relationships are stronger among more religious executives when conservatism is low. The study extends trust–commitment theory by showing how PSGMO influences relational outcomes and offers guidance for suppliers adopting sustainability‐oriented positioning.

papers.title: Climate Change Exposure and the Discipline of Capital Structure: Evidence From Managerial Leverage Distortion
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how climate change exposure affects corporate financing behaviour through the lens of managerial leverage distortion (MLD), defined as the absolute deviation of observed leverage from a benchmark implied by firm fundamentals. Using a large panel of the US firms and high‐dimensional fixed‐effects models with firm‐ and year‐fixed effects, the study finds that climate change exposure is associated with significantly lower MLD, indicating more disciplined, fundamentals‐aligned capital structure decisions. The effect is primarily driven by reductions in under‐leverage distortions, consistent with precautionary financial behaviour. The study documents that managerial incentives, business strategy and firm‐level risk conditions moderate this relationship, with weaker effects in high‐incentive and high‐risk environments. Further, the study reveals that higher MLD is associated with poorer firm performance, higher cost of debt and greater investment inefficiency. Overall, the findings suggest that climate risk improves financial discipline by constraining managerial discretion in capital structure decisions.

papers.title: Is competition good or bad for employee innovation? Examining the double-edged sword effect of team and individual responses
Measuring the value of blockchain adoption in supply chain management: an empirical analysis of key success dimensions
papers.abstract: Purpose Blockchain technology is widely discussed as an enabler of transparency, efficiency and trust in supply chain management (SCM). However, empirical evidence on which blockchain-related success dimensions translate into value perceptions remains limited. This study aims to examine how the perceived relevance of blockchain success dimensions relates to realized benefits and whether these benefits contribute to overall perceived blockchain value. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative survey of 41 companies with blockchain experience in SCM is conducted. Success dimensions are prioritized using best–worst scaling (MaxDiff). Relationships between perceived relevance, dimension-specific benefits and overall perceived value are analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Exploratory analyses assess company characteristics. Findings Contrary to dominant expectations in academic and practitioner narratives, even highly prioritized blockchain success dimensions fail to translate into measurable firm-level value perceptions. While transparency and traceability are associated with significant dimension-specific benefits, these improvements do not produce statistically significant direct or indirect effects on overall perceived blockchain value. This suggests that localized operational gains alone may be insufficient to generate overall perceived value and indicates that blockchain benefits may depend on broader organizational and technological complements. Originality/value The study moves beyond identifying potential blockchain benefits by empirically differentiating which success dimensions matter and which do not. By combining MaxDiff with PLS-SEM, it offers a structured, mechanism-oriented framework for evaluating blockchain success and highlights boundary conditions for value realization in SCM.
papers.journal_name: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

papers.title: What kind of brain strengthens the entrepreneurial creativity–intention link? Evidence from frontal alpha asymmetry
papers.abstract: Abstract Small business creation and self-employment depend critically on individuals’ motivation to pursue entrepreneurial entry under uncertainty. While prior research consistently shows that entrepreneurial creativity enhances entrepreneurial intention, substantial heterogeneity remains among creative individuals in their willingness to pursue small business entry. To address this gap, drawing on expectancy theory, we propose that entrepreneurial creativity primarily strengthens perceived feasibility, but that the translation of feasibility into intention depends on individuals’ affective–motivational readiness to act. We operationalize this readiness using frontal alpha asymmetry (FAA)—a resting-state neurophysiological index of relative left–right frontal cortical activity associated with approach-related affective tendencies. We conceptualize FAA as a dispositional boundary condition, rather than a driver of entrepreneurial intention. Using a multi-method design that combines validated self-report measures with resting-state electroencephalography (EEG), we test a moderation model in which FAA conditions the relationship between entrepreneurial creativity and entrepreneurial intention. Results indicate that entrepreneurial creativity is positively associated with entrepreneurial intention, and that this relationship is stronger among individuals exhibiting higher FAA. By identifying an affective–motivational boundary condition, this study advances micro-level explanations of entrepreneurial entry motivation and helps explain why some creative individuals pursue small business entry while others do not. The findings contribute to research on entrepreneurial decision-making under uncertainty and demonstrate how neuroscience-informed measures can complement traditional approaches in small business economics.

papers.title: When Firm Boundaries Meet Planetary Boundaries: Examining Corporate Land Use and Local Biodiversity With a Metacoupling Perspective
papers.abstract: We investigate the collective interactions between corporate land use and biodiversity using the lenses of the metacoupling framework. Focusing on corporations in English and Welsh local councils between 2014 and 2019, we find that land use by intensive land use corporations is associated with reduced local species richness through intracoupling processes and causes negative outward spillover interactions with species richness in neighbouring areas via pericoupling processes. These intra- and pericoupling effects are stronger for ectotherms, small-bodied, and low‑dispersal species. We also find telecoupling effects where declines in ectotherms, terrestrial species, small-bodied species, and low-dispersal species richness intensify when local councils are part of the neighbouring, regional, and national road and rail network. International connections via seaports and airports are associated with reduced endotherm richness. By adding a spatial dimension to the analysis, this study outlines the importance of tracing the impacts of corporate activities beyond their conventional firm boundaries.

papers.title: Institutional design and the financial resilience of credit guarantee schemes in SME finance
papers.abstract: Credit guarantee schemes are widely used policy instruments to expand SME access to finance, yet limited evidence exists on how their institutional design shapes long-term viability under credit stress. This study examines two distinct performance dimensions (operational sustainability and loss-based financial resilience) across 17 Latin American schemes using fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) and Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA). The findings show that performance stems from coherent configurations of governance, growth strategies, and risk-sharing mechanisms, rather than isolated best practices. Operational sustainability is achieved through two alternative pathways: a risk-buffered expansion model, where governance and loss-sharing mechanisms support scaling, and a governance-constrained model, where limited growth and structured risk allocation maintain stability. In contrast, loss-based resilience emerges from a single, more restrictive configuration centered on disciplined growth, independent governance, and explicit loss-sharing design. The analysis also reveals strong causal asymmetry: institutional fragility arises from misaligned configurations, including cases where commonly recommended features are present but not coherently combined.

papers.title: Legacy under threat: CEO entrenchment, power and governance dynamics in family firms
papers.abstract: This article examines whether CEO entrenchment and the accumulation of power negatively impact long-term social legacy-building practices. Utilizing data from 2,637 firms across 80 countries, we find that power-motivated CEOs undermine both the practice and continuity of these social initiatives. However, our findings suggest that ownership structures—specifically family involvement—serve as a vital internal governance mechanism. By monitoring executive behavior, family involvement mitigates the detrimental effects of CEO entrenchment on social legacy-building practices. These results underscore the critical role of ownership-based governance in aligning CEO actions with long-term firm goals.

papers.title: R&D Internationalization and Its Impact on Green Innovation: An fsQCA‐Based Comparison of Global R&D Divisions and Subsidiaries
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We examine the role of R&D internationalization in green innovation among Chinese firms based on two organizational modes of Chinese firms in Belt and Road (B&R) countries, which are overseas R&D divisions and overseas R&D subsidiaries. Based on institutional theory and dynamic capability theory, we examine how the external drivers (policy support, regulatory environment, market norms) interact with internal drivers (sensing, integration, reconfiguration, innovation). We find the configurations that would result in green innovation in various organizational structures using fuzzy‐set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA). There are four different models of green innovation. Policy sensing‐driven and regulatory integration‐driven green innovation models are mainly observed in overseas R&D divisions, whereas market reconfiguration‐driven and market innovation‐driven green innovation models are mainly observed in overseas R&D subsidiaries. Our findings extend the literature on R&D internationalization and green innovation by showing that the effectiveness of institutional and capability drivers depends on organizational form and by identifying multiple configurational pathways through which international R&D units achieve green innovation.

papers.title: The impact of local government debt on leverage adjustment speed: evidence from a quasi-natural experiment of local governmental debt governance reform
papers.abstract: Purpose This study takes China’s 2014 local government debt governance reform as a quasi-natural experiment. It aims to examine how the reform affects corporate leverage adjustment speed, and explores whether it eases the structural imbalance of corporate debt between state-owned and non-state-owned enterprises, to provide implications for local debt management. Design/methodology/approach This paper adopts a quasi-natural experiment design based on China’s 2014 local government debt governance reform. It conducts empirical tests to identify the reform’s impact on corporate leverage adjustment speed, and performs heterogeneity and additional analyses to verify the influencing mechanisms and effects. Findings The 2014 debt governance reform accelerates firms’ leverage adjustment speed by reducing firm risk and bank relationship costs. This effect is stronger in regions with larger implicit local debt and more new local government bonds. The reform also alleviates the debt structure imbalance between SOEs and non-SOEs in China. Originality/value This study offers new evidence from a quasi-natural experiment on how local government debt governance shapes corporate leverage dynamics. It reveals the real effect of the debt reform on micro-firms, and provides new insights for optimizing local debt governance and corporate capital structure.

papers.title: Salesperson performance in the wake of customer interest in digital technology: The role of job engagement as a resilience cushion
Adapting to generative AI in creative work: a technological frames perspective on creative advertising
The power of benevolence: A multilevel examination of how and when socially responsible human resource management shapes team responsible innovation
Forever Young? On the technological impact of green startups
papers.abstract: We study the technological impact of inventions developed by firms operating in the green domain at an early stage of their lifecycle, Green Technology-Based Startups (GTBSs). Building on a large dataset of US patenting firms from 1976 to 2019, we compare the inventive performance of GTBSs with that of other startups and incumbent firms. We find that GTBSs develop inventions with higher impact compared to the other groups. This premium is concentrated in green technologies, it is strongest among firms that develop both green and non-green technologies and it is limited in time. It declines as firms mature, consistent with the consolidation of organizational routines over the firm lifecycle. Inventor-team technological distance is found to be central: GTBSs exhibit inventor-team distance comparable to other startups but exceeding that of incumbents, indicating that the inventions with the highest impact is generated at intermediate levels of cognitive diversity. Our results suggest that firm type, lifecycle dynamics and knowledge recombination jointly shape technological impact of GTBSs. We conclude that policies supporting startups that integrate green and non-green capabilities are more likely to yield higher inventive returns.

papers.title: Beyond green claims: a social-ecological assessment of cruise tourism sustainability
Generative AI as a Scaffold in Travel Decision-Making: A Conceptual Framework
papers.abstract: Tourism decision-making is cognitively demanding. Travelers navigate fragmented information, coordinate interdependent choices amid uncertainty, and sustain planning. Although generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in travel decision-making, tourism research has not explained how it alters the cognitive organization of decision-making. This article presents a framework theorizing generative AI as a scaffold across travel decision-making. The framework encompasses three pathways: mitigating executive load by structuring information and managing task-related demands; supporting psychological processing balance across intuitive, deliberate, and reflective modes; and sustaining decision continuity across iterative planning cycles. Attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) tendencies serve as a theory-revealing case, where pronounced variation in executive function brings mechanisms into sharp relief. Grounded in task-based interviews with 30 UK adults, the framework extends tourism decision-making theory by explaining how generative AI redistributes cognitive work between travelers and digital systems and reorients AI design from efficiency optimization toward individualized cognitive and emotional support. Also available in Korean and Bahasa Indonesia.

papers.title: Fostering Regenerative Mountain Tourism Practices: A Participatory Action Research With High-Altitude Tourism Workers
papers.abstract: Nepal’s Himalayas provide the context for this research examining how frontline tourism workers adopt regenerative practices amid paradigmatic shifts. Despite growing interest in regenerative tourism, little is known about how such shifts occur. This study reveals that sustained adoption emerges from workers’ iterative interplay between professional identity reconstruction and multi-dimensional legitimacy evaluations, analyzed through identity work and legitimization as theoretical tools. Workers whose professional self-concepts shift toward stewardship orientations, through experimentation or elevation pathways, and who assess new practices as instrumentally effective, relationally just and morally aligned demonstrate sustained adoption. Those experiencing institutional distrust and resource constraints exhibit defensive entrenchment, understood as a rational adaptive response to structural betrayal rather than as personal deficiency. Theoretically, the study grounds regenerative tourism in socio-cognitive micro-foundations, extending identity and legitimacy theory to frontline tourism labor contexts. Practically, effective regenerative transitions require genuine agency, economic justice and institutional trust, not merely technical training.

papers.title: Business in Acute Crisis: A Humanitarian Impact Value Chain for Assessing Cross-Sector Partnerships
papers.abstract: Abstract Business–humanitarian partnerships are increasingly mobilised to respond to acute crises, yet in these extreme contexts even well-intentioned collaborations can harm crisis-affected populations and distort humanitarian action. In such settings, generic, outcome-focussed notions of impact fall short as tools for assessing cross-sector collaboration. This conceptual paper develops a normative framework—the Humanitarian Impact Value Chain (HIVC)—to assess the moral permissibility of business—humanitarian partnerships in acute crises. Building on the Impact Value Chain, we embed the humanitarian principles of humanity, impartiality, neutrality, and independence as explicit ethical constraints at each stage, from issue framing and mission design to inputs, throughputs, outputs, outcomes, and impact. The HIVC distinguishes principle-consistent positive impact paths from principle-violating negative impact paths and shows how specific partnership configurations generate predictable patterns of benefit, harm, and institutional effects for crisis-affected populations and humanitarian actors. The paper contributes to business ethics by developing a role-based account of corporate responsibility in humanitarian CSPs. It contributes to CSP scholarship by recasting recurrent implementation failures as patterned value-chain configurations, and introduces institutional harm to humanitarian space as a morally significant consequence of principle-violating partnerships.

papers.title: R&D investment, technology adoption and productivity dynamics: An empirical study of the productivity dispersion in Canada
Burning bridges or bridging divides: Geopolitics and collaboration in research and innovation
Toward a Gender Sensitive and Locally Rooted co‐Production Approach: Insights From Implementing Child Stunting Eradication Program in Indonesia
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Co‐production is a complex and nuanced field of social action that operates at multiple levels of the policy cycle, closely interconnecting the roles, motivations, and outcomes of different social actors. But how co‐production practices are shaped by gender is often overlooked. This article highlights the complexity of co‐production practices within Indonesia's ambitious national strategy to reduce child stunting. Based on qualitative research of three local government areas implementing stunting intervention programs, we draw on the ‘Four Co(s)’ framework to explore variations across co‐commissioning, co‐design, co‐delivery, and co‐assessment. Ongoing challenges to the eradication of stunting in some areas highlight the tense intersections between early marriage, poverty and rural and technological disadvantage. But as we argue, it is also dependent on social actors, especially women, who serve as catalysts. Future research that pays closer attention to the inherently gendered expressions of co‐production is both theoretically and practically necessary.

papers.title: American Society for Public Administration Code of Ethics
Conditional Autonomy, Discursive Gatekeeping, and Patterns of Action: How Experts Influence Policy in China's One‐Party System
Can cooperation between a city and a region lead to a robust solution during a polycrisis? – the case of Czechia
papers.abstract: The goal of this article is to explore whether municipal and regional cooperation can provide robust governance solutions during a polycrisis. The methodology of the article is based on a single-country case study from Czechia. The case study focuses on coping with the COVID-19 pandemic and the refugee crisis resulting from the war in Ukraine. We demonstrate how cooperation between a city and a region contributed to robust solutions and improved the lives of local communities. Although municipal and regional cooperation can potentially create significant positive effects that align with the definition of robust governance, this potential is not fully realized in Czechia. The main reasons for this untapped potential are failures of the central government, a lack of leadership and strategic focus, and the absence of formalized learning.

papers.title: Neighborhood Church Closure Density and Self-Reported Mental Health Diagnoses in Southeastern Pennsylvania: A Population-Based Analysis
papers.abstract: Yu-Tien Hsu, Taylor J Robinson, Insang Song, Hui Luan, Yusuf Ransome; Neighborhood Church Closure Density and Self-Reported Mental Health Diagnoses in Sout

papers.title: Structural Limitations of Early–Late Treatment Comparisons Under Target Trial Emulation: A Simulation Study
papers.abstract: Early versus Late (E-L) treatment initiation comparisons, which are prone to immortal time bias, are widely considered amenable to causal inference through target trial emulation (TTE) using clone-censor-weighting (CCW). However, whether standard CCW yields a well-defined causal estimand for the E-L comparison under ideal implementation conditions has not been formally examined. We conducted a structural simulation study to evaluate CCW-based TTE for E-L comparisons. The design varied along three dimensions: treatment-initiation mechanisms (random versus baseline-confounded timing), benefit-harm structures governing delayed-treatment harm and post-treatment benefit, and five distinct E-L initiation-window configurations. We implemented CCW as conventionally recommended and summarized estimated 12-month marginal risk ratios across settings. Depending on the placement and structure of the initiation windows, estimated risk ratios exhibited systematic window-dependent variation, including direction reversals across window specifications, even in settings where the true marginal causal contrast was 1 by design. These patterns were not consistently explained by weight instability or lack of support overlap. Our findings indicate that, in E-L comparisons, the window-defined strategy contrast estimated using CCW-based TTE can be strongly shaped by risk accumulated before treatment initiation under the specified windows, underscoring the need for caution when interpreting E-L analyses.

papers.title: When and how do governments succeed in introducing electronic voting (e-voting)? A qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) of 35 OECD countries
papers.abstract: Abstract Electronic voting (e-voting) is pivotal for modern democratic institutions in the digital age. Despite nearly six decades of e-voting technology development, significant disparities exist in its global introduction. Existing studies primarily focus on country-specific experiences, leading to limited generalizable insights into what defines successful e-voting introduction and its enablers. This study bridges this gap by proposing a comprehensive definition of successful e-voting introduction. We then explore on what grounds e-voting introduction succeeds or fails by applying fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to data from 35 OECD countries. Results reveal that the broader policy environments, digital readiness and citizens’ trust and ability to use technology significantly shape e-voting policies. Government commitment and policy alignment are identified as plausible complementary explanations for both success and failure. The study underscores the interplay of institutional and societal factors, rather than isolated influences, is the key driver of e-voting success.

papers.title: Psychotropic medication use in school-aged children in foster care and residential care within child protective services
Childhood psychological maltreatment and adolescent bullying victimization: The mediating role of core self-evaluation and moderating role of friendship quality
Not more harm, but less help: Dynamic associations among childhood emotional maltreatment, prosocial behavior, and bullying involvement in Chinese adolescents
Child sexual exploitation in a French child welfare cohort: Maltreatment histories, psychological and behavioural difficulties, and suicidal ideation
papers.abstract: Introduction Quantitative evidence on child sexual exploitation (CSE) in child welfare populations remains limited, particularly in France. This study examined CSE, associated maltreatment and psychological difficulties, and its indirect association with suicidal ideation. Method We conducted a retrospective cross-sectional study using case-file data for 1315 youth receiving child protection services in Essonne, France. Logistic regression models were adjusted for age, sex, age at entry into care, and school enrolment. Firth penalized logistic regression was used for restricted comparison, and exploratory mediation analyses used 1000 bootstrap simulations. Results CSE was identified in 62 youth (4.72%); 27.4% were boys. Youth with CSE were older, entered care later, and were more frequently not enrolled in school. Childhood sexual abuse showed the strongest adjusted association with CSE (aOR = 11.01, 95% CI [6.13–20.32], p < .001). Compared with youth who had experienced sexual abuse without CSE, those with CSE had higher odds of self-harm (Firth OR = 2.89, 95% CI [1.55–5.46]), aggression (Firth OR = 2.76, 95% CI [1.46–5.32]), alcohol use (Firth OR = 9.84, 95% CI [2.10–89.45]), and other substance use (Firth OR = 9.79, 95% CI [3.46–32.68]). In multivariable mediation analysis, CSE statistically accounted for 26.4% of the association between childhood sexual abuse and suicidal ideation (ACME = 0.026, 95% CI [0.007–0.044], p = .004). Conclusion CSE identifies a subgroup with extensive adversity and substantial psychological and behavioural difficulties, supporting gender-inclusive, trauma-informed, and coordinated assessment and intervention.

papers.title: Mandatory reporting on child abuse and neglect - many approaches, same name: Conceptualizing and understanding the mandatory reporting legislation
Does state eviction protection policy buffer the effect of housing instability on foster care entry? Evidence from IPV-exposed families
papers.abstract: Background Children exposed to intimate partner violence (IPV) face an elevated risk of foster care placement, yet the structural conditions shaping this pathway remain insufficiently understood. Objective This study examines whether caregiver housing instability increases the likelihood of foster care entry among IPV-exposed children and whether state-level eviction protection policies in the United States moderate this association. Participants and setting The sample comprised 53,159 children with documented IPV exposure across 17 jurisdictions, drawn from linked administrative data from the National Child Abuse and Neglect Data System (NCANDS) and the Adoption and Foster Care Analysis and Reporting System (AFCARS). Methods Multilevel logistic regression models were estimated to assess the relationship between caregiver housing instability and foster care entry, and to test whether U.S. state eviction protection policies moderated this association. Results Caregiver housing instability was associated with substantially higher odds of foster care entry (OR = 5.26, p < .001). This association was significantly attenuated in states with eviction protection policies (interaction OR = 0.47, p < .001). Conclusions U.S. state-level housing policies may serve as a structural buffer against foster care placement among IPV-affected families, highlighting the potential of housing stability interventions to reduce unnecessary child welfare involvement.

papers.title: The Impact of Past or Current Adult Industry/Sex Work Experience in Academia
papers.abstract: Although sex work in academia has been studied in the context of undergraduate student involvement, to date, no study has empirically examined the experiences of graduate students and academic faculty members involved in adult industry/sex work. Considering the potential negative impacts on the reputation and professional futures of those in academia who occupy professionalized spaces, it is important to understand how these individuals may be impacted in their careers. In this study, we distributed an online survey to graduate students and professional academics who had engaged in adult industry/sex work at some point, either currently or in the past. We thematically analyzed qualitative responses from 29 participants who reported on how their adult industry/sex work impacted their academic experiences. Five main overarching themes were identified, including impacts on their academic trajectory, attitudes toward academia, finances, and attitudes toward others, as well as no impact on their academic experience. No one theme dominated the responses, suggesting that the effects of adult industry/sex work on academic life are not universal, but instead may be shaped by intersecting identities and experiences.

papers.title: How We Mentalize Shapes Our Sexual Life: Evidence from a Cross-Lagged Panel Analysis
papers.abstract: The role of mentalizing – the ability to understand one’s own and other’s mental states – for sexuality is insufficiently understood. Thus, this study examined the longitudinal associations between sexual mentalizing and sexual function, activity, satisfaction, as well as general mentalizing in a cross-lagged panel design. German-speaking adults (N = 2650 [n = 1191 women] at T1; N = 1769 [n = 799 women] at T2) completed online measures on general and sexual mentalizing ability, sexual function, interpersonal and autoerotic sexual activity, and sexual satisfaction twice, four months apart. Cross-lagged effects were analyzed in gender-stratified path models. Largely reciprocal associations emerged: Sexual mentalizing predicted sexual function and interpersonal sexual activity in both genders, with significant reversed effects indicating reciprocal influences. Sexual mentalizing did not predict sexual satisfaction, while the reversed effect was significant in both genders. Among women, sexual mentalizing and autoerotic sexual activity were reciprocally associated, suggesting greater introspective involvement in women’s autoerotic activity. General mentalizing predicted sexual mentalizing only in men, while sexual mentalizing predicted general mentalizing in both genders, suggesting gender-specific developmental pathways. Findings highlight mentalizing as an important psychological ability shaping sexual function and behavior over time and signal the potential of mentalization-based approaches for improving sexual health.

papers.title: Instruments Used to Measure Sexual Identity Minority Stress: A COSMIN Systematic Review
papers.abstract: Abstract This systematic review evaluates the psychometric properties of instruments used to measure minority stress in lesbian, gay, bisexual, and queer (LGBQ) populations. A systematic search identified measurement instruments for dimensions of minority stress in adult LGBQ populations. The instruments were evaluated using the CO nsensus-based S tandards for the selection of health M easurement IN struments (COSMIN) methodology. Eight out of 105 instruments qualified for appraisal. The Lesbian, Gay, and Bisexual Identity Scale (LGBIS) and its German adaptation, LGBIS-DE, demonstrated the strongest psychometric properties and are recommended for use. However, the review indicated notable variation in how minority stress was conceptualized and operationalized across instruments. Additionally, content validity, as defined by COSMIN, has not been sufficiently explored, compromising the robustness of many instruments. This review highlights the need for greater standardization in the definition of minority stress constructs and a greater focus on content validity in future research. While the LGBIS and LGBIS-DE demonstrated strong psychometric properties, data were not available for all psychometric categories, particularly for reliability and responsiveness. Further research is needed to further validate the instruments included. PROSPERO Registration Number: CRD42021257995.

papers.title: J. Paul Fedoroff (1958–2023)
Subversive Amplification: Online Dissent and the Limits of Information Control in China
papers.abstract: Abstract Intensified information control severely constrains digital contention in China, yet online mass events occasionally occur. Using a dataset of 274,721 Weibo messages, this study examines mobilization, coordination and grievance articulation during a two-day episode of online dissent in the aftermath of the 2022 Urumqi residential building fire, which preceded the White Paper protests. It argues that users were activated by public communication failures that transformed manifold grievances into outrage, and that the associated hashtags provided anchors to which criticism could be attached. In a process this study terms “subversive amplification,” concentrated engagement amplified the hashtags’ visibility, and with it the critical content attached to them. However, absent the unifying function of opinion leaders, grievance articulation remained fragmented and did not converge on unified demands. The case illustrates the inherent vulnerabilities of information control but also the conditions and limits of their exploitation.

papers.title: A dynamic electrochemical impedance spectroscopy extraction method for PEM water electrolyzers considering time resolution
papers.abstract: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is an efficient in-operando characterization tool for analyzing the internal processes of proton exchange membrane water electrolyzers (PEMWE). However, conventional EIS requires the system to operate under steady-state conditions, which limits its applicability in real-world systems. Dynamic EIS (DEIS) provides a potential approach to capture the variation of internal physical states caused by changes in operating conditions over time. However, existing impedance calculation methods, such as fast Fourier transform and wavelet transform-based approaches, are limited in their ability to analyse nonstationary signals across the entire frequency range. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a hybrid method that combines the advantages of several existing time–frequency and instantaneous feature extraction techniques to accurately obtain DEIS under dynamic conditions. This study segments the perturbation signals based on operating variations and applies adaptive processing to ensure accurate impedance extraction. Simulation and experimental verification under different input power profiles to a PEMWE are conducted in this work. The results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid method achieves a DEIS accuracy exceeding 96%, verifying its effectiveness for PEMWE applications and potential for other electrochemical devices.

papers.title: Comfort-aware brain-emotional-learning coordination of battery storage and inverter air-conditioner fleets for microgrid frequency regulation
Optimizing risk-aware bidding strategies for photovoltaic systems in electricity markets through integrated forecasting and risk propensity
Reasoning-enhanced probabilistic electricity price forecasting using parameter-efficient large language models
Coordinated operation of power distribution networks considering impacts from electric taxi fleets under multi-stakeholder interactions
Modelling nonlinear heat pump part-load efficiency for optimal investment planning
Multiparametric optimization based decision making approach in energy systems planning under uncertainty
papers.abstract: Energy infrastructure planning confronts a fundamental temporal asymmetry in which capacity decisions must be committed before uncertainty materializes and yet must remain robust across all future operational scenarios. Traditional approaches either adopt worst-case hedging or ignore operational uncertainty. We address this through a Robust Optimization framework integrating data-driven uncertainty quantification with multiparametric programming, enabling design strategies as explicit functions of realized uncertainty without iterative re-optimization. We quantify forecasting errors via probabilistic deep learning technique to inform uncertainty bounds. Rather than worst-case designs, we model it as bilevel problem solved multiparametrically, deriving "wait-and-see" operations as piecewise affine functions of "here-and-now" decisions and uncertainty realizations.Applied to a multi-source, multi-sink energy system (wind, nuclear, natural gas, battery, electricity and hydrogen demands) under joint supply-demand uncertainty, the framework reveals a strategic shift in technology prioritization as uncertainty quantiles increase, optimal designs preferentially allocate capacity to expensive-but-reliable dispatchables even though economical renewables remain available. The complete parametric solution enables upfront cost-robustness trade-off exploration, providing a tractable and generalizable tool for risk-aware capacity expansion, supporting strategic investment decisions in uncertain and rapidly evolving energy landscape.

papers.title: Spectral intermittency regularization for photovoltaic ramp forecasting
Generalizable photovoltaic power forecasting under complex weather conditions: An adaptive decomposition-based hybrid network with physical consistency
Assessing the integration of climate change education in Sri Lanka’s secondary education system
papers.abstract: Climate change education is widely recognized as a cornerstone of global efforts to build climate resilience and sustainability. This study investigates the current status and integration of climate change education within Sri Lanka’s secondary school curriculum, evaluating the extent to which students are equipped with the knowledge, skills, and values necessary to engage in climate mitigation and adaptation. Using qualitative content analysis, the study examines a sample of national curriculum materials across three secondary education stages (Grades 6–13). The materials were assessed for thematic coverage, depth of climate change-related content, practical engagement strategies, and inclusiveness across student streams. The analysis reveals that while some references to climate change appear in subjects like Science and Geography, the content is largely theoretical, fragmented, and inadequately adapted to local contexts. Practical elements related to climate action, particularly community-based adaptation and mitigation strategies, are largely absent. This uneven distribution may result in fewer opportunities for students in subject pathways where climate-related content is less systematically represented. This study identifies critical policy and pedagogical gaps and provides timely recommendations as the country embarks on a major curriculum revision.

papers.title: Just transition policy implementation in Spanish coal mining communities: feedback effects on policy attitudes and voting intentions
papers.abstract: Implementing ambitious climate policies has presented significant political hurdles, particularly due to the concentrated adverse effects on communities reliant on fossil fuel industries. To address this distributive concern, proposals for ‘just transition’ strategies have emerged. While recent research suggests that just transition policy proposals can garner support from affected communities, whether political support can be sustained through such policies’ implementation remains largely unexplored. This study investigates the political consequences of the actual rollout of just transition policies among affected coal mining communities by the Spanish Socialist Party (PSOE) Government using a representative survey of individuals in a Spanish coal province a week before the 2023 general elections. We studied whether respondents continue to support the just transition policies, whether they perceived local changes, and the relationship between each of these and their intended support for PSOE in the 2023 election. We find that support for the coal mine closures and for worker compensation policies is stronger among direct beneficiaries (former coal workers), union members, those who trust mining unions, and those who are concerned about the environment. Support for those policies, moreover, is highly correlated with support for PSOE, with a slightly stronger pattern among former coal miners. We also find, however, that few respondents perceive changes linked to community-level just-transition projects – possibly due to delays in their roll-out – and that perceiving such changes is not correlated with support for PSOE. Our findings highlight the potential of just transition policies to generate positive feedback effects, with stronger impacts on those who directly receive material benefits than on those who benefit from community-level investments that may be harder to observe and to trace back to national government policies.Key policy insights Some governments are implementing ‘just transition’ policies to support workers and communities adversely affected by the closure of carbon-intensive industries, often with the support of labour unions.Government support measures for individual workers (financial and non-financial) are highly visible to the recipients and clearly linked to government policy. This creates the potential for reinforcing ‘policy feedback effects’: recipients are more likely to continue to support those policies and the party that implemented them.Government investment in communities (e.g. in industrial, cultural and environmental projects) also has the potential to generate reinforcing feedback effects, but this requires residents to notice these changes and attribute them to the policy.Climate-conscious parties implementing just transition policies need to clearly communicate to beneficiaries about the projects and their benefits, and link them to the government’s policy.

papers.title: Land price stabilization under Japan's LocatIon Optimization Plan: A propensity score matching analysis of Hachioji City
Analysis of synergies and trade-offs in sustainable development goals at the local scale: A case study of 2,063 counties in China
Powering progress: Clean energy and industrialization as pathways to sustainable development in Asia
The rise of renewable energy: How it shapes dependency, diversity, and geopolitical risk in the European Union
Low-carbon technology licensing under carbon taxes and green consumer preference
Ammonia-fueled marine engine: Enabling deep decarbonization of global shipping through full-chain technological innovation
Review of prognostics and health management for proton exchange membrane fuel cells based on interdisciplinary integration
Financial participation and compensation schemes in the European wind energy sector: A systematic classification and assessment (2006–2025)
papers.abstract: Wind energy is indispensable for achieving European climate targets, yet local resistance continues to delay or block projects. Financial participation and compensation (FPC) schemes are increasingly used to foster local acceptance by redistributing economic benefits to affected communities. While these schemes were initially implemented voluntarily by developers, an increasing number of countries and regions have incorporated them into binding legislation. Existing research suggests that FPC schemes can enhance local acceptance when designed in ways that increase perceived distributive, recognitional and procedural justice. To date, no systematic mapping and assessment of these schemes exists. Such an assessment is, however, essential to identify design blind spots, provide an empirical basis for EU-wide recommendations, and support future research on acceptance. We address this gap by providing a public dataset of regulatory and policy documents adopted in the EU27, Norway, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom between 2006 and 2025. We classify the schemes into four types for systematic comparison: fixed-payment compensation, profit-based compensation, debt-based participation, and equity-based participation. The analysis reveals a clear tendency towards fixed-payment compensation schemes, typically in the form of monetary transfers to host municipalities and local residents. In addition, we assess the schemes through an energy justice framework and contrast the findings with insights from the existing literature. Many schemes leave important justice dimensions underdeveloped, particularly recognitional justice aspects. While the paper focuses on onshore wind, the findings offer transferable insights for other infrastructure projects facing social acceptance challenges, such as large-scale solar photovoltaics, transmission grids or data centres.

papers.title: Energy intensity and economic performance: A semi-systematic review of historical dynamics, determinants, constraints, and future research pathways
papers.abstract: Energy intensity, commonly defined as energy use per unit of economic output, is widely used to assess efficiency improvements and progress toward decoupling. However, its interpretation is complicated by the fact that energy intensity is a composite, context-dependent indicator shaped by technological, structural, behavioral, infrastructural, and biophysical factors. This semi-systematic review synthesizes evidence from 147 studies across economics, engineering, industrial ecology, and biophysical analysis to clarify the drivers and limits of historical intensity trends. The review shows that observed declines often reflect structural change, sectoral reallocation, fuel switching, offshoring, and accounting conventions rather than genuine efficiency improvements. Rebound effects, infrastructural lock-in, material stock accumulation, and thermodynamic constraints further limit the potential for sustained long-term reductions. These mechanisms collectively elucidate why energy intensity cannot be regarded as a direct indicator of efficiency or as credible evidence of prospective decoupling. Building on this insight, the paper develops an integrated conceptual framework that links macroeconomic intensity dynamics with embodied energy, behavioral feedback, infrastructural inertia, and physical limits. This framework provides a more robust foundation for interpreting intensity-based indicators in modeling and policy contexts, particularly in scenarios that extrapolate past trends. The review also identifies several research priorities. Future research ought to amalgamate decomposition analysis with stock-based and material-flow methodologies, internalize rebound and behavioral feedback within macro-energy models, enhance multi-scale accounting of embodied energy and offshoring, and integrate biophysical constraints into long-term scenario formulation. Advancing these directions will strengthen the interpretive value of energy intensity and support more realistic assessments of long-term energy–economy pathways.

Delay-consistent adaptive incentive governance for circular beverage packaging systems: distinguishing structural and algorithmic limits in PET and returnable glass recovery in Mexico
papers.abstract: Mexico's 2030 target of 80% PET-container recovery under the ANNEP agreement remains 16 percentage points above the current national recovery rate, with returnable glass already operating near its infrastructure asymptote. Whether adaptive incentive governance can close this gap depends on distinguishing the mechanism sources of policy performance: the adaptive feedback timing itself, the average incentive intensity at which policies operate, or the underlying behavioral response of the recovery system. This paper investigates the distinction using a delay-consistent adaptive proportional–integral controller embedded in a system-dynamics closed-loop supply chain calibrated against four independent empirical sources for the Mexican beverage-container context. Four policies are compared in a 216-cell balanced factorial design: a no-incentive baseline, a constant deposit-refund, an adaptive proportional–integral controller, and a quarterly threshold rule. A new stratified matched-budget identification experiment decomposes policy performance into three analytically distinct levels — algorithmic effects, operating-point effects, and structural constraints — by comparing the adaptive controller against an equivalent-intensity fixed benchmark across baseline, demand-dip, and demand-whiplash regimes. The matched-budget analysis indicates that the adaptive controller and the equivalent-intensity fixed policy converge to essentially identical steady-state return rates (approximately 0.759) under all three demand regimes; the previously observed adaptive advantage is attributable to operating-point effects rather than to feedback timing. This identification supports interpreting the 2.1-percentage-point gap between the observed ceiling and the 0.78 composite target as structural rather than algorithmic in origin: the ceiling reflects the saturating Michaelis–Menten behavioral response of the recovery system, not a limitation of the control algorithm. Closing this gap requires policy instruments capable of expanding the behavioral elasticity envelope itself — reverse-vending densification, extended producer responsibility, informal-sector formalization, and consumer information campaigns — rather than stronger deposit-refund incentives alone. • Matched-budget identification experiment isolates algorithmic from operating-point effects in deposit-refund governance. • Adaptive controller and equivalent-intensity fixed policy converge to identical return rates across three demand regimes. • The 0.759 composite return-rate ceiling is structural, not algorithmic — reflecting behavioral elasticity limits. • Structural ceiling stops recovery 2.1 percentage points below Mexico's 0.78 composite target under current elasticities. • Closing the gap requires elasticity-envelope expansion, not stronger deposit-refund incentives.

Balanced use of recuperator in an MGT-powered eVTOL for extending cruise-stage flight time
papers.abstract: Although recuperators are not widely used in micro gas turbines for aircraft due to the concern of added weight, modern design and manufacturing technologies are able to make recuperators both compact and efficient, which makes the situation worth another assessment. The presented research systematically investigates the pros and cons of adopting a recuperative micro gas turbine for eVTOL applications. The research takes a 30 kW micro gas turbine power chain as an example and develops a system model consisting of the gas turbine, a recuperator, the weight and loading of the eVTOL, propellers and motors. A Pareto-based optimisation strategy is developed to identify the flight-time-optimal balance between the mass of the recuperator and the mass of the fuel under different cruise-speed and payload conditions. Under the long-duration forward-flight conditions considered, compared with the simple-cycle configuration in which the recuperator mass is replaced by an equal mass of fuel, the optimised recuperated configuration increases the calculated flight time by approximately 10–15 % over a broad low-payload range, with a maximum absolute gain of about 1.3 h. These findings demonstrate that recuperated micro gas turbines have clear advantages over simple-cycle micro gas turbines for some eVTOL applications. A well-balanced recuperator can therefore extend the flight time while reducing fuel consumption and direct CO 2 emissions under favourable operating conditions.

papers.title: Decarbonizing European refineries: GHG accounting framework and potential assessment for co-processed biofuels
papers.abstract: Co-processing of biogenic feedstocks in existing crude oil refineries is a promising, near-term option to decarbonize transport fuels by using existing fossil conversion infrastructure. This study quantifies the life cycle greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions of co-processed biofuels under an average European refinery configuration, using a policy-compliant approach consistent with the EU Renewable Energy Directive (RED), which has been integrated with a refinery-wide mass and energy balance model. Four case studies were selected: used cooking oil (UCO) co-processing in hydrotreating (HT) and hydrocracking (HC) conversion routes, and fast pyrolysis oil (FPO) and stabilized/hydrotreated pyrolysis oil (SPO/HDO) co-processing in fluid catalytic cracking (FCC) conversion pathways. Biogenic feed shares of 5–20 wt% at the conversion unit inlet were modelled, together with a full mass and energy balance for all pathways, derived to develop a comprehensive LCI for each pathway. Considered products comprised biogenic diesel, biogenic gasoline and biogenic kerosene. All pathways achieved substantial GHG savings relative to fossil fuels, with carbon intensities ranging from 3.9 to 25.8 g CO 2 e MJ −1 and GHG emissions savings of 73–96 %, thus remaining well above the 65 % RED minimum GHG emissions reduction threshold. UCO hydroprocessing delivered the lowest carbon intensities, while FCC pathways showed higher values, due to lower liquid-fuel yields and greater upstream burdens. Extrapolating the representative case-study yields to the entire EU refining system, a theoretical biofuel potential of up to 13.9 Mt y −1 at 5 % bio-share at conversion unit inlet is estimated.

papers.title: Data driven models for online tar monitoring in biomass gasification
papers.abstract: Reliable real-time monitoring of tar concentration remains a major barrier to process control and downstream syngas utilization. While online tar measurement is often constrained by high system complexity and associated costs, data-driven soft sensors offer a feasible and efficient alternative. Existing approaches often treat tar concentration in its raw form, despite its highly skewed distribution, which can compromise model stability, generalization, and the physical reliability of soft-sensor predictions. This study proposes a data-driven soft-sensor pipeline for the online estimation of tar concentration, combining domain-specific feature engineering, target-variable transformation, and deployment-oriented latency assessment across 11 ML algorithms, one DL model, and a Stacking Regressor ensemble, using a dataset comprising 221 literature-derived experimental records. The proposed pipeline systematically assesses the impact of four target variable transformations (logarithmic, Box-Cox, Yeo-Johnson, and untransformed raw data). Results demonstrate that target variable transformation is crucial for model stabilization and generalization. On the independent test set, the Stacking Regressor model coupled gradient and categorical boosting regressors achieves the best predictive performance (R 2 = 0.85, RMSE = 4.06 g/Nm 3 ). Similarly, the single categorical boosting regressor coupled with Box-Cox transformation proves to be a robust alternative (R 2 = 0.83). In addition, all top-performing models met the 1 Hz real-time monitoring constraint, indicating the feasibility of the proposed pipeline for soft-sensor deployment in biomass gasification systems. Overall, the findings show that boosting and ensemble nonlinear models combined with appropriate target-variable transformation offer a better balance between accuracy, generalization, and computational feasibility than more complex architectures, highlighting their potential for use as soft sensors for real-time tar monitoring in biomass gasification systems.

papers.title: Technical assessment of large-scale PCM packed beds for water-free gas turbine inlet air cooling and peak power enhancement
Process modelling of municipal solid waste gasification with non-thermal plasma tar-cracking unit for mass and energy recovery
papers.abstract: Growing municipal solid waste generation continues to outpace conventional disposal methods, and while gasification can turn waste into a synthetic gas, tar formation limits this gas mainly to combustion. Non-thermal plasma tar cracking can remove tar, but it has mainly been demonstrated at bench scale, with limited investigation of its integration into waste gasification systems. It was hypothesised that linking a gasification flowsheet to a regression model of non-thermal plasma tar cracking would reveal the trade-off between syngas quality and energy demand. A process model combining waste gasification with a non-thermal plasma tar cracking unit, represented using a multilinear-regression surrogate derived from plasma simulations, was built and tested across six pathways. The flowsheet predicted a syngas of hydrogen (52.3 %), carbon monoxide (25.3 %), carbon dioxide (14.0 %), and methane (3.9 %), in agreement with previous work, and the regression model achieved species-dependent coefficients of determination of 66.94–94.66 %. Overall non-thermal plasma removed most tar but added 1.80–2.00 kW per kilogram of waste, favouring methanol synthesis and fuel cells over conventional power generation.

papers.title: Ethanol steam reforming under engine exhaust-like conditions: energy recovery of reformate and coke-to-power integrated approach
papers.abstract: Ethanol steam reforming (ESR) was evaluated as an on-board energy recovery strategy for internal combustion engines under engine exhaust-like conditions using a bench-scale reactor and two catalysts: a commercial Ni/Al₂O₃ catalyst promoted with CaO and K₂O, and a Co catalyst supported on sepiolite. Experiments were conducted between 300 and 600 °C, selected according to exhaust temperature ranges experimentally obtained in a medium-duty compression ignition (CI) engine, and at steam-to-ethanol (S/E) ratios from 3:1 to 13:1. The nickel catalyst showed the broadest and most robust operating window, achieving complete conversion above 400 °C and positive energy recovery over a wide temperature range, although with significant coke formation at intermediate temperatures (400–500 °C), especially at low S/E ratios. The cobalt catalyst exhibited lower activity but higher hydrogen selectivity and lower methane formation, with optimal performance concentrated above 500 °C and negligible coke under high steam conditions. Considering the additional energy recovered from coke gasification, overall energy recovery reached values of 1.17–1.20 under optimal conditions, confirming the viability of ESR coupled with exhaust waste heat. This integrated reforming–regeneration analysis highlights that moderate coke formation does not necessarily penalize the overall energy balance, provided that effective regeneration strategies are implemented. However, bench-scale operation also revealed progressive mechanical degradation of the catalyst bed, including erosion, fragmentation, and pulverization caused by repeated coke formation–regeneration cycles, leading to increased pressure drop and operability limitations.

Limitations in the accuracy of satellite-derived Park Cooling Distances revealed by high-resolution airborne thermal data: A case study from Soest, Germany
papers.abstract: Urban parks are widely regarded as important mitigation elements for reducing urban heat stress, and their cooling influence is commonly quantified using Park Cooling Distance (PCD) derived from satellite-based land surface temperature (LST) data. However, the physical interpretation and robustness of these metrics remain uncertain because moderate-resolution satellite imagery may smooth fine-scale thermal heterogeneity and confound park-induced cooling with surrounding urban structure. This study critically evaluates the robustness and physical interpretation of satellite derived Park Cooling Distance (PCD) using very-high-resolution airborne thermal imagery in Soest, Germany. A multi-scale dataset consisting of 11 Landsat 8/9 summer scenes (30 m resolution) and airborne thermal imagery (20 cm resolution) from comparable meteorological conditions was analyzed. PCD and Park Cooling Intensity (PCI) were calculated using polynomial decay models for undifferentiated land surface temperature (LST) and also for ground-impervious surface temperatures which are more relevant to pedestrian heat exposure. Results show that isotropic PCD derived from Landsat and airborne data are similar (∼310 m). But directional PCD analysis showed distinct anisotropies with PCDs ranging from 165 to 401 m for both platforms. The analyses of ground-impervious surfaces revealed substantially shorter cooling distances (<200 m) and pronounced fine-scale thermal variability, largely caused by instantaneous shading. Multiple regression analyses of directional PCD segments demonstrated that vegetation cover, building density, building height, and shadow fractions explain most spatial temperature gradients, whereas distance from the park contributed only marginally. The results suggest that satellite-derived PCD may be strongly influenced by urban structure gradients surrounding parks. Consequently, part of the cooling distance identified in coarse-resolution thermal imagery may reflect underlying urban spatial heterogeneity in addition to physical park cooling processes. Similarly, satellite-derived PCD metrics may substantially overestimate effective street level cooling benefits from shading which are most relevant for human thermal comfort.

Estimation Accuracy Obviously Increased of Soil Organic Carbon Content Based on Habitat Patches Scale Using Interpretable Machine Learning in Southwest China
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Although machine learning models have been successfully applied to estimate soil organic carbon (SOC), the lack of interpretability research has resulted in the absence of mechanistic explanations for these models. Therefore, in this study, we adopted the following workflow: first, we divided the whole study area into several subregions using land cover types and habitat patch types based on cluster analysis, and then the model driving features of SOC estimation were selected using the recursive feature elimination (RFE) technique. Second, we compared the estimation accuracy and stability of three machine learning models, and explored the optimal feature combinations and model architecture. Finally, the Shapley additive interpretation (SHAP) model was introduced to interpret the selected SOC content estimation model to verify its reliability. The results showed that the divided modeling framework based on habitat patch type achieved the best performance in SOC content estimation: the maximum increase in R 2 reached 27%, and RMSE decreased by 20% (Habitat Patch 3 vs whole study area). The optimal model combination based on RFE‐RF demonstrated good estimation accuracy across the four habitat patches, with R 2 values of 0.36, 0.49, 0.62, and 0.59, and RMSE values of 22.04, 9.59, 11.67, and 14.57, respectively. Meanwhile, we analyzed the impacts of each input feature on the model prediction from both global and local perspectives. The results showed that DEM, precipitation, and air temperature were the key factors influencing the estimation of SOC content. The SHAP model successfully revealed the relationship between feature variables and SOC, effectively compensating for the limitations of the machine learning model in terms of interpretability.

papers.title: A more inclusive and sustainable mobility: Is Mobility as a Service (MaaS) a chimera or progress for Latin American cities?
papers.abstract: Currently, residents of large metropolitan areas in Latin America who do not own automobiles primarily rely on a multimodal mobility system to travel long distances. However, these transportation modes operate independently and do not interact effectively, resulting in high commuting costs that negatively impact the quality of life. This is particularly evident in the long travel times, necessary transfers, and the overall conditions of travel. In this context, this study assessed the feasibility of implementing a Mobility as a Service (MaaS) system in the city of Santiago (Chile), aiming to improve multimodal travel conditions and encourage the use of sustainable transportation options. To achieve this, we developed and applied a multi-criteria index for territorial suitability, which is structured around three dimensions: physical, temporal, and behavioral. The index was specifically used to assess the potential of Greater Santiago for future implementation of MaaS. The findings indicate that the city is moving away from the socioeconomic segregation that has shaped its growth model, highlighting a new East/West axis that is particularly beneficial for implementing a MaaS system.

papers.title: What comes after settler colonialism? Land, home and decolonizations in Palestine/Israel
papers.abstract: Following the idea that “decolonization is not a metaphor” ( Tuck and Yang 2012 ), this article examines how de-(settler)colonization might look in the case of Palestine/Israel. We consider settler colonialism as an organized form of “violent dwelling”: a mechanism of monopoly on the right to build a home, personal or national, and on the very sense of feeling at home, while denying such rights to the indigenous population. In Palestine/Israel, different configurations of settler colonialism exist simultaneously, stressing a need to consider decolonizations, in the plural, that are both unsettling and settling. On the one hand, decolonization must unsettle the current regime to make necessary transformations in the structure of citizenship, legislation, spatial configurations and reorganize the very notion of land and home. On the other hand, it also needs to settle issues of reparations, restitution and recognition through procuring dignity, security and futurity to all.

papers.title: Connectivity and Selective Rural Migration
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT How does infrastructure shape rural development? Using household panel data from a nationally representative sample of Chinese villages, matched to high‐resolution highway maps, we find that road expansion between 2000 and 2015 operates mainly through reallocation, with less productive farmers scaling down or exiting and more productive farmers remaining and expanding. We quantify the aggregate and distributional consequences in a dynamic spatial equilibrium model with heterogeneous households and endogenous migration. Improved connectivity not only accelerates urbanization but also increases aggregate rural output by 2.2%–5.3% in the long run, even as the rural workforce declines.

Survival after takeover entry: Effects of entrepreneurs’ domain experience and knowledge acquisition behaviour
papers.abstract: Entrepreneurs entering through takeovers are assumed to out-survive new venture founders as they inherit organisational structures. However, empirical findings remain inconsistent and founder-level conditions are rarely theorised. We introduce liability of misfit, defined as an inability to work with inherited organisational structures, which helps explain entrepreneurial exit, even when the firm remains viable. We argue that survival after takeover entry depends on whether entrepreneurs possess domain-specific experience at entry or engage in post-entry knowledge acquisition to avoid this misfit. Using 12 years of panel data on 903 entrepreneurs, we estimated discrete-time hazard models. Results show that lacking domain experience, prior industry and functional knowledge, is associated with higher risk of entrepreneurial exit following takeover entry, while knowledge acquisition such as market analysis, training and industry monitoring, may compensate for this lack. We contribute to research on entrepreneurial exit, entry modes and how human capital and post-entry learning shape post-entry outcomes.

Coordination Costs and Homelessness Housing Form Choice
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Local implementers have discretion in selecting forms of housing for the homeless, yet the determinants of these choices remain poorly understood. Using the institutional collective action (ICA) framework, this study examines California's Homekey program to assess how coordination demands shape decisions among hotel conversions, multifamily acquisitions, and modular or new construction. Drawing on binary logistic, generalized estimating equation (GEE), and multinomial logistic models, we find that larger projects and those designated as permanent housing are significantly more likely to pursue hotel conversions. Housing authorities—owing to their specialized missions and lower form‐specific coordination costs—are over six times more likely than cities to select multifamily acquisition. Local vacancy constraints further steer implementers away from modular or new construction and toward hotel conversions. These results demonstrate that implementation form is not a neutral technical decision but an institutional response to coordination challenges embedded in intergovernmental and interorganizational contexts.
