papers.title: Language and identity: Evidence from a schooling reform
The role of escape clauses: Firm response to thin capitalization rules
papers.abstract: Multinational firms can use internal debt to shift taxable income across jurisdictions. To limit such profit shifting and protect the corporate tax base, many countries use thin capitalization rules that restrict interest deductibility. These rules often include escape clauses that exempt firms below specified thresholds, but such thresholds may create incentives for avoidance within corporate groups. This paper evaluates Norway’s 2014 thin capitalization rule using difference-in-differences, bunching, and regression discontinuity designs. We find that exposed firms sharply reduce leverage after the reform, driven by lower intra-group borrowing and interest costs, with no detectable effects on firm performance. At the corporate-group level, leverage remains unchanged, indicating that firm-level responses primarily reflect intra-group debt reallocation. We document substantial bunching below the rule’s exemption thresholds, especially among newly created subsidiaries, and show that internal debt is disproportionately shifted to these bunching firms. Although firms eliminate most of their initial exposure to the rule itself, this happens largely through reduced internal lending, and we find suggestive evidence of higher taxable income in the medium run. Because we observe only the Norwegian parts of multinational groups, we cannot provide conclusive evidence on cross-border profit shifting. Overall, the findings show that firm-level escape clauses generate strategic avoidance responses within corporate groups, while also suggesting that the reform may have protected the Norwegian tax base.

papers.title: The Causal Effect of Parents' Education on Children's Earnings
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We develop and estimate a model of endogenous schooling and earnings to isolate the causal effect of parents' education on children's outcomes. Identification uses earnings differences among children with equal schooling whose parents have different schooling. Health and Retirement Study data indicate that the observed intergenerational schooling correlation is largely driven by correlated unobserved preferences for schooling. This is partly offset by a slightly negative structural relationship between parents' and children's schooling choices. Nevertheless, an exogenous one‐year increase in parents' schooling raises children's lifetime earnings by 2 % on average.

papers.title: The Macroeconomic Consequences of Competition for College Admissions
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT To study how college‐admissions competition shapes parental investment and child‐development policies, we develop a heterogeneous‐agent life‐cycle model in which parents invest in children's human capital to raise future labor productivity and compete for limited college seats. Because families ignore their spending's effects on others' admission chances, competition creates a rat race with overinvestment. Estimating the model with Chinese data, we find that this externality accounts for a substantial share of parental monetary investment. Policies that reduce competition raise current‐generation welfare but may diminish future human capital. Taxing private education spending while subsidizing public investment can balance this trade‐off and improve overall welfare.

papers.title: Two Two‐Tier Stochastic Frontier Replications
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We replicate the two foundational studies which proposed the two‐tier stochastic frontier model, first in the cross‐sectional setting and then for the fixed effects panel data model. We explore matters of software then and now, different mathematical formulations of the likelihood, and alternative current software tools. We also highlight several data issues that arose in both replications.

papers.title: Where and how is money spent on international migration and refugees in World Bank operational projects?
Environmental foundations of human capital: Deforestation’s impact on early childhood health
Retail ownership and earnings management
papers.abstract: Abstract We exploit the October 2019 abolition of trading commissions by major U.S. brokerages as a quasi‐natural experiment examining how retail ownership affects earnings management. Firms with high pre‐event retail interest earned positive abnormal returns, consistent with an expanded investor base lowering the cost of capital. Using a differences‐in‐differences design, we find these firms subsequently increased discretionary accruals and class‐action lawsuit likelihood. Earnings surprises relative to time‐series benchmarks rise for treated firms, while surprises relative to analyst forecasts do not, suggesting analysts anticipate the increased earnings management. Effects concentrate among firms with low analyst following and no industry cash‐flow shock.

papers.title: Mapping Barriers and Enablers to Institutional Lending for Smallholder Farmers: An Integrative Review and Research Agenda
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Millions of smallholder farmers in Asia and Sub‐Saharan Africa have been crowded out of institutional lending. While unclear property rights or illiquid collateral, isolation, the lack of tailored credit products, and agricultural endowment risks hinder their access to credit from formal channels, the extant literature is scant in mapping barriers and enablers to institutional lending for smallholders and presenting them in a unified framework by integrating theoretical perspectives into a conceptual synthesis. We bridge this gap by conducting an integrative review that combines a bibliometric analysis of 848 articles retrieved from the Scopus database, a systematic literature review of 83 articles, and 29 grey literature sources, utilizing an integrated Antecedents‐Decisions‐Outcomes (ADO) and Theory‐Context‐Characteristic‐Method (TCCM) framework. We identify supply‐side and demand‐side antecedents (barriers) that inform farmer borrowing decisions, lenders’ screening and credit appraisal, and the choice of intermediation channel, thereby shaping farmer credit availability and access, farm investment and agricultural yields, and social and environmental outcomes. The theoretical perspectives emerging from the TCCM framework are categorized into the structural, behavioural, and network layers that affect transaction‐cost attributes of institutional lending. We propose future research directions to address the conceptual and empirical gaps to deepen institutional lending to small‐scale farmers.

papers.title: Dependency, resource extraction and informality in Africa: how primarisation drives informal employment
papers.abstract: This study seeks to empirically demonstrate and theoretically articulate the relationship between extractive economies and informal labour in Sub-Saharan Africa. We utilise a multivariate OLS regression across a series of models which demonstrate a statistically significant relationship between countries’ reliance on the extraction of natural resources (i.e. primarisation) and the rate of informality in a country’s total workforce. Our findings and discussion demonstrate the theoretical and empirical shortcomings of the dominant liberal explanations for informality. Instead, we argue that a Marxist dependency theory framework aligns most closely with the reality of the nature of both informality and primarisation on the Continent. We argue that informality in Africa is significantly rooted in neocolonial relations of extractivism imposed upon the continent by the structures of global capitalism, including geopolitical and economic conditions of domination and unequal exchange that the global system entails.

papers.title: Credits for Exporters: How Firm Characteristics and Loan Frequency Shape Policy Effectiveness
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT We estimate the impact of Eximbank Hungary's working capital loans on firm exports using matching and panel methods. Loans increase export value by about 20% and export share by 6.5%. The strongest point estimates are associated with first loans. Export gains persist over time, but robust long‐run effects are detectable only at the full‐sample level, not among firms that receive a single loan. The estimated coefficients decline by initial export share but do not vary by firm size and productivity. Loans raise sales and employment by about 10% but do not affect productivity and profitability.
papers.journal_name: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

papers.title: Resolving the Performance Feedback Puzzle: CEO Psychopathy, Heterogeneous Emotional Responses to Aspiration Gaps, and Risk-Taking
papers.abstract: Theoretical perspectives provide conflicting predictions regarding how firms adjust risk-taking in response to performance–aspiration gaps. The behavioral theory of the firm attributes increased risk-taking to problemistic search under negative gaps, whereas threat–rigidity theory predicts a reduction in risk-taking. Under positive gaps, the behavioral theory of the firm’s satisficing logic implies decreased risk-taking, while slack search theory indicates the opposite effect. We integrate these competing theoretical logics through trait activation theory by introducing CEO psychopathy as a source of heterogeneity in responses to performance feedback. We argue that performance–aspiration gaps function as situational cues that activate differences in CEOs’ sensitivity to threat and reward cues, generating distinct emotional responses. The relationship between performance–aspiration gaps and risk-taking shifts from negative at lower levels of CEO psychopathy to positive at higher levels. Using fixed effects models on a longitudinal dataset of Finnish firms and a population-scale psychometric measure of CEO psychopathy collected independently of firm outcomes, we find empirical support for these predictions. Our theory reconceptualizes satisficing, threat–rigidity, problemistic search, and slack search as conditionally activated behavioral regimes rather than competing predictions tied solely to the valence of the performance–aspiration gap.

papers.title: Close Friends, Closer Comparisons: Regulating Envy in Multiplex Relationships
papers.abstract: Workplace envy is a socially embedded experience with important personal and relational implications. Yet, not all workplace relationships provide the same context for experiencing and regulating envy. In contemporary organizations, work is increasingly carried out within multiplex relationships that span both professional and personal domains. These relationships broaden the dimensions along which social comparisons occur and heighten the self-relevance of others’ successes, advantages, and favorable life circumstances, making envy especially likely. At the same time, friendship obligations, professional norms, and ongoing work responsibilities can constrain how envy is managed and expressed. Drawing upon emotion regulation theory and research on workplace relationships, we develop a theoretical model that explains how individuals regulate envy within multiplex relationships. We argue that envy simultaneously makes salient personal and relational motives—the desire to reduce the sting of envy and the desire to preserve a valued workplace relationship. These motives, in turn, activate a dual-motive appraisal process through which individuals arrive at key decision points that culminate in one of three regulatory pathways—experience-, situation-, or expression-level regulation—with each pathway producing distinct emotional and relational trajectories. In laying out this model, we seek to advance research on workplace envy and multiplex relationships.

papers.title: One of Few or One of Many? The Negative Affective Consequences of Family‐To‐Work Interruptions While Working Remotely
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT With expanded access to remote work, employees are spending a greater share of their time working from home. As a result, work and family demands increasingly intersect during the workday, creating more opportunities for interruptions from family members. Drawing on boundary theory, we argue that family‐to‐work interruptions differ from interruptions that originate within the work domain because they require employees to navigate a cross‐domain role transition involving distinct expectations, relationships, and role demands. To advance our understanding of the affective consequences of family‐to‐work interruptions, we leverage affective events theory to examine the effect of daily family‐to‐work interruptions on negative affect at the end of the workday and, in turn, emotional exhaustion in the evening. Importantly, we assess the role of individuals' general perceptions of family‐to‐work conflict and schedule autonomy as cross‐level moderators. We find that the positive effect of daily family‐to‐work interruptions on end‐of‐workday negative affect is stronger for individuals with higher overall perceptions of family‐to‐work conflict and with lower schedule autonomy. Finally, post hoc analyses suggest that gender further shapes these relationships, with the moderating effect of family‐to‐work conflict emerging only among women and the moderating effect of schedule autonomy being substantially stronger for women than for men.

papers.title: Staying Alive! Entrepreneurial Human Capital and Resilience of New Ventures
papers.abstract: Survival of new ventures has been shown to exhibit considerable heterogeneity both across and within industries. Some of the explanations for these differences have been attributed to firm size, organizational structure, and management practices. We add to this literature by showing how differences in employees’ abilities and their knowledge domain relate to survival. More precisely, we focus on the role of employees who in the past started and managed firms, referred to as an organization’s entrepreneurial human capital (EHC). Theoretically, we adopt an eclectic approach, while the empirical analysis is based on longitudinal register data for Sweden from 1997 to 2016. This allows us to identify EHC for all new ventures over the past 20 years. After controlling for a large number of confounders, our baseline results strongly suggest that a higher share of employees with entrepreneurial backgrounds is associated with an increased probability of new venture survival. We identify the following mechanisms through which former entrepreneurs contribute to survival: an enlarged resource base, magnified by learning from longer spells in entrepreneurship; an organizational fit conducive to absorbing and utilizing EHC; and a human capital fit in which entrepreneurial competencies align with the competence requirements of new ventures. We argue that our findings have both theoretical and practical implications for recruiters and managers and provide valuable insights for policymakers.

papers.title: Environmental responsibility in organizational life: A research agenda on goal displacement
How Leaders With Dark Personality Shape Their Climates: Developing a Theory of Influence Tactics and Follower Responses
papers.abstract: Abstract Despite burgeoning attention to dark leaders, we lack understanding about how they shape their climates. Using the dark triad (Machiavellianism, narcissism, psychopathy), we integrate social psychology and leadership research on interpersonal, romantic and leader–follower relationships to identify two predominant influence strategies: adversarial treatment and cunning deception. Developing a typological framework, we advance four influence scenarios and follower types: discerning observers, direct targets, devoted believers and ambivalent oscillators. These types determine constructive (voice, loyalty) or destructive (exit, neglect, retaliation) responses towards one's leader. These follower responses serve as social cues that influence the social power of the leader's ingroup and outgroup. Retaliatory responses, such as speaking up, will weaken the ingroup's relative social power, while constructive and other destructive responses will strengthen the ingroup's social power. These social power dynamics will determine work‐related and affective norms, whereby a wide power imbalance favouring the ingroup will produce high convergence on work‐related norms and high divergence on affective norms. Conversely, greater balance will produce high divergence on work‐related norms and high convergence on affective norms. Our theory contributes a holistic framework highlighting a complex and varying range of leader–follower interactions, which subsequently shape group member perceptions of social power and climate norms.

papers.title: Circular vs angular: “shaping” consumer responses to robot service failure
papers.abstract: Purpose This research aims to examine the effect of robot shape (circular vs angular) on consumer satisfaction in robot service failure contexts, explore the mediating effect of perceived warmth, and the moderating role of robot voice (child voice vs adult voice). Design/methodology/approach A pilot study based on secondary data from Ctrip and five experiments (n = 1287) examined the effect of robot shape on consumer satisfaction (Studies 1, W1, 2a, 2b, 3) and retention intention (Studies 1, 2a), the mediating effect of perceived warmth (Studies 2a, 2b), and the moderating effect of robot voice (Study 3). Findings Compared to angular robots, consumers respond more positively to service failures caused by circular robots. This effect is driven by warmth perception and is diminished when the robot uses a child voice (vs an adult voice). Practical implications This research offers insights for managers in the hospitality industry by showing that deploying circular robots can mitigate consumer dissatisfaction during robot service failures. When the robot shape cannot be easily modified, leveraging auditory cues, such as adopting a child voice for angular robots, can enhance perceived warmth and improve consumer satisfaction. Originality/value This research advances the robot service failure and shape symbolism literature by demonstrating how robot shape influences consumer satisfaction during robot service failures. Moreover, it introduces a multisensory perspective on robot design by revealing a novel cross-modal compensation effect between robot shape and voice.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

papers.title: A person-centered analysis of how hospitality employees cope with customer incivility
papers.abstract: Purpose Customer incivility is a pervasive stressor in hospitality organizations, yet prior research has largely examined coping strategies in isolation. This study aims to examine how frontline hospitality employees combine coping strategies in response to customer incivility and how these configurations relate to well-being and service performance. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping and Conservation of Resources theory, two studies used latent profile analysis. Study 1 identified coping profiles, while Study 2 replicated them and examined their antecedents and outcomes. Findings Four profiles emerged and were replicated: Problem-Solver, Balancer, Super-Coper and Drifter. Higher incivility intensity increased the likelihood of disengaged or moderate coping, whereas supervisor support promoted more active coping profiles. Practical implications Service organizations can develop targeted coping training and strengthen supervisory support to help employees respond effectively to customer incivility. Originality/value Extending prior profile-based research on emotion regulation, this study identifies broader coping configurations across five strategies. This study also shows how resource-related conditions are associated with these profiles and how the profiles differ in employee vitality and response performance.
papers.journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

papers.title: When Results Eclipse Sustainability: Supervisor Bottom-Line Mentality, Moral Disengagement, and the Ethical Climate of Environmental Responsibility in Logistics
papers.abstract: This study examines how supervisor bottom-line mentality (SBLM) shapes the ethical climate needed for environmental responsibility in logistics firms. Drawing on ethical climate theory (ECT) and self-determination theory (SDT), it argues that performance-focused supervisory signals weaken the moral conditions through which employees uphold environmental and compliance duties. Using time-lagged survey data from 379 employees in Pakistan’s logistics sector and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), results show that SBLM weakens workplace ethical climate directly and indirectly through moral disengagement. Job autonomy buffers these effects by reducing employees’ tendency to justify questionable operational choices under pressure. The findings reposition ethical climate as a workplace foundation for managing organizations’ environmental impact, showing that sustainability implementation depends not only on policies and reporting systems but also on moral regulation and autonomy in daily operations.

papers.title: Intergenerational Succession and Corporate Environmental Responsibility in Family Firms: Moderating Effect of Confucian and Clan Cultures
papers.abstract: Family firms are facing the dual challenges of intergenerational succession and green transformation. In this process, traditional cultural values such as Confucian and clan cultures rooted in collective responsibility and family reputation play a significant role in promoting family firms to fulfill corporate environmental responsibility (CER). Based on data from Chinese listed family firms from 2010 to 2021, we find that intergenerational succession significantly promotes family firms’ engagement in CER, and this effect is positively moderated by Confucian and clan cultures. Channel tests show that intergenerational succession promotes CER by enhancing the firm’s long-term orientation and reputation value. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that the positive effect of intergenerational succession on CER is more pronounced for successors who are male, highly educated, or possess an overseas background. Furthermore, this effect is more pronounced for firms in heavily polluting industries, in regions with stricter environmental regulations, and in regions with higher levels of green credit. From a cultural perspective, this article clarifies the boundary conditions for how intergenerational succession in family firms impacts their environmental performance, thereby extending the application of socioemotional wealth theory to the strategic decision-making in family firms.

papers.title: Enabling Systemic Trust in the Physical Internet: An eDSR Approach to Governance Model Design
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT The Physical Internet (PI) envisions a hyperconnected cyber‐physical logistics system inspired by the Digital Internet, yet adoption remains limited due to persistent trust and governance challenges. This study addresses these barriers by conceptualizing systemic trust as a foundational requirement for broad participation in the PI. We apply the echeloned Design Science Research methodology to develop the Governance and Trust Orchestration Layer (GTOL), an extension of existing layered PI models that incorporates mechanisms for rule enforcement, credentialing, dispute resolution, and fair matching. Based on empirical interviews with logistics practitioners and evaluated through scenario‐based walkthroughs, the GTOL addresses core commercial, institutional, and technological trust concerns. We contribute mid‐range design theory through six design principles that provide transferable guidance for embedding trust in decentralized logistics networks. They serve as a practical and theoretical blueprint for enabling governance structures that are transparent, enforceable, and adaptable across diverse logistics contexts.

papers.title: Pulling Back the Curtain: Using Dependability, Credibility, Transferability, and Confirmability as Evaluation Criteria for Literature Reviews
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Literature review articles play a crucial role in advancing knowledge by making sense of a body of research and setting a foundation for subsequent inquiry. Because much of the work is unobservable, some readers may wonder about the underlying rigor of a literature review. This hidden element creates parallels between literature reviews and qualitative research. In response to concerns about rigor, qualitative researchers have developed and rely upon a set of criteria by which qualitative work can be judged. In this essay, we adapt those criteria—dependability (analogous to reliability), credibility (analogous to internal validity), transferability (analogous to external validity), and confirmability (analogous to objectivity)—and explain how the criteria can be used to assess and improve the rigor of literature review articles. We then introduce the 2026 Special Topic Forum articles and spotlight examples wherein the articles excelled along the evaluation criteria.

papers.title: Disaster Relief Through a Complex Adaptive System Perspective: Firms' Motivations, Activities, and the Role of Operations Adaptability in Overlapping Landscapes
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Natural disasters disrupt the normal functioning of both communities and businesses. However, past literature often segregates the disaster relief view from the business continuity perspective, leaving a gap in understanding how firms can proactively support relief efforts. Using an embedded case, we focus on the operations of a multinational enterprise in the Fast‐Moving Consumer Goods sector to reveal these mechanisms. Its headquarters and geographic business units represent firms within and outside the disaster's vicinity and show how they work with NGOs and government counterparts in relief efforts. We find that firms within the disaster's vicinity (i.e., local firms or firms whose markets or supplies can be disrupted by the disaster) are motivated to proactively participate in the relief effort. These firms' goals to stabilize the market and economy are well‐aligned with NGOs and the government during disaster preparedness and response. Meanwhile, firms outside the disaster's vicinity mostly report philanthropic donations to support disaster relief, with underlying motivations for branding, tax benefits, and efficiency. Analyses of qualitative interviews and quantitative data under the Complex Adaptive Systems lens also reveal interesting insights into how the non‐profit and for‐profit landscapes overlap during disaster preparedness and response, and how firms within the disaster's vicinity can play a more central role in recovery if they have better operations adaptability capabilities (i.e., coordinated changes instead of changes in individual operations factors). Our findings contribute to both the disaster relief literature and the understanding of complex adaptive systems, especially in disaster contexts.

papers.title: From discovery to deployment: technology transfer as a supply chain process
The e-CNY and corporate tax avoidance: Evidence from China
Theodore J. Gordon (1930–2024): A visionary life spanning the cosmos and the future of humanity
Leveraging AI technology innovation for disaster risk reduction and resilience: Examining the mechanisms of financial development, globalization, and institutional quality
When Connection Feels Empty: Rethinking Consumer Loneliness Through Dual Presence in Digital Marketing
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Digital marketplaces sell connection, yet loneliness persists among their users. Marketing scholarship has largely examined loneliness as a consumer‐level deficit, studying how individuals compensate through consumption. How digital environments themselves structure the conditions under which loneliness is experienced has received less attention. This review addresses that gap by synthesizing 623 peer‐reviewed articles across marketing, psychology, communication, and information systems, using PRISMA procedures and topic modeling to map the field. Four research streams emerge, each addressing whether others feel accessible or whether one's own participation feels consequential, but rarely both together. These two perceptual conditions have been studied under different names across disciplines without being recognized as aspects of the same relational structure. When both are present, loneliness declines. When others are vivid but one's own visibility is uncertain, loneliness deepens. Digital environments can amplify this asymmetry by separating the perception of others from the perception that one's own participation registers. The review traces implications for customer engagement, brand communities, consumer‐brand relationships, and AI service design, and proposes an empirical agenda organized around how digitally mediated interaction constitutes or alters the relational conditions associated with loneliness.

papers.title: Home country institutional ties and Chinese SMEs ' OFDI : Institutional polycentrism and resource dependence perspectives
papers.abstract: Abstract Research Summary Combining institutional polycentrism and resource dependence perspectives, we theorize that small‐and‐medium‐sized enterprises' (SMEs) outward foreign direct investment (OFDI) depends on the types and levels of home institutional ties , and this relationship is moderated by technological resources. Analyzing a sample of 1123 Chinese listed SMEs from 2009 to 2019, we find that (1) SMEs with local political and industry association ties conduct fewer OFDI than those without such ties, (2) SMEs with central political ties conduct more OFDI than those without such ties, (3) SMEs' technological resources condition some of these relationships. We contribute to global strategy research by highlighting how different types and levels of institutional ties create dependencies that shape SMEs' OFDI, and how firms' technological resources moderate these effects. Managerial Summary This study offers practical guidance for SME managers operating in relationship‐based environments. Our findings show that the value of home institutional ties varies by type and level, shaping how firms design their OFDI strategies. First, managers should carefully assess the various resources available via ties to different institutional centers and the expectations attached to those ties. For instance, local institutional ties provide various domestic resources valuable in the home market and involve pressures to contribute locally, while central political ties facilitate OFDI by offering resources that can be leveraged abroad and aligning firms' strategies with global agendas. Second, such strategic decisions depend on a balance between internal and external resources available to firms. Managers should flexibly balance ties and technological resources when developing OFDI strategies.

papers.title: From Avatar to Activist: The Joint Effect of Virtual Influencer Prototype and Green Message Framing on Consumers’ Pro-environmental Behavioral Intention
Estimating Hedge Ratios in Shanghai Crude Oil Futures and Crude Oil Spot Under Multiple Uncertainties: A Dual Integrated Method with Noise Reduction-Mixed Frequency-Decomposition
papers.abstract: To address the problem of effectively estimating hedge ratios for Shanghai crude oil futures (INE) under multiple uncertainties, this study proposes a dual integrated method with noise reduction-mixed frequency-decomposition. The method optimizes hedge ratios between INE futures and crude oil spot markets under Climate Policy Uncertainty (CPU), Global Economic Policy Uncertainty (GEPU), and Geopolitical Risk (GPR). The proposed model first denoises crude oil prices and then integrates valuable information across uncertainties and time scales, thereby improving futures-spot hedging performance. The findings reveal the presence of noise in crude oil markets and highlight the heterogeneous effects of uncertainties on futures-spot relationships, with hedge ratios exhibiting distinct multiscale characteristics. The in-sample and out-of-sample results further provide evidence that the dual integrated method outperforms the control methods in terms of hedging performance in most cases. This study not only provides a novel hedging tool for developing effective risk management strategies but also offers a scientific basis for policy decision-making.

papers.title: Local Currency Borrowing Constraints and Firm Behavior: Evidence from an Emerging Market
papers.abstract: We analyze the financial and real effects of a 2022 Turkish regulation that restricts new local currency lending to firms whose asset dollarization exceeds specified thresholds. Using novel administrative data from January 2021–December 2023 and a difference-in-differences approach combined with propensity score matching, we find a medium-term decline in local currency borrowing among affected firms with a stronger impact for credit-constrained firms. We also document spillover effects, as firms substitute local currency loans with foreign currency loans, Turkish lira trade credit, and internal foreign currency liquidity. Extended analysis indicates that employment growth and net exports of affected firms declined, while operational volatility increased.

papers.title: The Impact of Population Aging on Commercial Banks’ Risk-Taking: Evidence from China
papers.abstract: This study investigates the impact of population aging on the risk-taking behavior of Chinese commercial banks and explores its underlying mechanisms. Using micro data from 403 commercial banks in China from 2007 to 2023, we find aging significantly increases banks’ risk-taking levels. Further analysis suggests that deposit–loan imbalances, the expansion of non-loan investments, and deteriorating asset quality are closely associated with population aging and further contribute to higher bank risk-taking. Moreover, the effect of population aging is more pronounced among rural banks and tends to be stronger in the central and western regions than in the eastern region.

papers.title: The Impact of Monetary-Fiscal Policy Coordination on Systemic Risk of Non-Financial Firms: Evidence from China
papers.abstract: Exploring the causal impact of monetary-fiscal policy synergy on systemic risk in non-financial firms (NFFs), we find a significant mitigating effect operating through four key channels: alleviating underinvestment, curbing corporate financialization, enhancing debt-servicing capacity, and reducing credit default risk. For NFFs with tighter financing constraints and more severe financial misallocation, the stabilizing efficacy of policy synergy is more pronounced—particularly during economic-financial contractions and as capital market openness advances, where the impact is strongest. Dynamic analysis further reveals a notable time-varying attenuation trend in this effect, underscoring the need for well-timed, precisely calibrated policy synergy to maintain resilience in the real economy.

papers.title: Capital Discipline: Party Organization Construction and Cross-Border M&A by Chinese Firms
Employee Stock Ownership Plans and Management Voluntary Earnings Forecasts
How Does ESG Internal Consistency Affect Its External Consistency: Evidence From Green Innovation and Executives’ Green Cognition
Urban Construction Investment Bonds and the Value Relevance of Corporate Earnings: Empirical Evidence from Chinese Local State-Owned Enterprises
papers.abstract: The impact of Urban Construction Investment Bond (UCIB) risks on the correlation between corporate earnings and value requires clarification. Using a fixed-effects model and generalized method of moments, this study finds that the UCIB scale expansion significantly reduces the earnings-value correlation for local state-owned enterprises (SOEs). More robust corporate governance and a more reasonable financing structure can mitigate negative effects, especially among local SOEs characterized by greater government intervention, lower marketization, and weaker oversight by non-state shareholders. The increase in UCIB greatly impacts firms’ unexpected operating cash flows. This study expands research on corporate earnings value and government debt.

papers.title: Corruption and Uneven Development: Why Anti‐Corruption Fails in the EU 's Most Vulnerable Regions
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT This article challenges the assumption that legal harmonization within the European Union ensures effective anti‐corruption governance. Despite EU‐compliant frameworks, institutional integrity remains highly uneven across subnational territories. We introduce the Regional Integrity Framework (RIF), a diagnostic approach that integrates citizen perceptions, procurement indicators, and enforcement activation measures to capture regional integrity performance. The analysis suggests that formal convergence can conceal functional divergence, as peripheral regions often exhibit weaker administrative capacity, limited oversight, and uneven institutional activation. A mixed‐methods application that combines panel analysis with an illustrative comparison of Sofia and Vidin, Bulgaria, demonstrates how the RIF can diagnose territorial integrity gaps within a shared legal framework. Conceptually, the study reframes anti‐corruption as a territorially embedded problem of institutional activation; methodologically, it offers a transferable framework for identifying enforcement asymmetries and governance disparities in multi‐level systems.

papers.title: Credit Attribution for Public Service Providers and Their Employees: Implications from Contracting Out
papers.abstract: Both government and government employees alike face negativity bias, but could conveying the exemplary work of public service help address declining public trust and engagement? While scholarly research has examined how the public assigns blame when the government or a contractor falls short, far less attention has been paid to the positive side. How is credit assigned to employees and agencies when they go above and beyond what is required in their jobs? This research addresses this gap through a vignette survey experiment, which is used to determine how contracting influences credit given to the service provider and the individual employee across levels of government –federal, state, and local. The results reveal that credit is more likely to be given to third-party providers than the government directly providing the service. However, at the individual employee level, the public prefers to give credit to public employees, especially at the federal government level, when outstanding work occurs. Findings have implications for contracting, performance, and accountability, where perhaps sharing more positive stories of public service can foster more positive public views.
papers.journal_name: The American Review of Public Administration

papers.title: Blindness and epistemic injustice: a critical autoethnography of digital disablement in Thailand
papers.abstract: Thailand’s digital transformation is presented as a route to inclusion, yet everyday accessibility remains unresolved for many disabled people. Combining policy document analysis with critical autoethnography, grounded in emancipatory disability research and analysed through a narrative approach, this article examines nearly thirty years of my experience as a blind person navigating education, public administration, banking, telecommunications, digital platforms, and generative AI in Thailand. Four interlocking patterns emerge: inaccessible documents and interfaces, conditional banking and biometric access, dependence on everyday platforms, and generative AI as compensatory access and epistemic risk. I develop the cycle of digital disablement to explain how these patterns persist despite formal accessibility commitments. The cycle is reproduced through three mutually reinforcing mechanisms: socio-epistemic exclusion, which limits the institutional force of disabled people’s knowledge of inaccessibility; techno-epistemic ableism, which embeds normative assumptions about bodies, perception, competence, and verification in technical systems; and socio-techonomic disadvantage, a term combining the technological and the economic, which transfers the financial, temporal, cognitive, relational, and privacy costs of accessibility failure to disabled users. Policy documents reveal that formal rights are diluted through regulatory silence, voluntary standards, weak enforcement, institutional discretion, and competing priorities. The analysis also shows workarounds widening immediate access while concealing the inaccessible arrangements that necessitated them. The article contributes an integrated account of digital exclusion as an epistemic, technical, material, and regulatory condition. Digital justice therefore requires enforceable accessibility duties, non-visual authentication, accessible materials and interfaces, accountable AI governance, effective remedies, and disabled people’s authority in design, regulation, and evaluation.

papers.title: Electoral targeting strategies during the 2022 election in Sweden: exploring the paid affordances of Facebook and Instagram
papers.abstract: Social media platforms have become central arenas for political communication, yet research has primarily focused on organic content rather than paid advertising. This study examines how Swedish political parties utilized Facebook and Instagram's paid affordances during the 2022 parliamentary election, analyzing a census sample (N = 2395) of ads from Meta's ad library. Combining content analysis with data on campaign spending and demographic targeting, the study identifies key differences in advertising strategies. We find that right-wing opposition parties engaged in more negative campaigning than left-wing incumbents, while calls to action were infrequent overall. The Center Party, the Sweden Democrats, and the Moderate Party emerged as the highest campaign spenders. Targeting strategies varied: left-leaning parties primarily targeted their messages toward women, whereas right-leaning parties focused on older male users. These findings contribute to the understanding of evolving party communication strategies, highlighting the role of paid social media advertising in contemporary election campaigns.

papers.title: Assessing and Adjusting for Selection Bias in Mendelian Randomization: the Effects of Body Mass Index, Education, and C-reactive Protein on Depression in UK Biobank
papers.abstract: Abstract Depression analyses in UK Biobank may be affected by selection bias due to incomplete participation in the optional Mental Health Questionnaire. We used one-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) to assess the causal effects of BMI, educational attainment (EA), and CRP on depression, applying inverse probability of selection weighting (IPW) and the instrumental variable for selection (IVsel) to adjust for selection into the MHQ sample. Sensitivity analyses included the use of psychiatrist consultation as a proxy outcome. MR analyses indicated that higher BMI increased the risk of depression (OR=1.09 [1.05, 1.13]), EA was protective (OR=0.81 [0.75, 0.88]), and there was limited evidence that CRP affected depression (OR=1.01 [0.92, 1.10]). Estimates obtained using IPW and IVsel were broadly consistent, although with IVsel estimates closer to the null, within BMI (ORIPW = 1.10 [1.05, 1.15], ORIVsel = 1.04 [1.02, 1.06]), EA (ORIPW = 0.81 [0.74, 0.88], ORIVsel = 0.93 [0.90, 0.96]) and CRP (ORIPW = 1.03 [0.92, 1.15], ORIVsel = 1.00 [0.97, 1.04]). Proxy outcome analyses suggested similar patterns of selection bias, supporting their utility for assessing potential bias in MHQ-restricted analyses. Bias-adjustment methods and sensitivity analyses provide a framework to assess the impact of selection bias in large cohort studies with optional components.

papers.title: The association between perceived neighborhood social cohesion and incident hypertension among older adults in the US Health and Retirement Study
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Despite the association between lower perceived neighborhood social cohesion (PNSC) and higher risk of hypertension, there is limited research on this relationship. This population-based study examined the association between PNSC and incident hypertension among a nationally representative population of older adults across racial and/or ethnic groups and sex. Methods: Data were obtained from 2,998 US older adult participants (mean age=62.5 years, SD=8.12) from the Health and Retirement Study. Normotensive participants at baseline (2006 or 2008) were assessed for hypertension incidence at 4- and 8-year follow-up visits. PNSC was classified into tertiles. Weighted Cox proportional hazards regression was used to estimate the association between PNSC and incident hypertension. Interaction terms (PNSC and racial and/or ethnic group, PNSC and sex) were included in models adjusted for appropriate covariates (sex, racial and/or ethnic group, education, body mass index, alcohol use, cigarette smoking status), and models were stratified by racial and/or ethnic group and sex. Results: Overall, 40.5% of the study population developed hypertension. Low perceived neighborhood social cohesion (versus high) was associated with increased hypertension risk (HR=1.22, 95% CI: 1.08-1.37). This association was the strongest among Black adults (HR=2.28, 95% CI: 1.23-4.25) and Black females (HR=3.40, 95% CI: 1.34-8.62), though the interaction terms were not statistically significant (p-values for interaction >0.05). Conclusions: Individuals perceiving low neighborhood social cohesion may have increased hypertension risk, particularly among Black females. Future studies could test potential underlying mechanisms that explain this association and implement community-based interventions promoting cohesive communities as a potential strategy for reducing disparities in hypertension risk.

papers.title: Does daylight saving time increase traffic crashes? Seasonal confounding and a morning fatality effect
Influences of paternal incarceration on children's maltreatment and polyvictimization risks
Sexual Passion Across Time: Patterns and Predictors Through Five Years of Marriage
papers.abstract: The purpose of this study was to explore how harmonious, obsessive, and inhibited sexual passion may change over five years of marriage, and to also evaluate whether sexual relatedness, sexual competence, and sexual autonomy-core constructs of self-determination theory (SDT)-at the beginning of marriage may be important predictors of sexual passion across time. With a nationally representative sample of 2106 mixed-sex recently married couples, we analyzed the intercepts and slopes of the three types of sexual passion over five years. The results indicated that the three types of sexual passion all had relatively stable means across time with small but significant positive slopes. Also, of the three SDT predictors of sexual passion, higher levels of sexual autonomy early in marriage were related to lower initial levels of inhibited sexual passion and higher levels of harmonious sexual passion over time. Curiously, sexual relatedness, though associated with lower levels of sexual inhibition across time, was associated with decreasing levels of sexual harmony.

papers.title: Getting Bullied in the Nonprofit Sector: The Dark Side of Public Service Motivation and Political Behavior
papers.abstract: Bullying is harmful and prominent in nonprofit organizations (NPOs), yet it remains understudied. This article investigates how public service motivation (PSM), which is trait-like, prosocial and vital to NPOs, may counterintuitively expose NPO workers to being bullied. Notwithstanding PSM’s many benefits, recent studies have identified a dark side of PSM that potentially may attract bullying from coworkers. This survey-based study in the New Zealand nonprofit sector ( N = 880) draws on social exchange theory and conservation of resources theory to examine the relationship between PSM and being bullied, the role of political behavior as a mediator, and constructive leadership as a moderator. Findings support all hypothesized relationships, except one. The article concludes with theoretical implications and practical recommendations to address challenges stemming from the dark side of PSM as well as to curb bullying in NPOs.

papers.title: Serving the Public as Civil Servants or Citizens? Public Employees’ Exposure to Public Participation, Job Satisfaction, and Volunteering
papers.abstract: Public employees serve the public interest through their work and extend this commitment through volunteerism. However, it remains unclear what motivates them to volunteer when professional roles already fulfill intrinsic prosocial motivations. Drawing on theories from multiple life domains and public service motivation, this study examines how public sector workplace experiences, specifically exposure to public participation and job satisfaction, are associated with volunteering behavior. Using cross-sectional, nationally representative survey data from U.S. local government managers, this study finds that the relationships vary by individuals’ prior volunteering status. Among non-volunteers, higher levels of public participation exposure and job satisfaction are both associated with a greater probability of initiating volunteering. Among current volunteers, lower levels are associated with greater time devoted to volunteering, whereas higher levels are linked to volunteering across a wider range of domains. Job satisfaction negatively moderates the relationship between public participation exposure and volunteering intensity. This study extends conventional understanding of public employee volunteering beyond public service motivation and sector differences by demonstrating a contingent work–volunteerism association, offering practical insights into managing workplace experiences to sustain public service both within and beyond organizational boundaries.

papers.title: Advancing the Sustainability Development Goals Through Workforce Professionalization in Public Procurement: The Case of Lebanon
papers.abstract: A capable public sector workforce is essential for sustainable development. In public procurement, the ability of procurement reform to support Sustainable Development Goals depends on a workforce with the competencies and professional standing needed to translate reform into administrative practice. Drawing on Institutional Theory and strategic PHRM, this study examines how workforce professionalization in public procurement is being constructed and institutionalized in Lebanon under Public Procurement Law No. 244 of 2021. Using a document-based qualitative case study, the study analyzes legal documents, technical reports, competency frameworks, and training materials produced between 2020 and 2025. The findings show that workforce professionalization in public procurement advanced through competency frameworks, certification initiatives, and professional training systems. However, workforce professionalization remains unevenly embedded across the civil service system. The study contributes to strategic public HRM and procurement governance scholarship and offers insight into workforce professionalization in governance-constrained settings in the Global South.

papers.title: Social Norms, State Punishment, and Motivation Crowding in Anti‐Corruption Messaging: Experimental Evidence From China
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT A growing body of scholarship views corruption not merely as a failure of monitoring and enforcement but as a resilient informal institution sustained by social perceptions—and misperceptions. When citizens believe others tolerate or engage in corruption, resisting it becomes a collective action problem, allowing corruption to perpetuate itself. Using a large‐scale survey experiment in China, this study tests whether correcting exaggerated perceptions of social tolerance for corruption can help break this cycle. We find that providing information about the actual (low) level of tolerance significantly strengthens anti‐corruption attitudes and intentions, especially among those who mistakenly believed a majority tolerated corruption. However, this effect is weakened when paired with punishment cues, suggesting that enforcement information can crowd out the motivational force of norm‐based messages. Our findings demonstrate both the potential and the limits of norm‐based informational interventions and offer implications for anti‐corruption messaging in comparable contexts.

papers.abstract: Passenger-transport decarbonisation raises distributional questions, but harmonised physical travel data by household group remain scarce. We attribute national mode-specific CO 2 totals from a bottom-up transport model to 60 household-consumption cells in each of 21 EU Member States in 2015. WILIAM cells combine five income quintiles, two settlement-density categories and six household compositions, constructed in LOCOMOTION by statistical matching and reconciliation to 2015 national accounts. This is an accounting attribution, not a direct measurement of group-specific travel activity or technical efficiency. Within each country–mode, attributed-emission ratios and Ginis reproduce the corresponding WILIAM consumption metrics by construction; multimodal totals instead weight modal consumption by distinct attribution intensities. The official-population-weighted resident mean for the covered 21-country sample is 1507 kg CO 2 /person/year. Across countries, the median total Q5/Q1 is 2.75, compared with 4.44 for air and 2.59 for private transport. Median grouped Ginis are 0.322 for air, 0.176 for private transport, 0.184 for rail and 0.082 for bus CO 2 attributed using road-passenger-service expenditure shares. A structured-scenario envelope gives a median national total Q5/Q1 of 1.57–4.76; it is not a confidence interval. Dense cells receive higher total and aviation attributions on average, whereas non-dense cells receive higher private attribution. The baseline identifies where transport CO 2 totals are attributed and formulates testable hypotheses about aviation concentration, car dependence, heterogeneous adjustment and public-transport pricing. Its policy contribution is diagnostic and hypothesis-generating: it specifies where credible incidence models need greater resolution and which price, accessibility, behavioural and compensation mechanisms they should test.

Integrated digital framework for wastewater treatment performance and sustainability assessment in low-income countries
papers.abstract: Modelling and simulation are widely used to optimise biological wastewater treatment processes, while life cycle assessment (LCA) is well established for evaluating environmental impacts. However, integrated modelling-LCA approaches have largely been developed for data-rich and well-resourced settings, limiting their practical application in developing countries where reliable operational data, technical capacity, and resources are often constrained. Moreover, few studies have demonstrated such integrated approaches using field-measured data and validated their recommendations through full-scale implementation. To address these gaps, an integrated digital framework linking metabolic activated sludge model (META-ASM) with LCA was developed and applied to optimise the Santa Catarina wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) in Cape Verde. The framework integrates systematic data collection and reconciliation, field-data-driven dynamic simulation, scenario-based optimisation, sensitivity analysis, and sustainability assessment. Model predictions were evaluated against observed plant performance, and operational and structural scenarios were sequentially assessed to identify improvements across individual treatment units. The recommended operational strategies were subsequently implemented at full scale, with field monitoring confirming reductions in effluent total chemical oxygen demand (COD Tot ), total suspended solids (TSS), total phosphorus (P Tot ), and total nitrogen (N Tot ) of 51.4%, 58.7%, 44.4%, and 21.5%, respectively, compared with baseline operation. LCA further demonstrated reductions of approximately 30% in human toxicity, freshwater ecotoxicity, and marine ecotoxicity, and 36% in eutrophication potential. Beyond improving treatment and environmental performance, the framework incorporates practical data-management tools, capacity building, and context-specific operational considerations. This field-validated, data-adaptive approach provides a scalable and transferable pathway for applying digital process modelling and sustainability assessment to WWTP optimisation in resource-constrained developing country contexts.

papers.abstract: Accurate assessment of lithium-ion battery ageing is complicated by cell-to-cell variability, heterogeneous cycling protocols, and limited transferability of data-driven predictors. This study develops a continuous ageing-trajectory framework in which coordinate-based multilayer perceptron (MLP) and sinusoidal representation network (SIREN) models represent state-of-health and voltage–capacity trajectories as differentiable functions of normalized trajectory coordinates. The framework combines continuous reconstruction, derivative-based knee descriptors, equivalent-full-cycle (EFC) harmonization, protocol-held-out early-life prediction, perturbation analysis, and conformal uncertainty quantification. Early-life prediction was evaluated in four protocol-held-out folds, repeated for three random seeds, using the first 𝑁 ∈ { 5 , 1 0 , 2 0 } available degradation observations rather than assuming that one observation represented one physical cycle. The pooled association between robust consensus knee location and the first crossing of the 80% SOH threshold was strong ( 𝑛 = 1 7 2 , Spearman 𝜌 S = 0 . 8 3 4 , 95% bootstrap CI [ 0 . 7 3 8 , 0 . 9 0 7 ] , Holm-adjusted 𝑝 = 3 . 3 6 × 1 ⁢ 0 − 4 5 ). Raw adapted cINR predictions exhibited substantial architecture- and window-dependent bias. A leakage-safe bias-corrected MLP-protocol blend achieved MAEs of 113.57, 107.79, and 112.82 EFC for 𝑁 = 5 , 10, and 20, respectively, compared with 116.66, 115.57, and 125.02 EFC for the protocol-median baseline. These numerical reductions were not statistically significant after multiplicity correction, although the blend significantly improved over raw MLP cINR predictions for 𝑁 = 5 and 𝑁 = 1 0 . Fold-external conformal intervals at the nominal 90% level attained empirical coverages of 90.3%, 91.0%, and 95.5%, but remained wide, reflecting substantial inter-cell uncertainty. Knee detection was comparatively stable under missing observations but sensitive to aggressive downsampling and measurement noise. The results support continuous trajectory representations as useful differentiable descriptors and components of calibrated hybrid predictors, but do not establish a uniform predictive advantage over a strong protocol-informed baseline.

Water footprint of low-tech digesters for bioenergy recovery from waste
papers.abstract: This study aimed to assess the water footprint of plastic tubular digesters to treat organic waste and recover bioenergy. Different scenarios in a small-scale dairy farm in Colombia were considered: i) scenario without the digester in which cow manure is piled up, and dairy wastewater is directly discharged into the environment, ii) scenario with a plastic tubular digester treating cow manure, and iii) scenario with a plastic tubular digester co-digesting cow manure with dairy wastewater. The ReCiPe 2016 – midpoint (H) method was used to assess the degradation of water bodies (i.e. eutrophication and ecotoxicity impact categories), while the AWARE 2.0 method was applied to evaluate the water scarcity impact category. Results showed that, in terms of water quality degradation, the co-digestion scenario exhibited impacts 10% to 45% lower than those of the other scenarios, depending on the impact category. In terms of water scarcity, the co-digestion scenario exhibited approximately 10% lower water scarcity than the other scenarios, which showed a similar water scarcity footprint. This indicates that implementing plastic tubular digesters, even under mono-digestion conditions, does not worsen water availability. These benefits are greater if co-digestion of different agri-food waste is applied, since it helps preserve water quality by valorising the intrinsic water content of food wastewater. It also decreases environmental impacts by reducing synthetic fertiliser use through the production of a higher-quality digestate. Overall, plastic tubular digesters provide a low-water footprint alternative to the direct discharge and uncontrolled storage of livestock waste and food-production wastewater in small-scale farms.

Compositional route types: Bridging configurational and urban tissue analysis
papers.abstract: In the context of the ongoing debates about the effects of vehicular traffic on urban environments, interest in street networks has increased across a broadening range of disciplines. With that increasing interest, there has been a proliferation of analytical methods and measures. A potential solution is to combine measures with types of urban tissue, seen as a common point of reference. The issue then arises that the definition of urban tissue is no less prone to proliferation of methods and attributes to consider. This paper proposes a general-purpose set of route and route aggregate types as a basis for the differentiation of street networks to facilitate comparative analysis, including correlations between network and urban tissue analysis as well as correlations with other aspects and attributes of human settlements. The method used starts with the abstraction of minimum topological attributes of streets, set within the mereological framework of the compositional hierarchy of built form, to arrive at a set of minimum elements. Possible combinations of the elements are then explored to identify distinct types at three levels: wide area inter-settlement routes, local area routes and local area route aggregates. The result is a consistent and coherent set of type families defined by their mereotopological attributes. The attributes in turn provide the basis for ordering the types and establishing the connection between network configurations and urban tissue. The types are applied in an analysis of the town of Leighton-Linslade to demonstrate the resulting differentiation of the street network and the relation between the route type and urban tissue. The paper concludes by assessing the potential for application of the types as well as further research.

papers.title: Employment-access constraints in the 15-minute city
papers.abstract: The “15-minute city” has emerged as an influential urban-planning paradigm, promoting proximity to work and essential services. Its feasibility for journey-to-work commuting, however, has rarely been examined quantitatively. Here, we show that employment proximity is constrained by heterogeneity in the number of employees per firm. Combining urban geometry with empirically observed firm-size distributions, we derive a lower bound on commuting time that holds even under optimal workplace placement. This bound reveals a sharp transition: when employment is sufficiently unevenly distributed across firms, no spatial rearrangement of workplaces can provide uniformly short commutes. Applied to Paris and its near suburbs, with area A = 762 km 2 and empirical firm-size exponent γ ^ ≃ 1.38 , the model predicts that only about 37% of workers can reach their workplace within 15 minutes by walking. Cycling increases this share to about 67%, but still leaves roughly one third of the workforce beyond the 15-minute threshold. Achieving universal short commutes would therefore require economic restructuring, differentiated mobility strategies, remote work, or a longer target time. Our results suggest replacing the universal 15-minute target, for commuting, by a city-specific benchmark determined by firm-size heterogeneity and urban scale.

papers.title: Disposing the unwanted: The UK-Rwanda deal and the resurgence of deportations to third countries
papers.abstract: The UK-Rwanda Deal sought to overhaul the UK’s migration policy by outsourcing the asylum process to Rwanda, a move that would have dissolved the state’s international protection for refugees. Whilst the incoming Labour Prime Minister scrapped the policy upon taking office, the question remains: Why did the UK-Rwanda Deal endure through two years of court injunctions and widespread criticism? A question that remains salient as Italy, the Netherlands, and the European Union attempt to pursue similar externalisation policies. Far from a failed experiment, we argue that the UK-Rwanda Deal was a calculated attempt to enact the historically enduring border politics of distancing. Physical distancing creates a spatial buffer to skirt legal obligations while isolating asylum seekers from support systems. Symbolic distancing functions as a deterrence, presenting the illusion that safety is unreachable while easing populist anxieties by framing the constructed ‘problem’ as resolved. Mental distancing normalises the violence of deportation by reducing asylum seekers to bureaucratic items. In practice, the externalisation of asylum functions both as a mechanism of control (physical) and the desire for racialised exclusion (symbolic and mental). By situating our critique within the historical context of deportations to third countries, we argue that the UK-Rwanda Deal is less a novel development than a resurgence of a longer standing practice. The cancellation of the UK-Rwanda Deal is therefore not the end of the story, but a chapter in the ongoing border politics of distancing, as former colonial powers in Europe, the USA and Australia eagerly seek to enact this practice of racialised exclusion.

papers.title: Rehearsing sovereignty through heritage infrastructure: State performance and cultural governance in Taiwan
papers.abstract: This study examines Taiwan’s Jianan Irrigation System as a rehearsal stage for sovereign performance under diplomatic constraints. It argues that state-led heritage preservation and historical reframing have produced a site through which sovereignty is simultaneously performed at domestic and local scales and rehearsed at the international scale. On one hand, this scaled practice expands existing conceptualisations of rehearsing stateness. On the other hand, it reexamines the relationship between heritage diplomacy and sovereign performance under diplomatic constraints. Drawing on fieldwork and discourse analysis, this paper traces how heritage preservation supports Taiwan’s sovereign legitimacy. These findings offer broader theoretical implications for understanding how diplomatically marginalised but functionally operative states rehearse sovereignty through cultural infrastructure.

papers.title: The Heterogeneous Impact of Short-Time Work: From Saved Jobs to Windfall Effects,
papers.abstract: Abstract This paper investigates the adoption of short-time work by firms and their participating employees. We present a model showing that short-time work can preserve jobs in firms facing severe negative revenue shocks, but not in less affected firms, where hours are reduced without preventing layoffs. Using data from all French establishments during the 2008-2009 Great Recession, we find that short-time work helped save jobs and increased hours worked in firms hit by significant revenue losses, facilitating a faster post-recession recovery. We also identify substantial windfall effects, which raise the policy’s cost per job saved. Nonetheless, short-time work is likely more cost-effective at preserving employment than wage subsidies, potentially resulting in a net negative cost to public finances.
